- 2025 sustainability targets: 80% of new offers to qualify as sustainable via an ESG checklist; 87% of Bank technical reserves assessed using the Impact Weighting Factor (IWF).
- ESG integration in products: Systematic use of shared tools (ESG checklist; green/social/sustainability bond framework) and methodologies (IWF, LBP AM’s GREaT) with innovation focus in 2024.
- Product and service examples for the just transition: financing for social home ownership, energy renovation and green vehicles; community finance (SIS) and SRI funds; transition-focused savings (e.g., Tocqueville Environnement SRI, green bonds); non-banking tools like Carbo carbon footprinting and Youth Pass. Tobacco cultivation/production revenues reported as zero.
- New impact card (Dec 2024, with WWF France): deposits fund mortgages with energy-efficiency works; card contribution supports WWF biodiversity programs; users receive carbon footprint tracking/advice via Carbo.
- Insurance and risk solutions: right to be forgotten for breast cancer survivors; microinsurance in Latin America; protection products (life, funeral, long-term care) and offerings tailored to seniors and people with chronic diseases.
- Sustainable investment offerings: launch of Tocqueville Biodiversity SRI (SFDR Art. 9) in July 2024; a green structured note (Green PAB 100 Autocall Nov 2032) linked to a Paris-aligned Eurozone PAB index under the Group’s Green/Social/Sustainability Bond Framework.
- Strategy and disclosure: Group transition plan; sectoral policies (coal, oil, gas, aeronautics, deforestation/ecosystem conversion); publication of a Climate and Nature report aligned with TCFD/TNFD, linking climate and biodiversity.
- Value chain and stakeholders: emphasis on collaboration across internal teams and external partners; stakeholder consideration through governance bodies—Mission Committee (18 members, 12 independent; meets at least 3 times/year; tracks 14 indicators and reports annually) and Customer Board (16 members; meets 3 times/year to inform offers, service quality, and customer experience).

nodes.title: Value chain
nodes.heading: 2.1.3.1.6 Value chain
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group’s value chain is presented in the following infographic.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on La Banque Postale Group’s sustainability strategy and ESRS 2 reporting context within the 2024 Universal Registration Document, with glossary reference for CSR terms.
- Launch of a new “impact card” with WWF France:
  - Deposits support financing/refinancing of real estate loans that include energy-efficiency renovations, particularly for poorly insulated housing.
  - The card’s additional contribution is fully donated to WWF France to fund biodiversity programs.
  - Cardholders receive tools and advice for responsible consumption via the Carbo carbon footprint calculator.
- Insurance and risk management solutions adapted to societal changes (longevity, retirement, social protection):
  - CNP Assurances initiatives: right to be forgotten for women with breast cancer; microinsurance in Latin America; coverage for life risks (life, funeral, long-term care); products tailored to the elderly and people with chronic diseases.
- Expansion of sustainable investment offerings:
  - Listing of Tocqueville Biodiversity SRI UCI (SFDR Article 9) for retail clients, investing in companies reducing human impact on biodiversity; links to SFDR monitoring indicators.
  - Green structured note issuance (La Banque Postale Green PAB 100 Autocall Nov 2032) to finance/refinance environmental transition projects per the Group’s Green, Social and Sustainability Bond Framework; uses Euronext Eurozone 60 PAB index aligned with the Paris Agreement.
- Embedding sustainability in strategy:
  - Group transition plan and sectoral policies guiding financing/investment (coal, oil, gas, aeronautics, deforestation and ecosystem conversion).
  - Publication of a combined Climate and Nature report aligned with TCFD and TNFD.
  - Tools and methods: ESG checklist for responsible products “by design,” the internal Impact Weighting Factor (IWF), and LBP AM’s GREaT SRI methodology.
- Value chain and collaboration:
  - Emphasis on internal and external collaboration to scale impact, share best practices, and ensure consistent, effective implementation of the sustainability strategy.
- Stakeholder engagement and governance:
  - Collaborative approach to decision-making; main stakeholders mapped via the value chain.
  - Mission Committee (18 members, 12 independent) oversees and advances sustainability strategy, meets at least three times annually, assesses progress via 14 indicators, and reports to the Supervisory Board.
  - Customer Board (16 members) partners with the Executive Committee to improve offerings, service quality, and customer experience by gathering customer input three times a year.

nodes.title: Consideration of stakeholders
nodes.heading: 2.1.3.1.7 Consideration of stakeholders
nodes.start_phrase: Details of how stakeholders are taken into account are presented in the following infographic “Main stakeholder challenges”.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and framing: Extract from La Banque Postale’s Universal Registration Document detailing ESRS 2 sustainability reporting, stakeholder integration, double materiality, and how sustainability is embedded in the Group’s strategy.
- New responsible offerings:
  - Impact card with WWF France: directs deposits to energy-efficient home renovation loans; channels card fee uplift fully to WWF biodiversity programs; supports responsible consumption via the Carbo carbon-footprint app and advice.
  - Insurance innovations by CNP Assurances: right to be forgotten for women with breast cancer; microinsurance in Latin America; coverage for life risks (life, funeral, long-term care); products tailored to seniors and people with chronic diseases.
  - Investment and structured products: Tocqueville Biodiversity SRI UCI (SFDR Article 9) added in July 2024; launch of a green structured note (Green PAB 100 Autocall November 2032) aligned with the Group’s Green, Social & Sustainability Bond Framework and Paris-aligned Euronext Eurozone 60 PAB index.
- Governance, tools and methodologies:
  - Group transition plan and sectoral policies (coal, oil, gas, aeronautics, deforestation/ecosystem conversion).
  - Climate and Nature report aligned with TCFD and TNFD, linking climate and biodiversity.
  - Product qualification via an ESG checklist; use of the Impact Weighting Factor (IWF) and LBP AM’s GREaT SRI analysis.
- Value chain and collaboration: Overview of upstream suppliers, own operations, and downstream customers/financed activities; emphasis on co-construction with teams, partners, and ecosystems to scale impact and consistency of the sustainability strategy.
- Stakeholder engagement architecture:
  - Mission Committee (18 members, 12 independent): meets at least three times a year, tracks 14 indicators, issues an annual mission report to the Supervisory Board.
  - Customer Board (16 members): triannual consultations to improve offer, service quality, and experience.
  - Initiative Against Banking Exclusion think-tank (25 members): financial inclusion, poverty insights, and solution co-creation.
  - Ongoing dialogue with NGOs and civil society (e.g., WWF) informing the IWF and sector policies; frequent consultation of public authorities, regulators, peers, and rating agencies.
- Stakeholder matrices: Detailed channels, purposes, and integration of feedback for shareholders/investors; public authorities and supervisors; NGOs/charities; industry peers; suppliers/subcontractors and their employees; employees and La Poste workers; financed entities and their employees; customers; planet; communities; and distributor/banking partners.
- Double materiality and IROs:
  - Positive impacts: access to bancassurance (including vulnerable populations), sustainable/positive-impact financing, strong corporate culture/working conditions, business ethics/general interest.
  - Negative impacts: own-operations climate/waste; environmental and human rights impacts from financed activities; customer impacts from cybersecurity breaches.
  - Risks: physical/transition climate and environmental risks and rising loss ratios; portfolio exposure to transition/physical risks; inadequate ESG integration in governance; HR health/safety risks; partner assessment gaps; customer protection risk.
  - Opportunities: growth in sustainable finance and employer attractiveness via culture.
  - Time horizons: environmental impacts assessed as current; social/governance as current or potential (short term for own operations/services; medium term for financed activities).
  - Trade-offs and dependencies acknowledged (e.g., home-loan decarbonization versus access to credit and pace of social housing renovation) within a just-transition approach; no material impacts from these dependencies identified in the analysis.
- Strategy linkage and execution:
  - Mission-led strategy centered on planet and people, a just transition, and transforming the bancassurance model; reinforces universal banking/insurance positioning and accessible banking mission.
  - Financed-activity impacts addressed through shareholder dialogue and financing of the public sector and social/solidarity economy.
  - Governance and business conduct treated as core to a regulated bancassurer.
  - 2030 strategic plan already aligned with most material ESRS topics; future updates will integrate double materiality results for the full conglomerate (including CNP Assurances); no near-term structural changes planned.
  - Strategic model emphasizes differentiation, diversification, and digitization across customers, co-workers, and communities, mapping objectives to ESRS E1–E5 and S1–S4, including access, impact financing, portfolio risk prevention, corporate culture, HR and customer-protection (including cybersecurity).

nodes.title: Description of material impacts, risks and opportunities (IRO)
nodes.heading: 2.1.3.2 Description of material impacts, risks and opportunities (IRO)
nodes.start_phrase: The positive and negative impacts, risks and material opportunities for La Banque Postale Group are set out in the diagram below presenting the list of IROs.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: ESRS 2 general disclosures in La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document covering material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs), their interaction with the business model, and related financial effects.

- Double materiality and IROs:
  - Identification of positive and negative IROs for own operations, service activities, and financed activities, with a reminder that actions to mitigate one impact may create trade-offs elsewhere.
  - ESG interdependencies are integrated into a “just transition” strategy; no material impacts from these dependencies were identified.
  - Time horizons: environmental impacts considered current; social and governance impacts can be current or potential. Potential impacts are assessed short term for own operations/service activities and medium term for financed activities.
  - A matrix summarizes which topics (E1–E5, S1–S4, G1) are material/non-material/not assessed across impacts and risks/opportunities for both own and financed activities.

- Interaction with the business model and strategy:
  - The Group is adapting its mission-led bancassurance model to enhance positive impact and resilience without questioning the core activity.
  - Adjustments include service offering changes, investment and commercial decision processes, and support to business lines; “impact” is added as a third decision axis alongside risk and return.
  - Example: CNP Assurances implements reinsurance coverage for excess mortality linked to climate risks (e.g., pandemics, heat waves). Internal functions (HR, purchasing, compliance) integrate climate-related social and governance considerations.
  - No immediate strategic overhaul is planned; ongoing stakeholder dialogue will keep the strategy relevant.

- Main impacts:
  - Negative environmental impacts largely stem from financed activities: GHG emissions, pollution, water and marine resource use, biodiversity impacts, and waste across supported sectors. Potential negative customer impacts include cybersecurity breaches or inadequate insurance.
  - Positive impacts arise from strategic choices: green loans for climate adaptation, favorable working conditions, financing for local authorities, accessible banking; as a responsible insurer, CNP seeks to enhance positive effects on people.

- Where impacts arise:
  - Environmental, employee, and governance impacts relate to own operations, service activities, and financed activities.
  - Social impacts on workers in the value chain, affected communities, and customers mainly arise through business relationships (e.g., La Poste workers, suppliers, local/regional authorities, customers).

- Financial effects of material risks:
  - 2024 provisions include climate-related risks in financed activities:
    - Transition risk in the Corporate portfolio (impact of carbon price increases on counterparties’ solvency).
    - Physical flood risk in the home loan portfolio (effects on expected recoveries in litigation).
  - Provisions will be refined each reporting period; details are in the consolidated financial statements notes.
  - Provisions for social factors (HR disputes) are recognized; no provisions for governance risks at 31 Dec 2024.
  - No assessment yet of the financial impact of material opportunities.

nodes.title: Interactions between material IROs and La Banque Postale Group's business model
nodes.heading: 2.1.3.3 Interactions between material IROs and La Banque Postale Group 's business model
nodes.start_phrase: In a context of environmental and social transition, La Banque Postale Group is adapting its business model to have a positive impact and ensure its resilience.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and context: La Banque Postale Group is adapting its mission-led bancassurance business model to environmental and social transitions, embedding sustainability into strategy, governance, and product design to enhance resilience.

- Integration of impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs): A third “impact” lens now complements the traditional risk-return analysis in strategic decisions. Current material impacts and risks are already factored into the strategy; stakeholder dialogue will keep it relevant, with no short-term strategic change planned.

- Business model and offering evolution:
  - Expansion of services and decision processes to address environmental and social issues.
  - Example: CNP Assurances’ global protection approach adds reinsurance against excess mortality (pandemics, heat waves).
  - Internal functions (HR, purchasing, compliance) integrate climate effects on social and governance aspects.
  - Financing and investment activities incorporate impact criteria across lending and asset management.

- Material impacts overview:
  - Negative: Primarily from financed activities—financed GHG emissions, pollution, water and marine resource pressure, biodiversity impacts, and waste; plus potential customer harm via cybersecurity breaches or inadequate insurance.
  - Positive: Driven by strategy and mission—green loans for climate adaptation/mitigation, favorable working conditions, financing local authorities, and accessible banking; responsible insurance for over 30 million policyholders.

- Impact linkages:
  - Environmental, employee, and governance impacts tied to own operations, service activities, and financed activities.
  - Social impacts on workers in the value chain, affected communities, and customers arise mainly via business relationships (La Poste workforce, suppliers, local/regional authorities, customers).

- Financial effects and provisions:
  - 2024 provisions added for climate risks:
    - Transition risk in the Corporate portfolio (counterparty solvency under higher carbon prices).
    - Physical flood risk in the home loan portfolio (impact on recoveries).
  - ESRS E1 risks addressed; methodology to be refined at each close.
  - Provisions for social factors (HR disputes) recorded under ESRS S1.
  - No provisions for governance risks as of 31/12/2024; no quantified assessment of opportunity financial impacts.

- ESRS-aligned risks and opportunities mapped across scopes:
  - Own operations/service activities: energy use and GHG (E1), waste (E5), employee health/safety, DEI, fair pay and work rights (S1), value chain labor risks and improvements (S2), societal sponsorship and local authority financing (S3), customer protection and cybersecurity (S4), governance, ethics, AML/CFT, supplier payment practices and culture (G1).
  - Insurance and own operations: physical and transition climate risks, customer protection risks, partner assessment failures, governance decision-making risks, and culture as a strategic asset.
  - Financed activities: portfolio exposures to physical/transition risks, energy price impacts, financed emissions and high-GHG sectors, financing of adaptation/mitigation and renewables, environmental pressures financed (E2–E5), labor and human rights in portfolios (S2, S3), consumer safety risks (S4), and governance failures in investees (G1).
  - Time horizons considered: current, short-, medium-, and long-term; impact finance IROs flagged.

- Strategy and business model resilience:
  - Anchored in long-term service to retail customers, accessible protection, and support for France’s public/private players; strengthened by Caisse des Dépôts shareholding, mission status, and CNP Assurances’ purpose.
  - Strong national footprint via the postal network; international growth through insurance; diversified activities (banking, insurance, asset management) bolster resilience.
  - IRO list established in 2024 and to be updated annually.

- Specific issues beyond ESRS:
  - Impact-awareness culture (G1), financing local/regional authorities (S3), and cybersecurity (S4) identified as additional material topics and integrated into the IRO set.

- IRO management methodology:
  - Two-part approach: impact materiality (using ENCORE) and financial materiality (ESG risk map).
  - Scope covers own operations, banking services, insurance, credit, and investment; aligned with CNP Assurances.
  - Inclusion of sectors significantly contributing to climate change for financing/investment analysis and linkage to duty-of-care risk mapping.
  - Validation through workshops with external stakeholders and internal experts (e.g., WWF France, EcoAct, I4CE, BL Évolution, OREE, INEC, HR, Caisse des Dépôts, LBP AM).

nodes.title: Strategy and business model resilience
nodes.heading: 2.1.3.4 Strategy and business model resilience
nodes.start_phrase: The resilience of La Banque Postale Group's strategy and business model is driven by:
nodes.summary:
- Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (CSR/ESRS 2), outlining strategy and sustainability reporting approach.
- Strategy and business model resilience built on: a mission-led, long-term vision serving retail customers and public/private players; ties to Caisse des Dépôts and CNP Assurances; strong national footprint via the postal network (nearly 10 million active retail customers; 12th-largest eurozone bank by assets end-2023); international growth through CNP Assurances; and diversification across banking, insurance, and asset management.
- Resilience reinforced by a structured view of impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs); first comprehensive IRO list created in 2024 with annual updates from 2025.
- Double materiality identified three Group-specific issues beyond ESRS requirements: impact-awareness culture (linked to ESRS G1), financing of local and regional authorities (ESRS S3), and cybersecurity focused on customer protection (ESRS S4). These IROs are integrated into the material IRO list; all other IROs are covered by ESRS disclosures.
- IRO methodology: two-pronged assessment—impact materiality using the ENCORE database; financial materiality based on the Group’s ESG risk map. Applied across Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit, and Investment; methodology aligned with CNP Assurances.
- Impact materiality carried out Group-wide and across geographies, including portfolio exposure to sectors with significant climate contribution for Credit and Investment. All CSRD topics assessed due to the bancassurance scope.
- Integration with the Company’s duty of care via due diligence risk mapping to ensure consistency.
- Stakeholder engagement through workshops with external experts and internal teams (e.g., WWF France, EcoAct, I4CE, BL Évolution, OREE, INEC, Caisse des Dépôts, LBP AM, HR) to validate methods and results.
- Cross-references provided to the Group business model/value chain section and to Section 6.8 on ESG risks for loan portfolio details.

nodes.title: Methodology for identifying and assessing IROs
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.1 Methodology for identifying and assessing IROs
nodes.start_phrase: The procedure for identifying and analysing IROs was carried out in two parts:
nodes.summary:
- Presents La Banque Postale Group’s strategy and business model resilience, anchored in its long-term mission to support retail customers, provide accessible insurance, and finance public and private players in France; its ties to the state-owned Caisse des Dépôts, mission-led status, and CNP Assurances’ purpose; strong French roots and nationwide presence via the postal network; international development through CNP Assurances; and diversified activities (banking, insurance, asset management) and geographies that enhance crisis resilience.
- Introduces the Group’s first formal list of impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) in 2024, to be updated annually, and explains that resilience is reinforced by understanding these IROs.
- Summarizes double materiality outcomes, highlighting three specific issues beyond ESRS: impact-awareness culture (linked to ESRS G1), financing of local and regional authorities (ESRS S3), and cybersecurity focused on customer protection (ESRS S4). These are mapped to relevant ESRS, and their IROs are included; all other IROs are covered by ESRS disclosures.
- Describes the methodology for identifying and assessing IROs: impact materiality using the ENCORE database and financial materiality using the Group’s ESG risk map, applied across Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit, and Investment, and aligned with CNP Assurances. The overall process is referenced in the governance section.
- Details impact materiality scope and approach: group-wide and all geographies; includes Own Operations (incl. Banking Services), Insurance, Credit, and Investment; assesses portfolio exposure to high climate-contributing sectors for Credit and Investment; analyzes all CSRD topics due to the breadth of bancassurance; integrates duty of care and due diligence risk mapping for consistency.
- Notes stakeholder engagement through workshops with external and internal experts (e.g., WWF France, EcoAct, I4CE, BL Évolution, OREE, INEC, Caisse des Dépôts, LBP AM, and Group HR) to validate methods and results.
- Provides cross-references to the Group business model/value chain section and ESG risk details (loan portfolios) in Section 6.8, and points to a glossary for key CSR terms.

nodes.title: Methodology for identifying and assessing IROs - Introduction
nodes.source_title: Methodology for identifying and assessing IROs
nodes.source_heading: Methodology for identifying and assessing IROs
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.1 Methodology for identifying and assessing IROs
nodes.start_phrase: The procedure for identifying and analysing IROs was carried out in two parts:
nodes.summary: Introduces the Group’s 2024 methodology for identifying and assessing IROs via a two-part approach: a materiality impact analysis using the ENCORE database (Exploring Natural Capital Opportunities, Risks and Exposure) and a financial materiality analysis based on the Group’s ESG risk map. The analyses cover Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit, and Investment to span all business areas, and the methodological approach is aligned with CNP Assurances. The end-to-end process (identification, rating, validation) is detailed in the infographic “Process of identifying, rating and validating IROs in 2024” referenced in Section 2.1.2.1 on governance of ESG impacts, risks and opportunities [IRO_1_01].

nodes.title: Impact materiality
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.1.1 Impact materiality
nodes.start_phrase: The impact materiality analysis was carried out on the Group scope, taking into account, in all geographic areas, Own Operations (including Banking Services), as well as the Insurance and Credit businesses and Investment.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (ESRS 2) covering strategy/business model resilience and the management of impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) via a double materiality approach.
- Strategy and business model resilience: Grounded in a long-term, mission-led vision tied to Caisse des Dépôts; strong French footprint through the postal network; international development via CNP Assurances; diversified activities (insurance, banking, asset management) that enhance resilience; first formal IRO list established in 2024 with annual updates.
- Scope and alignment: Double materiality spans Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit and Investment; methodological alignment with CNP Assurances.
- Entity-specific material topics beyond ESRS: Impact-awareness culture (linked to ESRS G1); financing of local and regional authorities (ESRS S3); cybersecurity focused on customer protection (ESRS S4). These are integrated into the IRO list; all other IROs are covered by ESRS requirements.
- Impact materiality methodology: 
  - Environmental impacts (ESRS E1–E5) for financed activities assessed using the ENCORE database at sector/portfolio level; a sector is material if ENCORE rates the impact High/Very High and technical reserves exceed defined thresholds.
  - Materiality criteria: scale, scope, irreversibility (negative only), probability (potential only), and long-term impact; for human rights, severity overrides probability.
  - Social/governance impacts assessed using internal management data and stakeholder interviews due to limited quantification tools.
  - Data gaps: several E2/E4 subtopics (e.g., microplastics, substances of concern, species state, ecosystem dependencies) not assessed this year pending external data.
- Stakeholder engagement: Workshops with external experts (e.g., WWF France, EcoAct, I4CE) and internal stakeholders (Sustainability, Group Risk, CNP Assurances, LBP AM, La Poste Group); no direct consultations with communities potentially affected by financed activities; in insurance, CNP operational teams integrate stakeholder views.
- Financial materiality methodology:
  - Risks mapped via the Group ESG risk map; opportunities identified by Risk and business lines; CNP conducts a coordinated assessment with governance review by its Executive bodies and committees.
  - Climate-related risks (physical and transition) emerge as material; other environmental risks currently not deemed material due to lack of methodologies linking them to economic variables.
  - Assessment criteria: potential financial effect, probability, and time horizon weighting; expert-based scoring where topics are not yet on the ESG risk map; opportunities include financing to mitigate environmental impacts (green loans, circular economy, decontamination).
- Materiality thresholds: Portfolio-based thresholds for technical reserves in Credit/Investment (e.g., €1 billion for banking portfolios ≈ 1.3% of outstanding loans); a unified scoring threshold applied to all IROs across scopes for consistency.
- Internal control and governance: No existing internal control procedure specifically for impacts; controls to be phased in after the first CSRD impact analysis; risk management overseen by independent committees within a three-lines-of-defense framework; clear separation between Executive Board (operations) and Supervisory Board (oversight).
- Cross-references: Business model and value chain; governance role in IRO management; ESG risks (Section 6.8).

nodes.title: Financial materiality
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.1.2 Financial materiality
nodes.start_phrase: The identification and assessment of La Banque Postale Group’s risks was based on the Group’s ESG risk map (see infographic Financial materiality assessment criteria below).
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (ESRS 2) detailing how the Group prepares sustainability reporting through a financial materiality lens, within a double materiality framework.
- Financial materiality approach: Group-level identification and assessment of risks and opportunities using an ESG risk map; opportunities (e.g., green loans, circular economy financing, decontamination) identified by Risk and business-line experts.
- CNP Assurances methodology: Uses risk and due-diligence impact mapping plus expert assessments; broad internal consultation (business lines, subsidiaries, shareholder sustainability reps); Sustainability and Accounting ensure consistency and set a materiality threshold; review by Executive Committee and Board, presented to Audit & Risk and CSR Committees; annual reassessment.
- Environmental topics: Climate-related negative impacts create both financing opportunities and material physical/transition risks. Other environmental risks currently deemed non-material due to lack of robust assessment methodologies and their limited reflection in economic variables/regulation/consumer behavior.
- Quantitative assessment: Risks scored on four levels (Minor, Moderate, Major, Critical) against three criteria—potential financial effect, probability, and time horizon (short/medium/long with weighting multipliers). Topics not yet on the ESG risk map and all opportunities are assessed using expert judgment.
- Materiality thresholds: Defined for Credit and Investment to determine material impacts using ENCORE; example threshold of €1 billion for banking portfolios (1.3% of outstanding loans). A consistent materiality threshold is also set on the IRO rating scale across all scopes.
- Internal control and governance: No internal control procedure yet for impact scope; controls to be integrated following the first CSRD impact analysis. Broader risk management relies on independent committees, clear separation of Executive vs. Supervisory Boards, and a three-lines-of-defense internal control framework.
- Decision rule: Material risk/opportunity determined via a composite score combining potential financial effect, probability, and time-horizon weighting against a defined materiality threshold.

nodes.title: Materiality thresholds used
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.1.3 Materiality thresholds used
nodes.start_phrase: In the Credit and Investment scopes, materiality thresholds have been defined in order to determine the material impacts: the impacts with material technical reserves higher than these thresholds were considered as material during the impact analysis, carried out using the ENCORE database (see Section 2.1.4.1.1 “Impact materiality”).
nodes.summary:
- Focus and framework: Explains La Banque Postale Group’s financial materiality assessment within ESRS 2 and the broader double materiality approach used for sustainability reporting.
- Risk and opportunity identification: Uses the Group ESG risk map; opportunities and topics not yet mapped are assessed by internal experts. CNP Assurances applies its own methodology (risk and due‑diligence impact mapping, expert input, consultations), with thresholds set by Sustainability and Accounting, reviewed by the Executive Committee and Board, and presented to Audit & Risk and CSR Committees; reassessed annually.
- Environmental lens: Financed activities’ environmental impacts create financing opportunities (e.g., green loans, circular economy, decontamination) and material climate-related physical and transition risks. Other environmental risks are currently deemed non‑material due to lack of methodologies and limited reflection of these impacts in economic variables, regulation, or consumer behavior.
- Quantitative assessment method: Group-wide scoring based on potential financial effect (0–3), probability of occurrence (0–3), and time horizon weighting (0.8 short‑term, 1 medium‑term, 1.1 long‑term). Materiality is determined via a combined score compared against a threshold; risks are categorized from Minor to Critical. Expert judgment is used where methodologies are pending; opportunities are also expert‑assessed.
- Materiality thresholds: For Credit and Investment, thresholds are set using ENCORE-based impact analysis and material technical reserves; example: €1 billion threshold for banking portfolios (1.3% of outstanding loans). A consistent materiality threshold is also defined on the IRO rating scale across all scopes to align portfolio thresholds with IRO ratings.
- Internal control and governance: No dedicated internal control over impacts yet; controls will be phased in following the first CSRD impact analysis. The Group relies on a three-lines-of-defense risk management framework, overseen by independent committees, with clear separation between the Executive Board (operations) and the Supervisory Board (oversight).

nodes.title: Internal control process
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.1.4 Internal control process
nodes.start_phrase: Currently, there is no internal control procedure concerning impacts.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and standards: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document under ESRS 2, detailing double materiality, IRO (Impacts, Risks, Opportunities) methods, governance, and data sources across Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit, and Investment.
- Financial materiality approach:
  - Group ESG risk map underpins identification and assessment, with risks/opportunities evaluated by the Risk team and business lines; topics not yet on the map assessed by experts.
  - CNP Assurances uses its own methodology combining risk mapping, due diligence impact mapping, and expert input; results reviewed by Executive bodies and presented to Audit & Risk and CSR Committees; annual review planned.
  - Environmental impacts of financed activities create financing opportunities (green loans, circular economy, decontamination), while climate-related negatives drive material physical and transition risks.
  - Other environmental risks (non-climate) deemed not currently material due to lack of methodologies and absence of economic/regulatory signals.
  - Quantitative scoring: potential financial effect, probability of occurrence, and time horizon weighting (short 0.8, medium 1.0, long 1.1). Materiality determined when (effect + probability) × time horizon exceeds threshold.
- Materiality thresholds:
  - Defined for Credit and Investment to flag material impacts via ENCORE; example threshold €1 billion for banking portfolios (1.3% of outstanding loans).
  - A cross-scope rating-scale threshold ensures consistency with IRO ratings.
- Internal control and governance:
  - No dedicated internal control yet for impacts; controls to be phased in following the first CSRD impact analysis.
  - ESG risks managed within existing enterprise risk framework and three lines of defense; clear segregation of duties between Executive Board (operations) and Supervisory Board (oversight).
  - ESG Risk unit within Group Risk assesses exposure, alignment with commitments, and reports to governance; ESG risks integrated into the Risk Appetite Framework and managed like other risks. Opportunities management not yet embedded in the overall framework.
- Data sources and updates:
  - ENCORE for environmental impact identification/assessment in Credit and Investment.
  - Internal management data for positive impacts and own operations.
  - Group ESG risk map for risk identification/assessment.
  - IRO assessment to be updated next financial year, incorporating ENCORE’s July 2024 update and ESG risk map refresh.
- Climate-related IROs:
  - Impact materiality: GHG impacts assessed across all scopes; ENCORE used for Credit/Investment sector impacts; 2023 carbon data for own operations.
  - Financial materiality—physical risks: portfolio- and operations-specific mapping of extreme events (floods, wildfires, storms, clay shrink–swell) and chronic risks (temperature rise, precipitation change, drought, heat waves), over short/medium/long horizons; CNP updated real estate physical risk and found low operational exposure; details in Pillar III (URD Section 6.8.8).
  - Financial materiality—transition risks: analysis via NGFS scenarios, focusing on exposure to carbon‑intensive sectors and financed emissions; details in Pillar III (URD Section 6.8.7).

nodes.title: Risk and opportunity management
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.2 Risk and opportunity management
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group treats Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) risks as a risk area in its own right, but also as a risk factor for other risk areas (credit, operational, market, etc.).
nodes.summary:
- ESG risk management approach: La Banque Postale treats ESG as both a standalone risk class and a cross-cutting factor for other risks (credit, operational, market). ESG risks are integrated into existing risk governance and the Group Risk Appetite Framework, overseen by a dedicated ESG Risk unit within the Group Risk Department that assesses exposures, ensures alignment with commitments, coordinates with subsidiaries, and reports to the Executive and Supervisory Boards. Opportunity management is not yet embedded in the overall framework.
- Data sources and scope: Analyses draw on the ENCORE tool (negative environmental impacts for Credit and Investment), internal management data (positive impacts and own operations), and the Group ESG risk map. Covered scopes include Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit, and Investment. The inaugural IRO analysis will be updated next year with the July 2024 ENCORE update and refreshed ESG risk map.
- Climate impact materiality: GHG impacts are assessed across all scopes. For Credit and Investment, sectoral impacts are evaluated using ENCORE; for own operations, 2023 carbon data underpin the assessment.
- Financial materiality—physical risks: Risk mapping quantifies physical risk scenarios over short-, medium-, and long-term horizons for Commercial and Real Estate Loans, covering extreme events (floods, wildfires, storms, clay shrink–swell) and chronic risks (rising temperature and precipitation, drought, heat waves). CNP Assurances updated physical risk assessments for its real estate in 2023 to inform 2024 adaptation plans. Own operations are judged not severely exposed to climate hazards likely to disrupt business.
- Financial materiality—transition risks: Transition risks are assessed using NGFS scenarios, focusing on exposures to carbon-intensive sectors and the Group’s financed emissions. Further methodological and indicator details are referenced in Pillar III sections of the Universal Registration Document.

nodes.title: Data sources used in the analysis and updating process
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.3 Data sources used in the analysis and updating process
nodes.start_phrase: The data sources used in the analysis are:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance, ESRS 2) detailing ESG risk and opportunity management, data sources for IRO analysis, and climate-related impact and financial materiality assessments.
- ESG risk governance: ESG risks are treated both as a standalone risk class and as drivers of other risks (credit, operational, market). They are integrated into existing risk management and control frameworks, aligned with the Group’s Risk Appetite Framework, and overseen by a dedicated ESG Risk unit within the Group Risk Department that reports to the Executive and Supervisory Boards and coordinates across subsidiaries.
- Opportunities: Management of opportunities is not yet integrated into the Group’s overall management framework.
- Data and scope for IRO analysis: Uses the ENCORE tool (negative environmental impacts for Credit and Investment), internal management data (positive impacts and own operations), and the Group’s ESG risk map. Analysis covers Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit, and Investment. This first-year exercise will be updated next fiscal year following the July 2024 ENCORE update and revision of the ESG risk map.
- Climate impact materiality: Assessment of GHG emissions impacts across all scopes; relies on ENCORE for Credit and Investment sectoral impacts and 2023 carbon data for own operations.
- Financial materiality—physical risks: Risk mapping quantifies scenario-based physical risks over short-, medium-, and long-term horizons for Commercial and Real Estate Loans, covering extreme events (floods, wildfires, storms, clay shrink–swell) and chronic risks (temperature and precipitation increases, drought, heat waves). CNP Assurances updated physical risk assessment of its real estate portfolio to inform 2024 adaptation plans; own operations are considered not severely exposed. Cross-references to Pillar III reporting for indicators.
- Financial materiality—transition risks: Assessed using NGFS reference scenarios, focusing on exposure to carbon-intensive sectors and financed emissions, with further details provided in Pillar III reporting.

nodes.title: Impact materiality
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.4.1 Impact materiality
nodes.start_phrase: The impacts on climate change related to the Group’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions were assessed across La Banque Postale’s various business scopes (Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit and Investment).
nodes.summary:
- Scope and standards: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance, ESRS 2) detailing general preparation of sustainability reporting and the IRO (Impacts, Risks, Opportunities) approach.
- ESG risk governance: ESG risks treated both as a distinct risk class and as factors affecting credit, market, operational risks; managed within existing Group risk frameworks and Risk Appetite Framework (no separate bodies). The Group Risk Department’s ESG Risk unit leads analyses, coordinates across subsidiaries, and reports to the Executive and Supervisory Boards. Opportunity management is not yet integrated into the overall framework.
- Data sources and perimeter: Analyses draw on the ENCORE tool (negative environmental impacts for Credit and Investment), internal management data (positive impacts and own operations), and the Group ESG risk map. Covered scopes: Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit, Investment. First-time IRO exercise to be updated next year with ENCORE (July 2024) and ESG risk map updates.
- Climate-related IRO assessment:
  - Impact materiality: GHG emissions impacts assessed across all scopes; ENCORE used for sectoral impacts in Credit and Investment; 2023 carbon data for own operations.
  - Financial materiality:
    - Physical risks: Portfolio-level risk mapping using scenario quantification across short/medium/long term; analysis of Commercial and Real Estate Loans exposures to extreme events (floods, wildfires, storms, clay shrink-swell) and chronic risks (temperature rise, precipitation, drought, heat waves). CNP Assurances updated physical risk assessment for its real estate portfolio in 2023; own operations not deemed highly exposed. Further details in Pillar III (Sections 6.8.8).
    - Transition risks: Assessed using NGFS scenarios, focusing on exposures to carbon-intensive sectors and financed emissions. Further details in Pillar III (Section 6.8.7).

nodes.title: Financial materiality – physical and transition risks
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.4.2 Financial materiality – physical and transition risks
nodes.start_phrase: To assess the physical risks related to climate change, La Banque Postale has carried out risk mapping work.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and governance of ESG risks: La Banque Postale treats ESG risks both as a standalone risk class and as drivers of other risks (credit, market, operational). ESG risks are integrated into existing risk appetite and control frameworks, not managed by separate bodies. A dedicated ESG Risk unit within the Group Risk Department coordinates analyses across subsidiaries and reports to the Executive and Supervisory Boards. Management of opportunities is not yet embedded in the overall risk framework.

- Data, tools and perimeter: The analysis uses ENCORE (for environmental impacts on credit and investment), internal management data (for positive impacts and own operations), and the Group ESG risk map. Coverage spans Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit and Investment. The IRO assessment will be updated next year with the July 2024 ENCORE refresh and the updated ESG risk map.

- Climate IROs:
  - Impact materiality: Assessment of GHG impacts across all scopes; portfolios evaluated via ENCORE, own operations via 2023 carbon data.
  - Financial materiality: Physical risks mapped for commercial and real estate loans, covering extreme events (floods, wildfires, storms, clay shrink-swell) and chronic risks (temperature rise, precipitation change, drought, heatwaves). CNP Assurances updated physical risk assessment for real estate; own operations considered not severely exposed. Transition risks assessed using NGFS scenarios, focusing on carbon-intensive sector exposures and financed emissions. Assets incompatible with the transition plan identified (fossil fuels, Paris-Aligned Benchmark exclusions). Opportunities from transition assessed qualitatively (no scenario analysis). Risk scenarios align with financial statement assumptions; provisions use NGFS short-term disorderly transition scenarios and a flood scenario for physical risks.

- Biodiversity and ecosystems IROs:
  - Impact materiality: ESRS E4 is non-material for own operations but material for credit and investment, based on exposure to high-impact sectors. Results align with the 2023 Climate and Nature report (TCFD/TNFD), which locates key impact areas.
  - Financial materiality: ESRS E4 not currently financially material, but a deeper analysis using the Global Biodiversity Score assessed dependencies on 21 ecosystem services via average and critical dependency scores. Four portfolios analyzed (commercial/residential real estate, corporate finance, public sector/social economy) covering 39% of exposures. Sectoral qualitative grids developed for five priority sectors: Real estate; Food and beverage manufacturing; Transport and warehousing; Energy production and distribution; Health and pharmaceuticals. CNP Assurances’ BIA-GBS analysis (covering 98% of directly held equities/bonds) shows low average but significant critical dependencies, indicating potential business model risks (e.g., water scarcity in leather). An initial assessment of nature-related physical and transition risks was completed; systemic risk not yet included.

- References: Further details on ESG risk governance, transition and physical risk indicators, and credit quality are provided in the Universal Registration Document (Sections 2.1.2.7.1, 6.8.2, 6.8.7, 6.8.8).

nodes.title: Impact materiality
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.5.1 Impact materiality
nodes.start_phrase: The impacts on biodiversity and ecosystems were examined, within the scope of La Banque Postale Group’s own operations, based on internal management data and on the Group’s ESG risk map.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document covering sustainability reporting (ESRS 2) and climate/biodiversity impact, risk, and opportunity (IRO) assessments.
- Transition alignment: Identification of assets/activities potentially incompatible with the Group’s transition plan, including exposures to fossil fuels and companies excluded from the Paris-Aligned Benchmark; further credit quality details referenced in Section 6.8.7.1.
- Transition opportunities: Assessed qualitatively on an expert basis without scenario analysis.
- Scenario use and financial alignment: Climate scenarios used are consistent with assumptions in the financial statements; transition risk provisions based on NGFS short-term disorderly scenarios; physical risk provisions use a flood scenario.
- Biodiversity and ecosystems (ESRS E4) – Impact materiality:
  - Own operations: ESRS E4 assessed as non-material based on internal data and ESG risk mapping.
  - Downstream value chain (credit and investment): ESRS E4 assessed as material; impact analysis focused on exposures to high-biodiversity-impact sectors per the document’s methodology; findings align with the 2023 Climate and Nature report (TCFD/TNFD), which maps the geographic location of impacts.
- Biodiversity and ecosystems – Financial materiality:
  - Currently not financially material for La Banque Postale, but deeper analysis conducted using the Global Biodiversity Score (GBS) across 21 ecosystem services and four IPBES pressures.
  - Two dependence metrics used: average dependency score and critical dependency score (indicating non-substitutable, high/very high dependencies).
  - Portfolio coverage: Four portfolios analyzed—commercial and residential real estate, corporate finance, public sector and social economy—covering 39% of on- and off-balance sheet exposures.
  - Sectoral deep-dives: Qualitative grids developed for five priority sectors—real estate; food and beverage manufacturing; transport and warehousing; energy production and distribution; health and pharmaceuticals.
- CNP Assurances’ analysis: Applied BIA-GBS to 98% of directly held equities and bonds; average dependency is low, but critical dependencies are significant for a share of companies, implying potential financial risks (e.g., water scarcity risks in the leather sector).
- Nature-related risk assessment: Initial assessment of physical and transition risks completed; systemic nature risk not yet incorporated.

nodes.title: Financial materiality
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.5.2 Financial materiality
nodes.start_phrase: The identification and assessment of risks related to biodiversity and ecosystems was carried out based on the methodology detailed in Section 2.1.4.1.2 “Financial materiality”.
nodes.summary:
- Context and framework: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document covering ESRS 2 sustainability reporting preparations and double materiality work, with links to glossary and cross-references to risk and exposure disclosures.

- Transition plan alignment: Identification of assets/activities potentially incompatible with the transition plan (including fossil fuel exposures and Paris-Aligned Benchmark exclusions). Transition opportunities assessed on an expert basis (no scenario analysis). Climate scenarios aligned with financial statements; transition risk provisions based on NGFS short-term disorderly scenarios and physical risk provisions using a flood scenario.

- Biodiversity and ecosystems (ESRS E4):
  - Impact materiality: Own operations assessed as non-material; material impacts identified in downstream value chain (credit and investment). Analyses align with the 2023 Climate and Nature report (TCFD/TNFD).
  - Financial materiality: Currently not material, but detailed dependency assessment performed using the Global Biodiversity Score across IPBES pressures. Two portfolio dependency metrics used (average and critical). Four portfolios analyzed (commercial/residential real estate, corporate finance, public sector, social economy) covering 39% of exposures. Sectoral qualitative grids developed for five priority sectors (real estate; food & beverage manufacturing; transport & warehousing; energy production & distribution; health & pharma).
  - CNP Assurances: BIA-GBS methodology applied to 98% of directly held equities/bonds; low average dependency but significant critical dependencies on at least one ecosystem service, implying potential financial risk (e.g., water scarcity in leather).
  - Nature-related risks: Initial assessment of physical and transition risks completed; systemic risk not yet included.

- Stakeholder engagement and operations context: Stakeholders consulted include WWF France, CDC Biodiversité, and BL Évolution. As a service bank, the Group does not source raw materials, has no production sites, and reports no biodiversity-sensitive sites or community impacts within own operations; therefore, no specific biodiversity mitigation measures (EU Birds/Habitats Directives, EIA, IFC PS6) deemed necessary for own operations.

- Pollution (ESRS E2):
  - Own operations: Non-material.
  - Downstream credit/investments: Material for impacts, non-material for financial materiality. High-impact sectors identified include metal products manufacturing; wearing apparel; paper; construction and civil engineering; pharmaceuticals; motor vehicles/trailers; aviation and defense; electric power generation/transmission/distribution; and IT services (programming/consulting).

- Water and marine resources (ESRS E3):
  - Own operations: Non-material.
  - Downstream credit/investments: Material for impacts, non-material financially. Sectors with very significant water use include paper; mineral and metal products manufacturing; renewable energy production; construction and civil engineering; mining and quarrying; leather manufacturing; and electric power generation/transmission/distribution.

nodes.title: Involvement of stakeholders and affected communities
nodes.heading: Involvement of stakeholders and affected communities
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the double materiality analysis, La Banque Postale Group consulted internal and external stakeholders on the various subjects.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance) detailing ESRS-based sustainability reporting preparations and double materiality outcomes.
- Methodology: Use of double materiality analysis with internal management data, ESG risk mapping, and references to methodologies in sections on impact materiality (2.1.4.1.1) and financial materiality (2.1.4.1.2).
- Stakeholder engagement: Consultation with internal stakeholders and external experts—WWF France, CDC Biodiversité, and BL Évolution—for topics including biodiversity and pollution.
- Biodiversity (ESRS E4):
  - Own operations: No raw material sourcing or production sites; no significant impacts on biodiversity or ecosystem services; no sites in/near sensitive areas; ESRS E4 deemed non-material for own operations.
  - Mitigation measures under EU nature directives and IFC PS6 considered unnecessary given activity profile.
- Pollution (ESRS E2):
  - Own operations: Not a significant source of pollution; not located in pollution risk areas; ESRS E2 non-material for these scopes.
  - Downstream value chain (credit and investment): ESRS E2 material for impact analysis but non-material for financial materiality. High-impact sectors identified include metal products manufacturing, apparel, paper, construction/civil engineering, pharmaceuticals, motor vehicles/trailers, aviation/defence, electric power generation/transmission/distribution, and IT services.
- Water and marine resources (ESRS E3):
  - Own operations: No significant water/marine resource use; ESRS E3 non-material for these scopes.
  - Downstream value chain: ESRS E3 material for impact analysis but non-material for financial materiality. High water-use sectors include paper, mineral and metal products manufacturing, renewable energy production, construction/civil engineering, mining/quarrying, leather products, and electric power generation/transmission/distribution.
- Overall conclusion: Environmental materiality for La Banque Postale largely resides in financed and invested sectors rather than the Group’s direct operations, with clear identification of high-impact sectors to inform risk and impact management.

nodes.title: Assessment of pollution‑related IROs
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.6 Assessment of pollution‑related IROs
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group’s own operations and service activities are not the source of significant pollution, and are not located in areas at risk of pollution.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document detailing sustainability reporting preparation under ESRS 2, with a focus on double materiality and impact/risk/opportunity (IRO) assessments.
- Stakeholder engagement: Internal and external stakeholders consulted; for biodiversity and pollution topics, external experts included WWF France, CDC Biodiversité, and BL Évolution.
- Biodiversity and ecosystems (ESRS E4): 
  - As a non-manufacturing bank, the Group does not source raw materials or operate production sites; its own operations do not negatively impact biodiversity, ecosystems, or related community ecosystem services.
  - No sites are located in or near biodiversity-sensitive areas.
  - Given the nature of activities, no specific mitigation measures (EU Birds/Habitats Directives, EIA Directive, IFC PS6) are deemed necessary for own operations.
  - ESRS E4 is not material for the Group’s operational scope.
- Pollution (ESRS E2):
  - Own operations and service activities are not significant pollution sources; ESRS E2 is non-material for these scopes based on internal data and the ESG risk map.
  - Pollution issues arise in the downstream value chain (credit and investment). For these scopes, ESRS E2 is material for impact analysis but non-material for financial materiality.
  - High-impact financed sectors identified: manufacture of metal products; wearing apparel; paper; building construction and civil engineering; pharmaceuticals; motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers; aviation and defence; electric power generation, transmission and distribution; programming/consulting/IT.
- Water and marine resources (ESRS E3):
  - Own operations require no significant water/marine resource use; ESRS E3 is non-material for these scopes.
  - In the downstream (credit and investment) scopes, ESRS E3 is material for impact analysis but non-material for financial materiality.
  - High water-consumption financed sectors identified: paper; manufacture of mineral and metal products; renewable energy production; building construction and civil engineering; mining and quarrying; leather and related products; electric power generation, transmission and distribution.
- Methodologies: Impact analyses based on exposure of technical reserves to high-impact sectors per Section 2.1.4.1.1 (Impact materiality); risk assessments per Section 2.1.4.1.2 (Financial materiality); own-operations assessments used internal management data and the ESG risk map.

nodes.title: Assessment of water and marine resources-related IROs
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.7 Assessment of water and marine resources-related IROs
nodes.start_phrase: As a commercial bank, La Banque Postale Group’s own operations and service activities do not require significant use of water or marine resources.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance), explaining how sustainability reporting is prepared under ESRS 2 and summarizing double materiality assessments.

- Stakeholder engagement: Internal and external consultations conducted. External stakeholders include WWF France, CDC Biodiversité, BL Évolution (biodiversity, pollution, water) and OREE (circular economy).

- Biodiversity and ecosystems (ESRS E4):
  - As a bank with no raw materials or production sites, own operations have no significant biodiversity impacts and do not affect communities or ecosystem services.
  - No sites in or near biodiversity‑sensitive areas.
  - No need for mitigation measures under relevant EU directives or IFC PS6 for own operations.
  - ESRS E4 is non‑material for the operational scope.

- Pollution (ESRS E2):
  - Own operations and services are not significant pollution sources and are not in high‑risk areas; ESRS E2 non‑material for operations.
  - Downstream (credit and investment) activities: material for impact, non‑material for financial materiality.
  - Very material sectors for pollution: manufacture of metal products; wearing apparel; paper; construction and civil engineering; pharmaceuticals; motor vehicles/trailers; aviation and defence; electric power generation/transmission/distribution; programming/consulting/IT.

- Water and marine resources (ESRS E3):
  - Own operations require limited water/marine resources; non‑material for operations.
  - Downstream activities: material for impact, non‑material for financial materiality.
  - High water consumption sectors: paper; mineral and metal products manufacturing; renewable energy; construction and civil engineering; mining and quarrying; leather and related products; electric power generation/transmission/distribution.
  - Significant marine resource use sectors: construction and civil engineering; mining and quarrying; agriculture/forestry/fishing; renewable energy.

- Resource use and circular economy (ESRS E5):
  - Operational scope: material for impact, non‑material for financial materiality.
  - Downstream (credit/investment) scope: material for impact, non‑material for financial materiality.
  - High waste‑producing sectors: real estate; renewable energy; automotive; pharmaceuticals; mining; aviation and defence; leather and related products; electric power generation/transmission/distribution.

- Disclosure framework:
  - EU legislative data points and coverage detailed in Sections 2.5.1.1 and 2.5.1.2.
  - Non‑disclosure choices include voluntary data points, delayed disclosure, non‑material topics, unmet disclosure conditions, and selection among alternative disclosures.
  - Minimum Disclosure Requirements applied for each ESRS.

nodes.title: Assessment of IROs related to resource use and the circular economy
nodes.heading: 2.1.4.8 Assessment of IROs related to resource use and the circular economy
nodes.start_phrase: The impacts, risks and opportunities identified in relation to resource use and circular economy were examined, within the scope of La Banque Postale Group’s own operations, based on internal management data and the Group’s ESG risk map.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document detailing ESRS-aligned sustainability reporting, with glossary reference and coverage of minimum disclosure requirements (MDR) for each ESRS.
- Marine resource use: Identifies financed sectors with the most significant impacts—building and civil engineering; mining and quarrying; agriculture, forestry and fishing; renewable energy production.
- Stakeholder engagement: Double materiality workshops consulted internal teams and external experts on water and resource topics, including WWF France, CDC Biodiversité, BL Évolution (water) and OREE (circular economy).
- IRO assessment (Impacts, Risks, Opportunities) on resource use and circular economy:
  - Own operations: ESRS E5 deemed material for impact materiality, non-material for financial materiality, based on internal management data and the Group’s ESG risk map.
  - Downstream value chain (credit and investment activities): ESRS E5 material for impact analysis; not financially material. Analysis used exposure to sectors with significant waste production.
- Sectors with very significant waste generation: real estate activities; renewable energy production; automotive, pharmaceutical, and mining industries; aviation and defence; manufacture of leather and related products; electric power generation, transmission and distribution.
- Disclosure scope and choices:
  - Sustainability sub-topics and coverage mapped in referenced tables (Sections 2.5.1.1 and 2.5.1.2).
  - Non-disclosure categories applied where relevant: voluntary data points; delayed disclosure; non-material topics; disclosure condition not met; alternative disclosures (choosing one among alternatives).
  - Confirms MDR implemented for each ESRS and inclusion of data points required by other EU legislative acts.

nodes.title: Disclosure requirements covered by the sustainability report
nodes.heading: 2.1.5 Disclosure requirements covered by the sustainability report
nodes.start_phrase: The data points required by other legislative acts of the European Union are presented in the table presented in paragraph 2.5.1.2 “Data points required by other European Union legislation”.
nodes.summary:
- Explains La Banque Postale’s ESRS-based sustainability reporting approach in the 2024 Universal Registration Document, confirming minimum disclosure requirements are covered and indicating where coverage tables and EU data point mappings are provided.
- Describes double materiality assessments for resource use, circular economy, and water/marine resources:
  - Own operations: ESRS E5 (Resource use and circular economy) is material for impact, not financially material.
  - Financed (credit and investment) activities: ESRS E5 is material for impact, not financially material.
  - Identifies sectors with significant impacts:
    - Marine resource use: building construction and civil engineering; mining and quarrying; agriculture, forestry and fishing; renewable energy.
    - Waste generation: real estate; renewable energy; automotive; pharmaceuticals; mining; aviation and defence; leather manufacturing; electric power generation/transmission/distribution.
- Details stakeholder engagement for topic scoping and IROs:
  - Water-related: WWF France, CDC Biodiversité, BL Évolution.
  - Circular economy: OREE.
- Outlines disclosure scope across ESRS sub-topics for own operations and financed activities, covering:
  - Climate (adaptation, mitigation, energy)
  - Pollution (air, water, soil, organisms/food, substances of concern/SVHC, microplastics)
  - Water and marine resources
  - Biodiversity and ecosystems (drivers, species, ecosystems, services)
  - Circular economy (resource inflows/outflows, waste)
  - Social topics for own workforce, value-chain workers, affected communities, customers/end-users (including cybersecurity)
  - Business conduct (corporate culture, corruption/bribery, supplier relationships and payment practices, political engagement/lobbying, whistleblower protection) and animal welfare.
- Specifies non-disclosure choices used where relevant: voluntary points, delayed disclosure, non-material topics, unmet disclosure conditions, and alternative disclosures.
- Presents entity-specific “impact-awareness culture” as part of its mission-led company status:
  - Governance via a Mission Committee and ESG responsibility embedded across the organization.
  - Integration of ESG targets into remuneration.
  - Training employees on ESG and supporting impactful actions.
  - Product and service offerings to enable environmental and social transition, including accessible banking for customers in difficulty.
  - Co-construction with independent third parties (e.g., NGOs) and an ambition to meet and exceed regulatory expectations to advance sustainable finance standards.

nodes.title: The impact-awareness culture at the heart of the mission-led company
nodes.heading: 2.1.6.1 The impact-awareness culture at the heart of the mission-led company
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale is committed to serving its purpose as a mission-led company.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on La Banque Postale’s mission-led model and impact-awareness culture, governed by a dedicated Mission Committee and embedded across the Group, including ESG-linked remuneration and comprehensive employee training.
- Commitment to exceed regulatory expectations and co-construct practices with independent third parties (NGOs, Mission Committee), while promoting accessible banking, and offers/services that enable customers’ environmental and social transitions.
- Strong ethics and compliance stance: zero tolerance for integrity breaches, fraud, anti-competitive behavior; adherence to sanctions, financial transparency, data protection, health, environmental safeguards, and human rights.
- Rising employee engagement in ESG: higher training completion, greater participation in sustainability initiatives, and a doubling of volunteer hours between 2023 and 2024.
- Impact culture metrics show 2024 progress and 2025 targets, including:
  - Employees trained in CSR/sustainable finance (69.7% in 2023 to 80% in 2024; 90% target).
  - Non-financial targets in remuneration (20% to 28.8%; target ≥20%).
  - Growth in customer carbon-footprint awareness initiatives.
  - CNP Assurances social inclusion and community impact: significant increase in internships/work-study for youth from deprived areas, higher sponsorship spending, and more employees mobilized for societal actions.
  - Other indicators: bank card carbon footprint tracked with refined LCA methodology (2023 restated; 2024 increase linked to higher card issuance), 100% SRI in employee savings (LBP AM range fully SRI), increased hours devoted to community outreach, and stable support for L’Envol.
- Detailed explanation of bank card emissions significance for the banking activity, methodological improvements in carbon accounting, and market context (high daily usage in France and higher new card issuance in 2024).
- Group-wide impact finance approach aligned with Finance for Tomorrow’s pillars (intentionality, additionality, measurement), steered by the Sustainability Department (DEC) since 2021 to ensure strategy coherence and avoid greenwashing.
- Strategic integration of impact finance in mission targets: transforming the bancassurance model through impact culture, developing products/services for environmental, social, and regional challenges, and advancing best practices and standards in sustainable finance.
- Application across financing and services: support for environmental solutions and local authorities, improving working conditions in the value chain, managing negative impacts of financed activities, and promoting access to bancassurance (accessible banking mission).
- Monitoring via CSRD indicators and concrete sector commitments: LBP AM’s leadership in research support, issuer transparency, SRI development, collaborative engagement, participation in impact/biodiversity/climate working groups, and governance roles.
- Methodological tools and innovations: Impact Weighting Factor for financing selection and LBP AM’s GREaT investment analysis methodology integrating sustainability considerations.

nodes.title: La Banque Postale Group’s impact finance approach
nodes.heading: 2.1.6.2 La Banque Postale Group’s impact finance approach
nodes.start_phrase: Finance for tomorrow defines impact finance as an investment or financing strategy that aims to accelerate the just and sustainable transformation of the real economy, by providing evidence of its beneficial effects.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance; ESRS 2) detailing impact finance strategy, governance, indicators, and selected CSR performance highlights.

- Customer and product CSR insights:
  - Bank cards: 94% of French adults use cards daily; while their share of total Group GHG is modest, it is material to banking activities. New card issuances rose 18% in 2024 vs. 2023. Methodology updates using life-cycle analysis improved accuracy; the 2023 baseline was revised from 563 tCO₂e to 408 tCO₂e.
  - Employee savings: 100% invested in socially responsible funds, as only LBP AM products are offered; LBP AM’s eligible range is fully SRI.
  - Social programs: Slight increase in employee participation and youth beneficiaries in the L’Envol program, confirming its long-term relevance.

- Impact finance approach:
  - Definition aligned with Finance for Tomorrow (intentionality, additionality, impact measurement).
  - Governance: Centralized in the Sustainability Department (DEC, created 2021) to steer the 2030 plan, ensure Group-wide consistency, and prevent greenwashing.
  - Strategic integration: Embedded in the mission-led company targets—transform the bancassurance model with impact culture, develop solutions for environmental/social/regional needs, and advance sector best practices and standards.
  - Scope of impacts: 
    - Positive impacts via financing environmental solutions, local authorities, and improving conditions in the downstream value chain.
    - Exemplary management to assess and mitigate negative environmental and social impacts in financing and investments.
    - Access to bancassurance services enhanced through regional networks and inclusive offerings (accessible banking mission).
  - Monitoring: Impact tracked through CSRD indicators.

- Tools, methodologies, and initiatives:
  - Impact Weighting Factor (IWF): An impact scoring tool co-developed with WWF France, used in retail and corporate lending to assess environmental, societal, and regional impacts alongside risk and financial performance; also a change-management lever for teams and customers.
  - LBP AM leadership: Supports academic research, issuer environmental transparency, SRI development, and advanced collaborative engagement; active in impact finance, biodiversity, and climate working groups at the Institute for Sustainable Finance (board member).
  - GREaT methodology: LBP AM’s Group-wide investment analysis framework integrating sustainable development issues.

- Impact finance instruments and offers (illustrative portfolio):
  - Regional financing for local authorities, social housing, charities, healthcare, and companies.
  - Green project financing; sustainability-linked corporate loans; Prêt Avance Rénovation; impact home loans.
  - Responsible current account and impact bank card; accessible insurance products (e.g., first insurance kit, carer guarantee).
  - Sector and exclusion policies; shareholder engagement.
  - Inclusive retail support: Livret A, Simplicité account, L’Appui; accessible branch network (including for people with disabilities).
  - Portfolio commitments and pathways for GHG emissions reduction.
  - Overarching commitment to provide universal access to bancassurance services and support customers in financial difficulty.

nodes.title: The Impact Weighting Factor (IWF)
nodes.heading: The Impact Weighting Factor (IWF)
nodes.start_phrase: The Impact Weighting Factor is an impact scoring tool used to grant loans to retail customers and for Corporate and Investment Banking.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document under “Sustainable performance” and “General information on the preparation of sustainability reports [ESRS 2],” with references to CSR glossary and terminology.

- Impact finance framework: Overview of La Banque Postale’s approach to “impact finance” aimed at accelerating a just and sustainable transformation of the real economy, covering:
  - Regional financing for local authorities, social housing, charities, healthcare, and companies, plus shareholder engagement.
  - Consumer impact offerings (impact home loans, renovation loans like Prêt Avance Rénovation, responsible current account, impact bank card).
  - Sector and exclusion policies; financing of green projects.
  - Accessibility and inclusion in bancassurance (universal access, support for financially vulnerable customers, accessible products such as first insurance kits, carer guarantees; services like Livret A, Simplicité account, L’Appui; accessible branch network).
  - Portfolio commitments tied to concrete GHG reduction pathways.

- Impact Weighting Factor (IWF): A proprietary impact scoring tool co-developed with WWF France to guide lending and investment decisions by assessing environmental, territorial, and inclusion impacts.
  - Scope and use: Applied at counterparty level or by financing purpose across retail and corporate activities; embedded in onboarding, credit analysis, annual reviews, and portfolio management; data from customers, external providers, public sources, and sector inputs.
  - Operational effects: Influences retail loan pricing (preferential rates for positive-impact or energy-efficiency renovation financing); in corporate real estate/asset/project finance, unfavorable scores escalate decisions to higher approval levels.
  - Deployment: Already built for five priority lines (home loans; commercial real estate; asset and project finance; large corporate loans; trading room). Next phases include local authorities, social housing, public health, SMEs/mid-caps, and consumer loans. Progress tracked by a mission-led metric (share of activities covered by the IWF).
  - Strategic outcomes: Steers capital toward positive environmental and social sectors and away from high-negative-impact activities (e.g., fossil fuels, polluting counterparties). Incorporated into Executive Board variable remuneration.
  - Structure: Three pillars—Environment (aligned with EU Green Deal, Taxonomy, SFDR: climate, biodiversity, water, pollution), Territory (economic and social characteristics within France/EU: regional economic development, sustainable territorial development), Inclusion (human rights, diversity and inclusion, universal product/service accessibility).
  - Impact scale: Five levels from Very negative (1) to Very positive (5).

- LBP AM GREaT methodology: Integration of ESG in La Banque Postale Asset Management’s investment processes through its SRI approach.
  - SRI pillars: (1) Integrate sustainable development issues in investment selection; (2) Engage companies to improve practices; (3) Exclude firms in major controversies or sensitive sectors (controversial/prohibited weapons, tobacco, gambling, thermal coal, certain oil and gas).
  - GREaT analytical framework: G – responsible Governance; R – sustainable management of natural and human Resources; E – Energy transition; T – Territorial development.
  - Consumer-focused criteria: Data protection, product/service quality and safety, customer relationship management (privacy), mitigation of negative impacts on customer rights, access to essential services, and human rights respect.
  - Application: Covers all asset classes with SRI ratings for ~12,000 companies; ratings used via quantitative methods and certified thresholds in portfolio construction. The GREaT Committee oversees engagement and exclusion policies, including exclusion decisions.

nodes.title: The GREaT methodology
nodes.heading: The GREaT methodology
nodes.start_phrase: LBP AM, La Banque Postale Group’s asset management company, places responsibility at the heart of its strategy.
nodes.summary:
This excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document outlines how sustainability reporting is prepared under ESRS 2 and details LBP Asset Management’s integration of ESG across all investment processes. It presents LBP AM’s SRI approach—built on (1) embedding sustainable development in investment selection, (2) engaging issuers to improve practices, and (3) excluding sensitive sectors and major controversies (e.g., controversial/prohibited weapons, tobacco, gambling, thermal coal, and certain oil and gas).
