nodes.title: Policies related to water and marine resources
nodes.heading: 2.2.4.1 Policies related to water and marine resources
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, La Banque Postale Group, as a subsidiary, adopted the Caisse des Dépôts Group’s water policy to address the three major challenges it faces:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and materiality: Water is not a material topic for La Banque Postale’s direct operations but is material in its financed activities (downstream value chain). Resource use/circular economy is material through waste for both own operations and financed activities.

- Water policy (adopted 2024 from Caisse des Dépôts):
  - Key challenges: scarcity of water, water quality and infrastructure, flooding/soil sealing.
  - Pillars: understand impacts/risks; drive water savings; preserve water quality and infrastructure.
  - Governance: Group Risk Management Committee oversees; first implementation steps in 2025.

- Water-related commitments:
  - By end-2025: produce a water footprint or dependency assessment.
  - By end-2027: estimate aquatic pollution from operations/financed counterparties; assess portfolios’ exposure to drought/water stress (France, overseas, international as relevant).
  - Contribute to France’s 10% water-use reduction by 2030 via financing, ESG integration (by 2025 include water-saving and local water-stress in ESG analysis), and tools for efficient water management; ensure projects in high-stress areas align with best practices.
  - Preserve ecosystems: combat aquatic pollution, support the water cycle, avoid wetland damage; exclude financing/investment in companies with >20% revenue from pesticides; provide loans improving water quality (e.g., sanitation services, water agencies).
  - Marine/ocean policy: none yet; to be developed with Caisse des Dépôts in 2025 ahead of UNOC 2025.

- Action plans and tools:
  - Water as an indicator in the Impact Weighting Factor (with WWF France).
  - Green loans for local authorities’ water/sanitation; bridging loans tied to water-agency subsidies (leak reduction, reuse); Climate & Biodiversity Impact Fund supports water consumption reductions.
  - Subsidiaries: CNP Assurances’ real-estate “Green Works” (limit consumption, ensure quality); LBP AM in CERES Valuing Water; Louvre Banque Privée enhances PAI monitoring (emissions to water).

- Water risk mapping:
  - 2024 financing location analysis: ~65% of financed areas have at least two high-risk criteria (biodiversity importance, ecological integrity, water stress).
  - Priority areas: Île-de-France (significant potential building land, average risk) and parts of South-East France (very high risk).
  - Next steps: define actions to limit impacts. CNP Assurances to map portfolio assets in high/very high water-stress areas by 2027, and its sites/real estate by 2026; LBP AM engages companies to map abstraction sites and assess local impacts.

- Targets/results:
  - Following 2023–2024 impact/dependency/risk/opportunity assessment, quantified impact-reduction targets will be set progressively.

- Circular economy policy (2024):
  - Scope: La Banque Postale SA and main subsidiaries (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, LBP Consumer Finance, Louvre Banque Privée, Domiserve, Easybourse, LBP Leasing & Factoring).
  - Aim: reduce at source and optimize use and end-of-life of resources by 2030, using a life-cycle approach; applies to operational activities.
  - Governance: validated/monitored by the Sustainability Department; financing/investment considered but without specific targets; policy and targets shared internally and externally on request.

nodes.start_phrase: Water is one of the environmental indicators under the Impact Weighting Factor (IWF), an impact scoring tool developed by La Banque Postale in partnership with WWF France to guide financing and investment strategies (for more information on the IWF, see focus point: The Impact Weighting Factor (IWF)).
nodes.summary:
- Focus on water and marine resource management within La Banque Postale’s sustainability strategy, using the Impact Weighting Factor (IWF) developed with WWF France to guide financing and investment decisions.
- Deployment of water-focused financing tools:
  - “Green loans” for local authorities targeting sustainable water and sanitation investments (small water cycle).
  - Bridging loans to pre-finance water agency subsidies (supply security, leak reduction, treated wastewater reuse).
  - Climate and Biodiversity Impact Fund supporting projects to reduce water consumption.
- Subsidiary initiatives:
  - CNP Assurances’ Green Works Charter to limit water use and ensure water quality in directly owned real estate.
  - LBP AM’s participation in CERES’s Valuing Water initiative to promote water resource protection.
  - Louvre Banque Privée’s enhanced monitoring of SFDR PAIs, including emissions to water.
- Water risk mapping and prioritization:
  - Analysis of financed activities’ locations identified sensitive areas, with ~65% of financed areas meeting at least two high-risk criteria (biodiversity significance, ecological integrity, or water stress).
  - Priority geographies: Île-de-France (significant potential building land, average overall risk) and parts of South-East France (very high overall risk).
  - Next steps include defining concrete actions to limit impacts in water-risk areas.
- Commitments and timelines:
  - CNP Assurances to map portfolio assets in high/extremely high water-stress areas by end-2027, and its sites/real estate by end-2026 (France and internationally).
  - LBP AM engaging investee companies to map abstraction sites, identify high-stress areas, and assess local impacts, with targeted engagements for highest-risk firms.
- Targets and results:
  - Following 2023–2024 impact/risk assessment, La Banque Postale will progressively set quantified impact-reduction targets for water and marine resources.
- Circular economy policy (2024):
  - New Resources and Circular Economy policy covering La Banque Postale SA and key subsidiaries (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, La Banque Postale Consumer Finance, Louvre Banque Privée, Domiserve, Easybourse, LBP Leasing & Factoring).
  - Commitment to reduce at source and optimize resource use and end-of-life by 2030, integrating waste management within a life-cycle approach.
  - Policy applies to operational activities; financing and investment activities were considered but have no specific targets or commitments.
  - Governance by the Sustainability Department, with targets and policy communicated internally and available externally on request.

  - Subsidiary actions: CNP Assurances’ Green Works Charter (limit/ensure quality of water use in real estate), LBP AM’s participation in CERES’ Valuing Water initiative, Louvre Banque Privée’s strengthened monitoring of “emissions to water” (SFDR PAIs).
  - Post-2023/2024 impact measurement will inform expanded impact-reduction actions.

- Water risk mapping and priorities:
  - 2024 analysis identified financed activities in sensitive areas using criteria including water stress; about 65% of financed areas have at least two high-risk criteria.
  - Priority locations: Île-de-France (significant potential building land, medium overall risk) and parts of South-East France (very high overall risk).
  - Next steps: define concrete actions to limit impacts in water-risk areas.
  - CNP Assurances to map financial assets in high/extremely high water-stress areas by end-2027 and real estate/sites by end-2026; LBP AM engaging portfolio companies to map abstraction sites, identify high-stress areas, and study local impacts.

- Targets and results for water:
  - Quantified impact-reduction targets to be set progressively following 2023–2024 assessments.

- Circular economy strategy:
  - 2024 Resources and Circular Economy policy covering La Banque Postale SA and main subsidiaries (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, LBP Consumer Finance, Louvre Banque Privée, Domiserve, Easybourse, LBP Leasing & Factoring).
  - Commitment to reduce at source and optimize resource use and end-of-life by 2030, with a life-cycle approach and subsidiary-specific roadmaps.
  - Promotion of recycled and renewable materials; eco-design of products (e.g., bank cards) prioritizing recycled content and recyclability.
  - Financing/investment activities considered but without specific targets; policy governed and monitored by the Sustainability Department and shared internally/externally.
  - No waste policy yet for Corporate & Investment Banking due to measurement methodology gaps; collaborative work with La Poste Group to develop resource footprint and reduction pathways.

- Action plans for resource use and waste:
  - Reduce consumption and waste:
    - Plastics: identify high-consuming suppliers, implement reduction plans, integrate material criteria in procurement, raise buyer/specifier awareness.
    - Paper/cardboard: trace waste origins, embed criteria in tenders, train influencers/buyers on alternatives.
    - Electrical/electronic equipment (EEE): optimize allocation policies and raise user awareness.
  - Optimize end-of-life:
    - Comprehensive waste mapping, supplier progress plans prioritizing reuse and recycling over energy recovery/landfill, employee training on sorting/recovery.
    - Reduce undelivered bank cards; integrate recovery with providers; consider extending card validity.
    - Promote reuse via stricter supplier requirements, donation channels, life-cycle analyses, and awareness.
  - Annual roadmap coordinated by the Sustainability Department; no specific budget allocation; no waste roadmaps for credit/investment portfolios.

- Waste management practices:
  - Contracts apply the waste hierarchy; reuse considered before recycling.
  - Majority of waste handled by operators committed to 100% recycling (e.g., Recygo, Les Joyeux Recycleurs).

nodes.title: Action plans related to resource use and the circular economy
nodes.heading: 2.2.5.2 Action plans related to resource use and the circular economy
nodes.start_phrase: The main actions deployed under the Resources and Circular Economy policy include:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and policy: La Banque Postale’s environmental/CSR approach includes a Group-wide Resources and Circular Economy policy, translated into subsidiary-specific roadmaps based on operational needs and resource use.
- Eco-design and materials: All products placed on the market (notably bank cards) follow an eco-design approach prioritizing recycled inputs, recyclability of plastics/cardboard/IT equipment, and promotion of renewable resources. Procurement supports systematic use of recycled materials for paper/cardboard, plastics, and WEEE.
- CIB perimeter: No waste management policy currently applies to Corporate & Investment Banking due to the absence of robust methodologies to measure resource footprints. Group-level work (with La Poste Group) is underway to establish footprints and reduction pathways, which should enable better integration of waste impacts in CIB in the future.
- Action plans to reduce resource use and waste:
  - Plastics: Identify highest-consuming suppliers, deploy plans to reduce plastic supply, embed materials criteria in tenders, and raise awareness among specifiers/buyers.
  - Paper/cardboard: Map waste origins across activities, add dedicated procurement criteria, and raise awareness of alternatives.
  - Electrical/electronic equipment (IT): Review allocation/management policies, optimize allocation processes, and train employees on responsible use.
- End-of-life optimization:
  - Waste management: Assess volumes and types across sites; implement supplier progress plans; favor reuse and recycling while avoiding incineration and landfill; train employees on sorting and recovery.
  - Bank cards: Reduce undelivered cards, organize recovery of non-delivered products, and consider extending card validity to limit renewals.
  - Reuse: Strengthen supplier requirements for WEEE reuse, set up internal/external donation channels, conduct LCAs, and train specifiers on reuse methods.
- Governance and implementation: Actions are consolidated in an annual roadmap shared across entities and adapted to each operational scope. The Sustainability Department leads execution; efforts focus on human-resource prioritization and influencer awareness. No specific budget allocations were attached to these roadmaps.
- Exclusions: No waste management roadmaps exist for the credit and investment portfolio.
- Waste handling: Contracts apply the waste treatment hierarchy, systematically considering reuse before recycling. Most waste is processed by operators committed to 100% recycling (e.g., Recygo, Les Joyeux Recycleurs).

nodes.title: Targets and results related to resource use and the circular economy
nodes.heading: 2.2.5.3 Targets and results related to resource use and the circular economy
nodes.start_phrase: A number of operational targets have been set and are managed annually by the Sustainability Department.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Sustainable performance and environmental information, specifically strengthening the circular economy across La Banque Postale Group.
- Strategy and governance: Establish a Group-wide donation hierarchy and internal/external donation rules to enhance materials circularity; Sustainability Department leads, with quarterly steering committees and annual target reviews; subsidiaries have dedicated quarterly monitoring.
- Stakeholder engagement: Collaboration with institutional actors (e.g., CITEO) to track Extended Producer Responsibility; employee awareness initiatives; supplier engagement via annual reviews and progress plans; internal sustainability experts coordinate actions.
- CNP Assurances integration: Circular economy and resource use embedded in ESG filters for listed equities and bonds, assessing waste and circularity across design/production/use; in real estate, a “Green Works” Charter promotes deconstruction, reuse/recovery, and materials from redeployment channels; management companies handle associated risks case by case.
- 2030 operational targets (base year 2023) for entities under the Resources and Circular Economy policy:
  - Reduce plastic waste by 50% and paper/cardboard waste by 30%.
  - Sort and recover 100% of non-plastic waste on sites, prioritizing recycling.
  - Ensure 100% of plastic waste generated is recyclable, reusable, or compostable.
  - Reduce WEEE volumes by 30% vs. 2021 and keep WEEE recovery rates above 85%.
  - Maintain at least a 50% “second life” rate (one-third reuse, two-thirds redeployment).
  - Apply eco-design to 100% of products put into circulation.
  - Collect 30% of expired bank cards; recover 100% of collected expired cards.
  - Recover 100% of undistributed bank cards (NPL).
- Target-setting process: Developed by the Sustainability Department with Purchasing and Marketing; roadmaps monitored quarterly; annual performance assessment follows data collection.
- Scope notes: Subsidiaries e Zyness, Sofiap, and 115K have no specific targets due to size and limited materiality.
- Portfolio scope: No waste management targets set for the loan and investment portfolio.

nodes.title: Targets
nodes.heading: 2.2.5.3.1 Targets
nodes.start_phrase: A number of operational targets have been set and are managed annually by the Sustainability Department.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale’s Resources and Circular Economy policy within its 2024 Universal Registration Document, covering governance, targets to 2030, eco-design and procurement practices, waste management approach, and performance metrics.
- Governance and engagement:
  - Strengthens circular economy via a shared donation hierarchy and specific internal/external donation rules.
  - Works with institutional actors (e.g., CITEO) to monitor Extended Producer Responsibility and coordinates ecosystem actions.
  - Engages all employees through awareness initiatives; involves suppliers via annual reviews and progress plans.
  - CNP Assurances integrates resource/circular-economy criteria into ESG filters for listed assets and applies a “Green Works” Charter in real estate (deconstruction, reuse/recovery, priority for redeployed materials), with risk management by asset managers.
- Targets to 2030 (base year 2023; set by the Sustainability Department; monitored quarterly; annual assessments):
  - Reduce plastic waste by 50% and paper/cardboard by 30%.
  - Sort and recover 100% of site-generated waste (excluding plastic), prioritizing recycling.
  - Ensure 100% of plastic waste is recyclable, reusable, or compostable.
  - Reduce WEEE by 30% vs 2021 and maintain recovery rates above 85%.
  - Achieve a minimum 50% “second life” rate (one-third reuse, two-thirds redeployment).
  - Apply eco-design to 100% of products put into circulation.
  - Collect 30% of expired bank cards; recover 100% of expired and 100% of undistributed cards.
  - Note: No waste-management targets for loan and investment portfolios.
- Eco-design and procurement:
  - All offers/services pass an internal ESG project grid assessing resource use and waste.
  - Purchasing embeds circularity, especially for IT: repairability indices, spare parts availability, take-back of replaced/EOL equipment, and robust redeployment/recycling/destruction channels.
- Waste management approach:
  - Prioritizes reduction at source and follows the European waste hierarchy (recycling, then material recovery, then energy recovery).
  - Voluntary, mission-driven policy exceeding regulatory requirements.
- Key metrics and results:
  - Total waste generated: 1,435 tonnes.
  - Waste diverted from disposal: 1,325 tonnes; waste sent for disposal: 110 tonnes.
  - Non-recycled waste: 253 tonnes (17.6% of total).
  - WEEE: 575 tonnes; classified as hazardous waste under EU Directive 2008/98/EC. No radioactive waste.
  - 36 tonnes of electrical/electronic equipment reused.
  - Main streams: office paper; WEEE (batteries, bulbs, phones, computers), containing rare metals, aluminum, plastics.
- Reporting:
  - Centralized by DEC teams using service-provider data; estimates used for some multi-tenant sites based on employee counts.
- Additional:
  - Targets mapped to circular economy levers (eco-design, circular material use, minimization of primary raw materials, sustainable sourcing, waste management).

nodes.title: Metrics
nodes.heading: 2.2.5.3.2 Metrics
nodes.start_phrase: The waste generated mainly covers three specific streams: paper/cardboard, WEEE (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) and non-hazardous industrial waste, in connection with the bancassurance activities of our various entities.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Environmental information). References a glossary of CSR terms (p. 808).

- Waste management scope and priorities:
  - Main waste streams: paper/cardboard, WEEE (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment), and non-hazardous industrial waste linked to bancassurance activities.
  - Priority on reuse and recycling, especially for paper, cardboard, and glass.
  - Non-recycled waste (including reuse and energy recovery where recycling is unavailable or constrained by contracts) represents 17.6% of total waste.

- WEEE specifics and circular practices:
  - La Banque Postale mainly generates paper and WEEE; WEEE includes batteries, light bulbs, telephones, and IT equipment (computers, printers, cartridges) containing rare metals, aluminum, and plastics.
  - All WEEE is treated as hazardous waste per Directive 2008/98/EC Annex III; all hazardous waste at the bank is WEEE; no radioactive waste produced.
  - 36 tonnes of electrical and electronic equipment were reused.
  - A Resources footprint study (La Poste Group scope) will provide an exhaustive material composition of WEEE.

- Governance and reporting methodology:
  - Waste data reporting and circular economy implementation are centralized by DEC teams for La Banque Postale and subsidiaries.
  - Data based on service providers’ feedback; where unavailable (e.g., multi-occupant sites where the bank is a minority), estimates are used based on total volumes and headcount.

- Quantitative waste metrics (tonnes):
  - Total waste generated: 1,435.
  - Waste diverted from disposal: 1,325.
    - Hazardous waste diverted: preparation for reuse 1; recycling 471; other recovery 0.
    - Non-hazardous waste diverted: preparation for reuse 0; recycling 711; other recovery 142.
  - Waste for disposal: 110.
    - Hazardous waste for disposal: incineration 72; landfill 17; other disposal 13.
    - Non-hazardous waste for disposal: incineration 0.005; landfill 8; other 0.
  - Non-recycled waste: 253 (17.6%).
  - Total WEEE (entity-specific): 575.
  - Total hazardous waste: 575; radioactive waste: 0.

- European Green Taxonomy (EUTax) background and implementation:
  - Regulation (EU) 2020/852 defines sustainable activities via substantial contribution criteria to at least one environmental objective, DNSH to the others, and Minimum Social Safeguards.
  - Six objectives: climate change mitigation; climate change adaptation; sustainable use/protection of water and marine resources; transition to a circular economy; pollution prevention and control; protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.
  - Article 8 requires disclosure of how activities align with environmentally sustainable economic activities.
  - Technical criteria set by Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139 (climate objectives) and 2023/2486 (other four objectives).
  - Integration into the bank’s business model: green loan and green bond frameworks reviewed; front-office equipped to help customers meet green criteria.
  - Reporting scope and roadmap: alignment published for the first two objectives; remaining four considered non-material for current portfolios—analysis to be pursued next year subject to data availability.
  - Acknowledges uncertainties in interpretation and data gaps; future publications will refine disclosures.
  - Notes EC FAQ published on 8 Nov 2024; timing prevented incorporation this year; process under review to integrate at next reporting date.

nodes.title: Background and regulatory requirements of the European Green Taxonomy
nodes.heading: 2.2.6.1 Background and regulatory requirements of the European Green Taxonomy
nodes.start_phrase: The European Green Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852 dated 18 June 2020 defines sustainable economic activities by establishing substantial contribution technical criteria (CCS), for at least one of the environmental and Do No Significant Harm (DNSH) targets and five other targets.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: La Banque Postale’s Universal Registration Document outlines how the European Green Taxonomy applies to the Bank’s activities, focusing on environmental information and sustainable performance.
- EU Green Taxonomy framework: Explains Regulation (EU) 2020/852, defining sustainable activities through substantial contribution criteria, Do No Significant Harm (DNSH), and Minimum Social Safeguards (MSS). Notes Article 8 disclosure obligations and the technical screening criteria set by Delegated Regulations 2021/2139 (climate objectives) and 2023/2486 (the other four environmental objectives). Lists the six environmental objectives (climate mitigation, climate adaptation, water/marine, circular economy, pollution prevention, biodiversity/ecosystems).
- Implementation at the Bank: Integration of the Taxonomy into the business model, including updates to green loan and green bond frameworks and front-office enablement to help clients meet green criteria.
- Reporting perimeter and timing: The Bank currently discloses eligibility/alignment for the first two objectives (climate mitigation and adaptation). It deems the remaining four objectives non-material for current portfolios but plans best-efforts analysis from next year. Acknowledges interpretation and data limitations; cites the EC FAQ of 8 Nov 2024 that could not be incorporated this cycle and will be addressed in future reporting.
- Green Asset Ratio (GAR) methodology:
  - Definition: GAR measures the share of Taxonomy-aligned assets in total assets; key KPI under the Taxonomy.
  - Denominator (covered assets): Total assets minus sovereign, central bank, supranational exposures, and trading book.
  - Numerator scope: Applies technical criteria to selected products/counterparties; excludes certain items only from the numerator (e.g., companies not subject to the NFRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank loans), ensuring eligibility/alignment ratios are inherently below 100%.
  - Eligibility boundaries: Only activities with defined technical criteria are eligible; some sectors (e.g., farming) are currently out of scope.
  - Alignment rules: Specialized/project financing that meets criteria is treated as aligned; general-purpose loans rely on counterparties’ published alignment ratios. Each asset can align to only one environmental objective to avoid double counting.
  - Stepwise calculation flow: Total assets → covered assets (after exclusions) → assets analyzed for eligibility → Taxonomy-eligible assets (after removing non-eligible portions) → Taxonomy-aligned assets (after removing non-aligned portions), based on project- or counterparty-level indicators.
- Disclosures: Results of the analyses and required qualitative information are provided, with a commitment to refine future publications as data quality and regulatory guidance improve.

nodes.title: Alignment analysis principles
nodes.heading: 2.2.6.2 Alignment analysis principles
nodes.start_phrase: The GAR is the ratio of Green Taxonomy-aligned assets to total assets, and is the Taxonomy’s key performance indicator.
nodes.summary:
- Source and context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Environmental information) detailing EU Green Taxonomy alignment analysis and Green Asset Ratio (GAR) methodology and results.
- GAR definition and purpose: GAR measures the share of total assets aligned with the EU Green Taxonomy; it is the Taxonomy’s key KPI identifying investments in sustainable economic activities.
- Scope and calculation principles:
  - Denominator (covered assets): Total assets excluding exposures to sovereigns, central banks, supranationals, and the trading book.
  - Numerator: Assets meeting Taxonomy technical screening criteria among selected products/counterparties.
  - Scope differences: Certain exposures (e.g., companies not subject to NFRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank loans, some interbank loans) are excluded from the numerator or from eligibility analysis, ensuring eligible/aligned ratios are always below 100% (e.g., an SME wind farm loan cannot enter the numerator if the SME is outside NFRD scope).
  - Eligibility constraints: Only activities with specified technical criteria can be assessed; some (e.g., farming) are not yet Taxonomy-eligible.
  - Alignment rules: Specialized (project) financing aligned when it meets criteria; general purpose financing included based on counterparties’ published alignment ratios; each asset is aligned to only one environmental objective to avoid double counting.
- Process flow: Total assets → Covered assets → Assets analyzed for eligibility → Taxonomy‑eligible assets → Taxonomy‑aligned assets.
- Four-stage Taxonomy assessment:
  1) Eligibility (activity listed in the Taxonomy),
  2) Substantial contribution (to one of six environmental objectives),
  3) DNSH (no significant harm to the other five objectives),
  4) MSS (minimum social safeguards).
- Mandatory vs voluntary GAR:
  - Mandatory GAR: Asset-by-asset assessment without estimates, per regulation.
  - Voluntary GAR: Supplementary indicator with estimates and a slightly broader scope; includes special purpose SME green loans excluded from mandatory GAR; complemented by Pillar III ESG Table 10 on green products not in GAR.
- Portfolio-specific application principles:
  - Households – Real estate:
    - Mandatory: Uses actual energy use data and a physical risk model aligned with Pillar III ESG (for DNSH); MSS presumed met for French financing.
    - Voluntary: Uses estimated energy use from external data provider with the same risk model; MSS presumed met.
  - Other household loans (e.g., motor vehicles, home renovation): Included in eligibility per regulations where applicable, but generally excluded from alignment if treated as general purpose financing.
  - Corporates:
    - Special purpose financing: Mandatory uses actual client data; voluntary may use estimates or partial analysis (e.g., only substantial contribution).
    - General purpose financing: Mandatory collects alignment ratios published by NFRD-reporting counterparties.
- Methodology governance: Despite unresolved interpretive issues in the texts, the Bank developed an internal reference framework to operationalize the Taxonomy’s technical screening criteria.
- Reported outcome: As of 31 December 2024, the regulatory GAR is 5.7% (€10.3bn) based on turnover, mainly from energy‑efficient household real estate financing aligned with climate change mitigation; includes some general purpose financing where counterparties publish alignment indicators; level is stable versus 5.5% (31 Dec 2023) and 5.9% (30 Jun 2024).

nodes.title: Alignment indicators
nodes.heading: 2.2.6.3 Alignment indicators
nodes.start_phrase: At 31 December 2024, the Bank’s regulatory green asset ratio was 5.7% (€10.3 billion) based on turnover.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Environmental information on La Banque Postale’s Green Asset Ratio (GAR) and EU Taxonomy alignment within the 2024 Universal Registration Document, including methodology, portfolio treatment rules, key indicators, results, data limitations, and reporting format.
- Taxonomy methodology:
  - Four-stage analysis: eligibility; substantial contribution to environmental objectives; Do No Significant Harm (DNSH); Minimum Social Safeguards (MSS).
  - Bank-developed reference framework to operationalize technical screening criteria, addressing unresolved methodological interpretations.
- Mandatory vs. voluntary GAR:
  - Mandatory GAR: asset-by-asset assessment without estimates; includes general purpose lending when counterparties publish alignment ratios (per regulation).
  - Voluntary GAR: broader scope using estimates; includes certain SME special purpose green loans excluded from the mandatory GAR because SMEs are outside NFRD scope; supplemented by Pillar III ESG Table 10 for green products not in GAR.
- Portfolio-based alignment principles:
  - Households (real estate): mandatory uses actual energy use and a physical risk model aligned with Pillar III ESG; MSS presumed met in France. Voluntary uses estimated energy data with the same DNSH model and MSS presumption.
  - Other retail (vehicle loans since 1 Jan 2022, home renovation): eligible base per regulation but excluded from alignment calculations as general purpose financing.
  - Corporates:
    - Special purpose financing: mandatory uses customer’s actual data; voluntary may use estimates (e.g., energy performance diagnostics) or partial substantial contribution-only analysis.
    - General purpose financing: relies on alignment ratios published by NFRD counterparties.
- Key 2024 alignment indicators (as of 31 Dec 2024):
  - Regulatory GAR: 5.7% (€10.3bn) based on turnover, mainly household real estate aligned to climate change mitigation. Stable vs. 5.5% (Dec 2023) and 5.9% (June 2024).
  - Voluntary GAR: 8.0% (€14.2bn), of which 2.3% is the voluntary component.
  - Off-balance sheet: 0.0% for financial guarantees; 3.0% for assets under management at LBP AM.
  - Additional KPIs: a flow GAR figure is provided (1.7%; value shown as 679 in the template), plus template-based disclosures on KPI coverage and assets excluded from GAR numerator/denominator.
  - Trading book and fee/commission KPIs only apply from 2026.
- Data constraints and improvements:
  - GAR reflects limited availability of reliable alignment data for existing portfolios (notably technical reserves), unlike new production where data are obtained at origination.
  - Ongoing enhancement of data collection, prioritizing real estate, asset financing, and project finance; coordinated with broader ESG initiatives (Impact Weighting Factor, low-carbon pathway, Equator Principles).
- Reporting and templates:
  - Disclosures follow Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178; exposures shown twice using counterparties’ turnover and then CapEx alignment ratios; other exposures treated consistently.
  - To avoid redundancy, overlapping Green Taxonomy and Pillar III ESG tables (6, 7, 8) are published once using the Green Taxonomy format.
  - Insurance and asset management Taxonomy metrics are detailed separately (Section 2.5.1.7); glossary references provided for CSR terms.

nodes.title: Alignment indicators - Introduction
nodes.heading: 2.2.6.3 Alignment indicators

nodes.title: Summary of key performance indicators
nodes.heading: 2.2.6.3.1 Summary of key performance indicators
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents the main key performance indicators (KPIs), as calculated using the information reported in the Taxonomy tables presented in Section 6.8.9.3. “Alignment indicators”.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on sustainable performance reporting in La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, covering environmental (EU Taxonomy) and social (workforce) disclosures.
- Environmental information:
  - Green Asset Ratio (GAR) reflects limited reliable data for Taxonomy alignment on existing technical reserves; data is available for new production at issuance.

- Social information:
  - Scope covers La Banque Postale Group (banking, insurance, asset management). Many distribution employees are La Poste SA staff working “for and on behalf of” La Banque Postale and are treated as value chain workers, with HR management by La Poste SA.

nodes.title: Scope taken into account
nodes.heading: 2.3.1.1.1 Scope taken into account
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale, a subsidiary of La Poste Group, is structured around a multi-business line organisation, which includes banking, insurance and asset management functions.
nodes.summary:
- Document context: Social information section of La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, focusing on guaranteeing favourable working conditions for employees.
- Scope: Covers La Banque Postale Group (SA and subsidiaries). Many front-line distribution roles are performed by La Poste SA staff; these “value chain workers” are outside the Group’s headcount and are addressed separately, with HR risks managed by La Poste SA.
- Double materiality IROs for the Group’s workforce:
  - Negative impacts: harmful working conditions affecting physical/mental health (stress, burnout, MSDs); discrimination/inequality/harassment; potential deterioration in pay, employment levels or contract types reducing purchasing power; non-compliance with work-related rights under EU regulations.
  - Positive impacts: initiatives on inclusion, protection, equal opportunities, skills and career development; favourable working conditions (hours, social dialogue, fair pay, social protection, collective agreements).
- Risk and opportunity profile:
  - Risks: potential failure in employment, health and safety, diversity and inclusion practices; heightened vigilance on diversity, inclusion and equal pay due to bancassurance model.
  - Opportunities: workforce upskilling driving innovation and new products/services; mission-led company model supports employment, diversity and inclusion goals.
- Strategy and governance:
  - Emphasis on the employee experience, diversity and inclusion, strong social dialogue.
  - 2025–2030 strategic plan targets cultural transformation and a new managerial culture focused on efficiency and employee well-being.
- Climate aspect: No specific employee adaptation risk identified; a 2025 transition plan includes cross-business projects and training for 2025–2029.

nodes.title: Note on La Poste employees working for and on behalf of La Banque Postale
nodes.heading: Note on La Poste employees working for and on behalf of La Banque Postale
nodes.start_phrase: To develop its distribution activities, La Banque Postale relies on a network located in post offices and in remote customer relations centres (retail customers), and lastly on its business centres (professional customers).
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Social information on guaranteeing favorable working conditions for all employees within La Banque Postale Group (LBP), part of a multi-business bancassurance organization (banking, insurance, asset management).
- Scope: Workforce covered is LBP SA and its subsidiaries. A large portion of distribution activity is performed by La Poste SA employees (retail and business centers), classified as “value chain workers,” not part of LBP’s own workforce; their HR management and risk prevention are handled by La Poste SA. Details provided separately in Section 2.3.2.1.
- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) from a double materiality analysis:
  - Negative impacts: harmful working conditions affecting physical/mental health (stress, burnout, MSDs); discrimination, inequality, harassment; potential deterioration in remuneration, job levels or contract types reducing purchasing power; non-compliance with work-related rights.
  - Positive impacts: actions supporting inclusion, protection, equal opportunity, skills and career development; favorable working conditions (working hours, social dialogue, fair pay, social protection, collective agreements).
- Sector-specific emphasis: Given bancassurance exposure, strict monitoring of inclusion, diversity, and equal remuneration. “Employee experience” is a strategic priority, aiming for strong working conditions, diversity and inclusion, and robust social dialogue.
- Risks and opportunities:
  - Risks: potential failure in employment, health and safety, diversity and inclusion practices; H&S risks seen as limited; higher risk around D&I, including wage inequality and discrimination.
  - Opportunities: upskilling employees to drive innovation and new product/service development; leveraging the mission-led company model and the 2025–2030 strategic plan to strengthen employment, D&I, and cultural transformation, including a project to evolve managerial culture toward efficiency and employee well-being.
- Climate aspect: No climate adaptation risk identified for employees; a 2025 transition plan includes projects and training across banking lines from 2025–2029 (referenced in Section 2.2.1).

nodes.title: IRO relating to the Group’s workforce
nodes.heading: 2.3.1.1.2 IRO relating to the Group’s workforce
nodes.start_phrase: Various positive and negative impacts, as well as risks and opportunities, relating to the Group’s workforce were identified during the double materiality analysis.
nodes.summary:

- Scope: Reporting covers LBP SA and its subsidiaries. La Poste SA employees who work for and on behalf of LBP are not part of LBP’s own workforce; they are treated as “value chain workers” and covered elsewhere.
- Material IROs: Results of a double materiality analysis identifying workforce-related impacts, risks and opportunities.
- Negative impacts identified: harmful working conditions affecting physical/mental health (stress, burnout, MSDs); discrimination, inequality or harassment; potential deterioration in pay, jobs or contract types affecting purchasing power; non-compliance with EU work-related rights.
- Positive impacts identified: actions promoting inclusion, protection, equal opportunities, skills and career development; favourable working conditions (working hours, social dialogue, fair remuneration, social protection, collective agreements).
- Governance focus: Strong monitoring of inclusion, diversity and equal pay; “employee experience” is a strategic priority supported by a culture of social dialogue.
- Risks and opportunities: Risk of shortcomings in employment, health and safety, and diversity/inclusion practices; opportunity to develop employee skills that drive innovation and new products/services. Health and safety risks are limited for bancassurance, but D&I and pay inequality/discrimination risks require attention.
- Strategy: Mission-led company model seen as an opportunity for employment, diversity and inclusion; embedded in the 2025–2030 strategic plan aimed at cultural transformation and a new managerial culture focused on efficiency and well-being.
- Climate dimension: No specific climate adaptation risks identified for employees; a 2025 transition plan includes cross-business projects and training from 2025 to 2029.

nodes.title: Scope taken into account

nodes.summary:
- Focus of the section: ensuring favorable working conditions for all La Banque Postale Group employees within its multi-business bancassurance model.
- Scope: covers La Banque Postale SA and subsidiaries; La Poste SA staff working for and on behalf of La Banque Postale are treated as value chain workers, with their HR management overseen by La Poste and detailed elsewhere in the report.
- Double materiality results—negative impacts: risks to physical/mental health (stress, burnout, musculoskeletal disorders), discrimination/inequality/harassment, potential deterioration in pay/jobs/contracts affecting purchasing power, and potential non-compliance with work-related rights.
- Double materiality results—positive impacts: initiatives on inclusion, protection, equal opportunity, skills and career development; favorable working conditions (working hours, social dialogue, fair pay, social protection, collective agreements).
- Governance and monitoring: heightened oversight of inclusion, diversity, and equal remuneration due to bancassurance exposure; “employee experience” is a strategic priority backed by strong social dialogue.
- Risks and opportunities: HR risk from failures in employment, health and safety, diversity, and inclusion practices; opportunities from employee upskilling driving innovation and new offerings. Health and safety risks are limited; diversity and inclusion risks (e.g., pay gaps, discrimination) are more material.
- Strategic alignment: mission-led company model and the 2025–2030 strategic plan support employment, diversity, inclusion, and cultural transformation, including a program to foster a managerial culture focused on efficiency and employee well-being.
- Climate dimension: no employee-related adaptation risk identified; a transition plan (published in 2025) includes cross-business projects and training from 2025 to 2029, with further detail provided in the climate change section.

nodes.title: IRO relating to the Group’s workforce
nodes.heading: 2.3.1.1.2 IRO relating to the Group’s workforce
nodes.start_phrase: Various positive and negative impacts, as well as risks and opportunities, relating to the Group’s workforce were identified during the double materiality analysis.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and organization: La Banque Postale (LBP) Group—covering LBP SA and subsidiaries across banking, insurance, and asset management—is the perimeter for social reporting. Many frontline distribution roles are performed by La Poste SA employees, treated as “value chain workers” and addressed separately.
- Value chain workers: La Poste SA staff working on behalf of LBP are managed under La Poste’s HR strategy; their impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) are integrated there.
- Double materiality IROs for LBP’s own workforce: 
  - Negative impacts: risks to physical/mental health (stress, burnout, MSDs); discrimination/inequality/harassment; potential deterioration of pay, jobs, or contracts affecting purchasing power; non-compliance with work-related rights.
  - Positive impacts: inclusion, protection, equal opportunities; skills and career development; favourable working conditions (hours, social dialogue, fair pay, social protection, collective agreements).
- Risk and opportunity profile: Limited health and safety risks typical of bancassurance; higher focus on diversity, inclusion, and equal pay to prevent discrimination and wage gaps. Strategic emphasis on employee experience, strong social dialogue, and a cultural transformation (2025–2030) to build a managerial culture centered on efficiency and well-being. Skills development seen as a lever for innovation.
- Climate dimension: No specific employee climate-adaptation risk identified; 2025 transition plan includes cross-business projects and training through 2029.
- Forced and child labor: Assessed as not at risk; adherence to international labor standards; 88% of workforce in France/Europe where such risks are tightly regulated.
- Vulnerable groups: While job roles do not create higher H&S risk, older employees, ethnic minorities, and people with disabilities may face higher exposure to discrimination risks.
- Policy framework (covers permanent and fixed-term staff within LBP’s Economic and Social Unit and Group/subsidiaries):
  - Quality of Work Life and Working Conditions: comprehensive QWLWC and occupational risk prevention.
  - Diversity and Inclusion: disability, intergenerational diversity, gender parity, LGBT+ inclusion, social and ethnic inclusion; dedicated disability policy; anti-sexism/discrimination/harassment measures.
  - Health & Safety Prevention: risk assessments, accident analyses, workstation adjustments, traffic risk awareness, annual prevention plan.
  - Remuneration: fairness and equal pay (notably gender), recognition of performance, support for professional development.
  - Employee Experience: career progression, daily work-life improvements, commitment to a just transition.
  - Social Dialogue: strong framework for employee representation and consideration of employee interests.
  - Training: skills development aligned with the Group’s strategic plan.

- Training: skills development aligned with the Group’s Strategic Plan.

nodes.title: Employee policies

nodes.summary:
- Focus: Social information from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, detailing employee-related CSR risks, impacts, and policies.

nodes.heading: 2.3.1.2.1 Policies regarding quality of life and working conditions
