LBP’s HR Director (Executive Committee member) leads the interface with La Poste. Effectiveness of dialogue assessed via engagement survey outcomes, which inform operational management.
- Reporting and remediation: Concerns can be raised via the engagement survey, annual appraisals, direct manager dialogue (when managed by LBP), and the Group whistleblowing system (independent, accessible platform, managed by Compliance, with whistleblower protections). LBP HR accesses survey and appraisal results to monitor issues and act as needed. No significant negative impacts identified; remediation would follow due diligence if they occur.
- Actions and 2024 initiatives: Regular HR coordination between LBP and La Poste; joint work on variable remuneration and workforce matters; a co-led monitoring committee addressing workplace “niggling” issues; evolution of employee representative bodies with social dialogue overseen by LBP HR within La Poste’s rules. Effectiveness tracked through engagement survey results.

nodes.title: Dialogue mechanisms
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.1.3 Dialogue mechanisms
nodes.start_phrase: The point of view of La Poste employees working for and on behalf of La Banque Postale is important for La Banque Postale in order to ensure the smooth running of these activities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Social information on workers employed by La Poste but working for and on behalf of La Banque Postale (LBP), within LBP’s CSR framework.
- Dialogue mechanisms: use of La Poste Group’s engagement survey and annual appraisals/professional interviews to capture expectations and concerns; information also flows via La Poste’s social bodies; both entities respect legal obligations on social dialogue.
- Governance/interface: the Human Resources Director of LBP Group (Executive Committee member) is the most senior point of contact with La Poste on these workforce issues.
- Effectiveness monitoring: dialogue effectiveness is assessed indirectly through results of the annual engagement survey, which inform operational management actions.
- Reporting channels: workers can raise concerns through the engagement survey, mandatory annual appraisals, and direct dialogue with LBP managers when applicable.
- Data access and follow-up: LBP’s HR Department accesses survey and appraisal results to monitor significant issues and implement measures as needed.
- Whistleblowing: a Group-wide, independent, confidential platform managed by the Compliance Department is available to all employees; communicated via the code of conduct and protects whistleblowers.
- Impacts and remediation: no significant negative impacts identified to date; therefore no specific remediation effectiveness procedure yet, but due diligence would apply if needed.
- Material risk identified: potential negative impacts linked to poor working conditions (including unequal pay and safety), and forced or child labor in the value chain related to own operations and services.
- Action plans (2024): joint HR work with La Poste on variable remuneration and workforce issues; a co-led monitoring committee addressing workplace “niggling issues”; adjustments to employee representative bodies with social dialogue managed by LBP HR under La Poste’s rules.
- Evaluation of actions: effectiveness measured via engagement survey outcomes.

nodes.title: Reporting and remediation process
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.1.4 Reporting and remediation process
nodes.start_phrase: As mentioned in Section 2.3.2.1.3 “Dialogue mechanisms”, workers can raise their concerns via:
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Practices related to workers employed by La Poste but working for and on behalf of La Banque Postale (LBP), within LBP’s CSR/Sustainability reporting.
- Dialogue mechanisms: Employee voice captured mainly via La Poste Group’s engagement survey and mandatory annual appraisals; if the manager is from LBP, assessments still follow La Poste rules and tools. LBP is informed of concerns raised by La Poste’s social bodies. The most senior interface with La Poste on these issues is LBP’s Group HR Director, a member of the Executive Committee. Effectiveness of dialogue is assessed indirectly through engagement survey results and integrated into operational management when needed.
- Reporting and remediation: Workers can raise concerns through the engagement survey, annual appraisals, or directly via managers. LBP’s HR has access to survey and appraisal results to monitor significant issues and take action. Significant negative impacts can also be reported through a Group whistleblowing platform managed by the Compliance Department; it is accessible to all employees, publicized via the code of conduct, independent, and protects whistleblowers. No significant negative impacts have been identified to date; if they occur, they will be handled with due diligence.
- Action plans and resources: A key potential material risk identified is poor working conditions (including unequal pay and safety), and forced and/or child labor in the value chain for own operations and services. LBP’s HR works with La Poste’s HR in regular meetings to design and implement actions based on issues surfaced through the dialogue channels, at both operational and management committee levels.
- 2024 actions: Joint work on variable remuneration and workforce topics; a co-led monitoring committee to address workplace “niggling issues” and define corrective actions; changes to employee representative bodies with social dialogue for workers acting for LBP (Financial Services) managed by LBP HR under La Poste’s social dialogue rules.
- Monitoring effectiveness: Measured primarily via engagement survey outcomes.

nodes.title: Action plans and resources
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.1.5 Action plans and resources
nodes.start_phrase: The following negative impact is considered material for workers working for and on behalf of La Banque Postale: "negative impact of poor working conditions (unequal remuneration, safety, etc.), forced labour and/or child labour in companies in the value chain for own operations and service activities."
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Social information) focusing on La Poste employees who work for and on behalf of La Banque Postale (LBP).

- Dialogue mechanisms:
  - Employee voice captured primarily via La Poste Group’s engagement survey and annual appraisals conducted under La Poste rules.
  - Social bodies’ concerns shared with LBP; both entities comply with legal requirements for social dialogue.
  - The LBP Group HR Director (Executive Committee member) is the senior interface with La Poste.
  - Effectiveness of dialogue assessed indirectly through engagement survey results and integrated into operational management.

- Reporting and remediation:
  - Concerns can be raised via the engagement survey, annual appraisals, and direct dialogue with LBP managers where applicable.
  - LBP HR accesses survey and appraisal outcomes to monitor significant issues and take action.
  - A Group whistleblowing system (managed by Compliance, accessible via a dedicated platform, independent, with whistleblower protection) is available to all employees and promoted through the code of conduct.
  - No significant negative impacts identified to date; no specific remedial verification procedure in place but due diligence would be applied if needed.

- Action plans and resources:
  - Material potential risk identified: adverse working conditions (e.g., unequal pay, safety), forced or child labor in the value chain for operations/services.
  - Actions developed jointly by LBP HR and La Poste HR through regular meetings and governance forums.
  - 2024 actions:
    - Joint work and decisions on variable remuneration and workforce issues.
    - A co-led monitoring committee to address recurring workplace issues and define corrective actions.
    - Adjustments to employee representative bodies, with LBP HR managing social dialogue for affected workers within La Poste’s rules.
  - Effectiveness measured via engagement survey outcomes.
  - Resources include dedicated interface functions with La Poste, management actions for affected workers, and costs related to survey analysis and action plans.
  - No severe human rights incidents reported.

- Targets:
  - No specific LBP targets for these workers; potential impacts are managed by La Poste as LBP’s parent company, making LBP not directly responsible for target-setting on this topic.

- Workforce characteristics and methodology:
  - La Poste employees working for LBP support the Banking Advice Line (in post offices), remote Customer Relations Centres, and IT/other head office support.
  - La Poste pursues an active gender equality policy aligned with LBP’s.
  - All relevant employees are based in France; only male/female genders recognized under French law.
  - Workforce counted as active headcount at 31 Dec 2024; calculation methods align with those used for LBP’s own employees.
  - Costs for these services are invoiced between entities and recognized under “External services” in LBP Group’s consolidated statements.

- 2024 workforce figures (La Poste workers for LBP):
  - Total: 19,382
  - Women: 11,854 (9,106 full-time; 2,748 part-time)
  - Men: 7,528 (6,247 full-time; 1,281 part-time)

nodes.title: Targets
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.1.6 Targets
nodes.start_phrase: No specific target has been set for employees working in the name and on behalf of La Banque Postale.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Social information), referencing a glossary of CSR terms (p. 808).
- Resources allocated to managing potential negative social impacts: dedicated functions interfacing with La Poste; managerial oversight for employees working for/on behalf of La Banque Postale; expenses for the employee engagement survey and related action plans.
- Human rights: No severe human rights incidents reported for employees working for and on behalf of La Banque Postale.
- Targets: No specific targets set by La Banque Postale for these workers; potential impacts are managed by the parent company, La Poste, so La Banque Postale is not directly responsible.
- Workforce covered: La Poste employees working in the name and on behalf of La Banque Postale support Banking Advice Lines in post offices, remote Customer Relations Centres, IT teams, and other head-office support; they are essential to banking services. La Poste pursues a gender equality policy aligned with La Banque Postale’s.
- Methodology and accounting: All Financial Services and Banking Advice Line employees are located in France; genders reported as male/female per French law; workforce is the headcount of active employees as of 31 Dec 2024; calculation methods align with the Group’s workforce indicators. Costs for these services are invoiced between La Banque Postale and La Poste and recorded as “External services” in the consolidated income statement (Note 7.3, Section 5.2).
- 2024 key figures (La Poste workers serving La Banque Postale, all in France; total 19,382):
  - By gender: 11,854 women; 7,528 men.
  - By work pattern: Full-time 15,353 (9,106 women; 6,247 men); Part-time 4,029 (2,748 women; 1,281 men).

nodes.title: Additional indicators specific to the entity
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.1.7 Additional indicators specific to the entity
nodes.start_phrase: La Poste employees working for and on behalf of La Banque Postale work for:
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Social information on workers employed by La Poste but working “for and on behalf of” La Banque Postale (LBP), plus oversight of workers in the upstream value chain.
- Governance and resources:
  - Potential negative impact management handled via: dedicated functions interfacing with La Poste, managerial oversight for these workers, and engagement survey analysis/action plans.
  - No specific LBP targets for these workers; impacts are managed by La Poste (LBP not directly responsible).
- Workforce scope and characteristics:
  - 19,382 La Poste workers dedicated to LBP, all located in France, across Banking Advice Line (post offices), remote Customer Relations Centres, IT and head-office support.
  - Gender split reported as 11,854 women and 7,528 men (only male/female recognized in France).
  - Data and methods aligned with LBP Group workforce indicators; related costs invoiced between entities and booked as “External services.”
  - La Poste pursues an active gender equality policy consistent with LBP’s.
- Collective bargaining and social dialogue:
  - 75.8% covered by collective agreements (La Poste–France Télécom agreement for permanent, fixed-term, and work-study contracts).
  - 24.2% are civil servants, represented under La Poste’s social dialogue framework (appear as not covered by collective agreements in the chart).
- Training, careers, and performance:
  - Skills development supported through École de la Banque et du Réseau and La Poste Group training catalog.
  - Targeted onboarding for La Poste banking advisors on marketing green offers.
  - High take-up of annual performance/career reviews (about 97.7% overall; women 98%, men 97.3%).
  - Average training hours per worker: total 49.9 (women 49.4; men 50.8).
- Health, safety, and work-life balance:
  - Dual responsibility: La Poste as employer; LBP as host when workers are on LBP sites, governed by an agreement between entities.
  - 100% covered by a health and safety policy.
  - 100% eligible for family leave; uptake reported at 5.7% overall (women 6.7%, men 4.0%).
- Human rights, discrimination, and grievances:
  - No severe human rights issues reported for these workers; no related fines or penalties.
  - 29 incidents of discrimination/harassment recorded; 10 complaints received through LBP channels; no national contact point complaints; zero fines, penalties, or compensation.
  - La Poste Group (including LBP) complies with a Human Rights Policy and maintains specific anti-discrimination agreements; note that additional complaints may be filed via La Poste channels (not included in LBP’s breakdown).
- Upstream value chain workers (scope and risk management):
  - Covers non-LBP workforce present on LBP sites and supplier workers.
  - Risk differentiation by sector: building/maintenance/logistics more exposed to safety risks; consulting more to mental workload; vulnerable groups (older workers, people with disabilities, ethnic minorities) recognized as more exposed to discrimination/inequality.
  - ESG risk ratings applied to suppliers to identify specific working conditions and tailor prevention/due diligence.
  - Risks vary by geography, segment, and contract (notably for CNP Assurances); mitigations include contractual clauses, targeted audits, and a whistleblowing system.
  - Impacts identified: positive (improving working conditions, protection, inclusion) and potential negative (poor conditions, unequal pay, safety issues, forced/child labor).
  - Responsible purchasing strategy supports improved conditions and contributes to LBP’s mission-led commitments and SDGs monitoring; no severe human rights incidents or related fines reported for La Poste workers.

nodes.title: Material IROs and links with strategy and business model
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.2.1 Material IROs and links with strategy and business model
nodes.start_phrase: Workers in the upstream value chain are key stakeholders for La Banque Postale.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and stakeholders: Focus on workers in the upstream value chain—non-payroll workers on La Banque Postale sites and supplier employees; downstream workers covered elsewhere.
- Risk exposure: Higher exposure in building, maintenance, and logistics; vulnerable groups (older workers, people with disabilities, ethnic minorities) face greater risks of discrimination and inequality.
- Supplier ESG assessment: ESG risk rating differentiates by activity (e.g., consulting vs. maintenance) and considers geography, business segment, and contract type to tailor prevention and due diligence.
- Mitigation tools: Contractual clauses, targeted audits, and a whistleblowing system to address social and safety risks, especially in sensitive regions.
- Impacts identified:
  - Positive: Responsible purchasing strategy improves working conditions and inclusion; aligns with mission-led status (since 2022) and supports selected SDGs with published indicators.
  - Negative (potential): Poor working conditions (unequal pay, safety lapses), discrimination, forced labour, and child labour within suppliers and subcontractors.
- Performance indicators: Reported zero severe human rights incidents and zero related fines, penalties, or compensation for La Poste workers operating for/on behalf of La Banque Postale.
- Operating context: Significant outsourcing primarily to French/European suppliers, limiting potential negative impacts due to EU labour standards and UN Global Compact alignment.
- Governance and certifications: Adoption of La Poste Group Purchasing Policy; “Responsible Purchasing Approach”; RFAR charter signed in 2022; RFAR certification obtained in 2023 for La Banque Postale SA and CNP Assurances; rollout to banking subsidiaries from 2025; promotion of responsible purchasing culture across the group.
- Material risks: Financial losses from inadequate partner assessment amid social transition and regulatory change; operational/financial impact from termination or slowdown of major suppliers; risks integrated into group risk mapping with emphasis on limiting supplier dependency.
- Forced and child labour: Overall low risk in main operating regions (France/Europe); continued vigilance, notably for CNP Assurances’ activities including Latin America.
- Policies and supplier obligations: Responsible and Ethical Purchasing Charter requires suppliers (and their subcontractors) to:
  - Ensure dignified management and working conditions, prevent psychosocial risks, and safeguard health and safety.
  - Comply with laws on working hours, remuneration, training, and trade union rights.
  - Adhere to the UN Global Compact, ILO core conventions, and ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work.
  - Cascade these requirements across their own supply chains, including in countries not signatory to ILO conventions.

nodes.title: Applicable policies
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.2.2 Applicable policies
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group is actively committed to the workers in its upstream value chain, in order to limit the negative impacts and develop the positive impacts that it may have on this group of people.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale’s responsible purchasing approach and management of social impacts on workers in its upstream value chain within La Poste Group’s CSR framework.
- Positive impacts: Embedding CSR criteria and requiring adherence to the UN Global Compact and ILO conventions improves health, safety, inclusion, and overall working conditions across the value chain.
- Operating model context: A tertiary-sector business largely outsourcing in France/Europe (except CNP Assurances with activities in Europe and Latin America), where forced/child labor risks are generally low; vigilance maintained.
- Governance and alignment: Adoption of La Poste Group’s Responsible Purchasing policy; participation in ObsAR; reference to ISO 20400 responsible purchasing standard.
- Certifications and milestones: Signing of the Supplier Relations and Responsible Purchasing (RFAR) charter in Sept 2022; RFAR certification for La Banque Postale SA and CNP Assurances in Sept 2023; certification rollout to banking subsidiaries from 2025.
- Core policy instruments: La Banque Postale Group’s Responsible and Ethical Purchasing Charter (approved by the Executive Committee), appended to all supplier contracts and managed by the Purchasing Department.
- Supplier obligations under the Charter: Respect human dignity and worker rights; prevent psychosocial risks; ensure safe work; comply with laws on hours, pay, training, and union rights; uphold UNGC and ILO fundamental conventions; extend these principles throughout their own supply chains, including in non‑ILO signatory countries.
- La Poste Group policy pillars: (1) Enforce/promote human rights in supply chains; (2) Reduce environmental impacts of purchases and encourage positives; (3) Promote social inclusion and regional economic/social development via purchasing; (4) Build responsible, ethical supplier relationships.
- Inclusion through purchasing: Seek suppliers engaged in integrating people far from employment; facilitate access to markets for inclusive structures; encourage positive regional inclusion impacts throughout subcontracting chains.
- Supplier assessment and due diligence: Pre‑contract and in‑contract assessments covering financial risk, anti‑corruption (Sapin II), documentary and ESG due diligence (French duty of vigilance); criteria include financial health, supplier dependency, environmental compliance, and human rights risks.
- Processes and tools: A Purchasing Manual (from 2025) detailing organization and multi‑criteria tender assessment to manage risks of financial loss from inadequate partner assessments; procedures and templates available on intranet.
- Identified potential negative impacts on value‑chain workers: Poor implementation of security measures; unequal remuneration (gender and executive pay) at subcontractors; discrimination; forced or child labor.
- Risks and mitigation: Material risks include financial loss from failures in partner assessment amid evolving social expectations/regulation, and disruption from key supplier/distributor failure; supplier dependency addressed via the Purchasing Charter and included in Group risk mapping; risks considered gross if dependency is poorly managed.
- No material opportunities identified related to impacts on value‑chain workers.
- Engagement mechanisms with suppliers: Establishment of a Supplier Relations Mediator (2023); creation of an SME Officer role (2024) to support SMEs; ongoing “supplier listening” with annual interviews, notably in intellectual services.

nodes.title: Commitments to workers in the upstream value chain
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.2.3 Commitments to workers in the upstream value chain
nodes.start_phrase: The relationship between La Banque Postale and its suppliers, who are employers of workers in the value chain, is framed by the Responsible and Ethical Purchasing Charter between La Banque Postale and its suppliers.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale’s responsible purchasing and human rights framework within the La Poste Group’s CSR strategy, governance, tools, and supplier expectations across the value chain in France and internationally.

- Governance and scope:
  - Responsible and Ethical Purchasing Charter appended to all contracts and linked via General Purchasing Conditions; approved by the Executive Committee; implemented and monitored by the Purchasing Department.
  - Alignment with La Poste Group’s Responsible Purchasing policy; active membership in ObsAR; policy published online; documents available on intranet.
  - ISO 20400 definition adopted: maximizing positive environmental, social, and economic impacts over the life cycle.

- Responsible purchasing pillars:
  1) Enforce and promote human rights across supply chains.
  2) Reduce negative environmental impacts and foster positive ones.
  3) Promote social inclusion and regional socio-economic development through purchasing.
  4) Build responsible and ethical supplier relationships.

- Inclusion through purchasing:
  - Preference for suppliers integrating people distant from employment and contributing to vulnerable regions; encouragement to drive inclusion through subcontracting chains; facilitated market access for inclusive structures.

- Supplier risk assessment and tools:
  - Formal supplier assessment pre- and in-contract covering financial risks, anti-corruption (Sapin II), documentary due diligence, and ESG risks.
  - Criteria include financial health, dependency, environmental compliance, and human rights risks.
  - Purchasing Manual (from 2025) standardizes organization, macro-processes, and tender multi-criteria assessment to manage loss and transition risks.
  - Procedures and templates accessible on intranet.

- Commitments to workers in the upstream value chain:
  - Supplier Relations Mediator (2023) to handle disputes, including worker well-being issues.
  - SME Officer (2024) to support SMEs whose workers face higher risks (role being finalized).
  - “Supplier listening” system with annual interviews in intellectual services categories.
  - Confidential whistleblowing website for suppliers and their employees to report serious fundamental rights infringements; suppliers must inform employees and cooperate on investigations.
  - CNP Assurances provides additional concern-raising channels (whistleblowing and mediation).

- Human rights framework and initiatives:
  - La Poste Group Human Rights policy covering operations and value chain; regular social agreements with unions.
  - References to ILO core conventions and UN Global Compact principles.
  - Responsible Purchasing policy validated January 2023; directly supports SDGs 3, 5, 8, and 10.
  - Diversity and inclusion commitments: AFMD StOpE initiative (2023) against everyday sexism; L’Autre Cercle LGBT+ Charter (2024).

- Supplier obligations via the Charter:
  - Ensure decent working conditions and prevent psychosocial risks.
  - Prohibit discrimination and promote equal treatment.
  - Comply with anti-corruption laws and standards.
  - Cascade Charter requirements to subcontractors and suppliers.
  - Accept external audits and implement corrective actions (process effective since Q4 2024).
  - Take appropriate measures following human rights incident reports at postal sites.
  - Reinforces buyer conduct: adherence to Code of Ethics, fair treatment, transparency, and independence.

nodes.title: Human rights
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.2.4 Human rights
nodes.start_phrase: La Poste Group has adopted a Human Rights policy that embodies its commitments to the protection, respect and promotion of human rights in all of its activities, in its value chain, both in France and internationally.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance/Social information) detailing human rights, responsible purchasing, supplier oversight, and grievance mechanisms across the upstream value chain, including CNP Assurances.

- Human rights and policy framework:
  - La Poste Group Human Rights policy applied across activities and value chains, in France and internationally.
  - Alignment with ILO core conventions, UN Global Compact principles, and UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.
  - La Banque Postale’s Responsible Purchasing policy (validated Jan 2023) built on four pillars; Pillar 1 commits to enforcing and promoting fundamental rights in supply chains and contributes to SDGs 3, 5, 8, and 10.
  - Diversity and inclusion commitments, including AFMD’s StOpE initiative (2023) and L’Autre Cercle LGBT+ charter (2024).
  - Explicit references to ILO Conventions 29 (forced labor) and 182 (child labor), and UNGC principles 4 and 5.

- Supplier obligations and charters:
  - Responsible and Ethical Purchasing Charter sets reciprocal commitments on human rights, labor law, environment, and anti-corruption; flow-down to subcontractors; acceptance of external audits (rolled out from Q4 2024); cooperation in case of reported human rights issues.
  - Contractual “due diligence” clauses require risk identification and mitigation of fundamental rights infringements.
  - Group code of conduct (zero tolerance on corruption) annexed to contracts and published online; aligned with ILO standards.
  - CNP Assurances policies mirror UN human rights guidelines; Responsible Supplier Charter deployed Dec 2024 and rolled out/translated in foreign subsidiaries from Jan 2025; suppliers sign upon onboarding from Jan 2025.

- Supplier risk assessment and monitoring:
  - Pre-onboarding and annual assessment for all suppliers (with thresholds noted), covering financial risk, corruption/AML-CFT (Sapin II), documentary due diligence, and CSR risks (including human rights).
  - Use of AFNOR risk mapping (segment exposure rated 1–4), translated into high/medium/low CSR risk levels; supplier CSR ratings integrated in mapping.
  - Deployment of La Poste Group’s e-compliance with EcoVadis ratings and a CSR maturity questionnaire; potential escalation to documentary or on-site audits.
  - “Due diligence” clauses mandate corrective actions where risks are identified.
  - No upstream value chain non-compliance reported to date.

- Dialogue and grievance mechanisms:
  - Ongoing dialogue with suppliers through compliance analyses, mediation, listening systems, and whistleblowing channels; consultations report high satisfaction and no significant issues thus far.
  - Independent Supplier Mediator (shared with La Poste Group), accessible online, participates in the Responsible Purchasing Committee (ARCOM), publishes annual reports; usage monitored monthly with no cases recorded to date.
  - Supplier listening system for intellectual services (PM/PMO/consulting) via questionnaires, annual meetings, and KPIs; since Oct/Nov 2024 includes questions on working conditions and internal whistleblowing; informs action plans where needed.
  - Confirmation of purchasing function’s responsibility for responsible purchasing and supplier compliance; “Supplier Relations and Responsible Purchasing” certification achieved Sep 2023, follow-up audit Jun 2024.

- Reporting and remediation:
  - Whistleblowing platform covers all upstream workers (suppliers and their employees), accessible via La Banque Postale’s website; suppliers must inform their employees and provide access.
  - Workers can also access the Supplier Mediator; channels rely on availability of digital equipment.
  - Processes allow for investigation, corrective actions, and continuous improvement based on findings and audits.

nodes.title: Dialogue mechanisms
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.2.5 Dialogue mechanisms
nodes.start_phrase: As part of its ESG approach and its “Responsible Purchasing” policy, La Banque Postale ensures that the views of workers in its upstream value chain are incorporated into its decisions and activities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale’s CSR governance of its upstream value chain, emphasizing supplier dialogue, responsible purchasing, and worker voice mechanisms.
- Ongoing supplier dialogue: Initiated pre-contract via compliance analysis and maintained throughout the relationship; annual compliance reviews for all suppliers invoicing ≥€10,000; existing channels include mediation, supplier listening, and whistleblowing.
- Mediation system: Independent supplier relations Mediator (shared with La Poste Group), accessible online, participates in the Responsible Purchasing Committee (ARCOM), issues annual reports, and proposes out-of-court solutions; usage is monitored monthly with no cases to date.
- Supplier listening program: Structured engagement with intellectual services suppliers (project management/assistance/consulting) via questionnaires, annual meetings, relationship committees, and KPI tracking; assesses CSR maturity and drives improvements. Since Oct 2024, includes questions on working conditions and internal whistleblowing systems. Results inform action plans where needed.
- 2024 updates: Nov 2024 questionnaire to verify suppliers’ own worker-voice systems; related questions integrated into third-party audit tools from Nov 2024; the listening program is conducted annually for the specified supplier panel.
- Governance and compliance: The purchasing function owns Responsible Purchasing and ensures contractual and GPC compliance; this was validated by “Supplier Relations and Responsible Purchasing” certification in Sep 2023 and confirmed in a Jun 2024 follow-up audit.
- Reporting and remediation: All workers in the upstream value chain can access the whistleblowing platform and supplier mediator via the corporate website; the whistleblowing system covers suppliers and their workers. Suppliers are contractually required to inform their employees about the platform and ensure access.
- Outcomes to date: Supplier consultations indicate high satisfaction and no significant issues regarding working conditions or impacts, so no decision changes have been needed, while maintaining vigilance and continuous dialogue.

nodes.title: Reporting and remediation process
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.2.6 Reporting and remediation process
nodes.start_phrase: In addition to the dialogue mechanisms with suppliers described above, workers in the upstream value chain also have access to the whistleblowing system set up by La Banque Postale.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale’s ESG/Responsible Purchasing approach to integrating upstream value chain workers’ perspectives, managing reporting and remediation, and maintaining targets.
- Supplier dialogue mechanisms:
  - Pre-engagement and ongoing compliance reviews, including annual analyses for suppliers billing ≥€10k.
  - Multiple channels: supplier mediation, supplier listening, and whistleblowing.
- Mediation system:
  - “Supplier relations” Mediator established in 2023, shared with La Poste Group, accessible online, independent, part of the Responsible Purchasing Committee (ARCOM), issues annual reports.
  - Usage monitored monthly; no cases to date.
- Supplier listening system:
  - Engagement via supplier representatives, with pilots among project management/consulting firms.
  - Questionnaires, annual meetings, relationship committees, and KPI monitoring assess CSR maturity and identify improvements.
  - Since Oct 2024, includes questions on working conditions and whistleblowing; results can trigger action plans.
  - Nov 2024: questionnaire and third‑party audits expanded to check such systems at intellectual services suppliers; process repeated annually on a defined panel.
- Governance and assurance:
  - Purchasing function accountable for Responsible Purchasing policy and supplier compliance (contracts and GPC).
  - Confirmed by “Supplier Relations and Responsible Purchasing” certification audit (Sept 2023) and follow‑up (June 2024).
- Reporting and whistleblowing:
  - Whistleblowing platform covers all upstream value chain workers; access via LBP website.
  - Suppliers must inform their employees and provide access per contracts/GPC.
  - Ethics Officer manages reports; Purchasing Director involved for supplier-related cases; protection against reprisals ensured.
  - LBP assesses risk to certain worker categories as limited; current system deemed sufficient.
- Remediation approach:
  - LBP will remediate if it caused or contributed to negative impacts on value chain workers.
  - No formal written remediation process yet due to no proven negative impacts; commits to implement appropriate, proportionate remedies with monitoring and stakeholder feedback if needed.
- Subsidiaries:
  - CNP Assurances: buyers trained to identify/report impacts; cases handled by Compliance/HR/Procurement/Legal; reporters informed; external mediation possible; focus on non‑recurrence.
  - LBP AM: procedure for non‑compliance; can terminate supplier relationships and notify relevant authorities (e.g., HALDE, CNIL).
- Targets and performance management:
  - Three‑year action plan with regularly monitored targets informed by supplier feedback and monitoring systems; reviewed by the Responsible Purchasing Committee.
  - Maintain established levels: 100% inclusion of CSR criteria in tenders and 100% worker coverage by a charter guaranteeing healthy and safe working conditions.
  - Effectiveness assessed via supplier listening questionnaires and analysis of providers’ CSR criteria.

nodes.title: Targets
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.2.7 Targets
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale's Responsible Purchasing approach is based on targets that are regularly monitored.
nodes.summary:
- Governance of reports and ethics: La Banque Postale’s Ethics Officer oversees reports; supplier-related cases are processed with the Purchasing Director, who reports to the Managing Director (Finance & Strategy) on the Executive Board. Whistleblowers are protected from reprisals.
- Scope and risk profile: Given LBP’s business nature and locations, specific worker-category risks are considered limited; existing mechanisms are deemed sufficient and inclusive for value chain workers.
- Report handling and remediation: If alerted by a supplier of a negative impact on workers, LBP manages remediation. While no formal written remediation process exists due to no proven negative impacts to date, LBP commits to implement appropriate, proportionate remedies with best practices, stakeholder engagement, and monitoring if needed.
- Subsidiary practices:
  - CNP Assurances: Buyers trained to identify/report impacts; cases handled by Compliance/HR/Procurement/Legal; stakeholder meetings, possible external mediation; prevention of recurrence required.
  - LBP AM: Procedure for non-compliance with Responsible Purchasing policy; may terminate supplier relationships and inform relevant authorities (e.g., HALDE, CNIL) for breaches related to human rights or ethics.
- Targets and monitoring (Responsible Purchasing):
  - Maintain inclusion of CSR criteria in 100% of tenders.
  - Ensure 100% of supplier workers are covered by charters guaranteeing healthy, safe working conditions.
  - LBP AM supplier CSR adoption: ≥75% of eligible suppliers in 2024; ≥80% in 2025–2026.
  - Inclusion Market platform: increase buyer use; currently monitored via dashboards and stakeholder feedback; plan to formalize quantitative targets.
- Human rights safeguards in the value chain:
  - 100% of upstream workers covered by a charter aligned with UN Global Compact and ILO conventions.
  - Zero cases of forced or child labor in 2024; target is to maintain zero and full coverage.
- Supplier financial risk management:
  - Annual financial risk analysis for 100% of suppliers invoicing >€10k (N-1) and 100% of prospects.
  - Dependency threshold at 25% triggers an action plan; goal is to maintain full coverage and annual cadence.
- Action plans and resources:
  - A structured, three-year Responsible Purchasing action and improvement plan defines actions, targets, and deadlines.
  - Plan aligned with RFAR certification; initiated in 2022, validated by the Purchasing Director, independently audited, running through 2025; new 2026–2029 roadmap to be prepared in 2025.
- Supplier awareness and contractualization:
  - Systematic communication of the Responsible Purchasing Charter; reinforced via training and contractual clauses on worker rights and social standards.
- CSR integration in procurement:
  - Tenders include social/CSR criteria (e.g., ethics/anti-corruption training, CO2 data for hardware/software, equipment sustainability/compatibility).
  - CSR criteria carry significant weight (≥10%) in evaluations to drive responsible supplier practices.

nodes.title: Action plans and resources
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.2.8 Action plans and resources
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group deploys a structured strategy to ensure that matters related to workers in the value chain are taken into account, based on a number of practical and coordinated actions.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale’s responsible purchasing and social performance regarding workers in its upstream value chain and financed activities, within the 2024 Universal Registration Document.
- Supplier CSR targets: LBP AM aims for at least 75% of eligible suppliers with CSR approaches promoting fundamental rights in 2024, rising to 80% in 2025–2026.
- Inclusion Market platform: recently launched tool to source inclusive suppliers; usage is being monitored via dashboards and ARCOM meetings every four months, with plans to formalize quantitative targets and increase buyer adoption.
- Human rights safeguards: targets to keep 100% of upstream value chain workers covered by a charter aligned with the UN Global Compact and ILO conventions; zero cases of forced or child labor in 2024 and goal to maintain this.
- Financial risk management of suppliers: 100% of suppliers invoicing >€10k and all prospects receive annual financial risk analyses; supplier dependency >25% triggers systematic action plans; objective is to sustain full coverage annually.
- Governance and action planning: Group Purchasing Department leads a structured, three-year responsible purchasing action plan under the RFAR certification; current plan runs 2022–2025 with a new roadmap planned for 2026–2029.
- Supplier engagement: widespread communication of the Responsible Purchasing Charter, use of training and contractual clauses to embed CSR expectations.
- CSR in tenders: social and environmental criteria integrated into RFPs (e.g., ethics/anti-corruption training, CO₂ data, product longevity/compatibility), weighted at least 10% of overall scoring.
- Audit regime: internal/external audits (Provigis, Indued) and third‑party audits (via La Poste–selected firms) on anti‑corruption and due diligence; annual third‑party audits from December 2024.
- Inclusion initiatives: systematic access to the Inclusion Market for buyers since 2024 and promotion of inclusive purchasing, including suppliers supporting social inclusion and disability employment.
- Internal awareness: ongoing ESG dissemination via Just Transition ambassadors and Sustainability; 2023–2024 awareness for specifiers on responsible purchasing criteria.
- SME access: creation of an SME Officer role planned for 2025 to facilitate SME engagement with purchasing.
- Incidents and remediation: no forced or child labor incidents or other human rights breaches reported in 2024; updated purchasing documentation includes due‑diligence clauses and whistleblowing links; no remediation required.
- Risk management tools: annual ExCo reviews of portfolio and risk map; specific risk sheets and corrective action plans for working-condition and compliance risks; responsible purchasing procedures and manual to be updated in 2025.
- Resources and budget: Supplier Mediator, Ethics Officer, Purchasing Department involved; external audit budget €20k (2024) and €100k (2025); ~0.5 FTE allocated in 2024–2025 for supplier assessment.
- Monitoring effectiveness: indicators tracked via a Responsible Purchasing dashboard; progress reviewed by a committee every four months; annual external RFAR audits with employee/representative consultations; RFAR label obtained in Sept 2023 (based on standard 20400).
- Safeguards and grievance: contractual clauses on worker rights and data protection; internal/external audits, risk mapping, and a confidential whistleblowing system in place; no severe human rights incidents reported.
- Financed activities scope: material impacts on workers in the value chain considered across financing by CNP Assurances, LBP AM, and Louvre Banque Privée; use of the Impact Weighting Factor and controversy management to assess issuers.
- Strategic linkage: human rights, climate, and biodiversity commitments inform risk controls and sector policies; while considered, these topics do not directly reshape the business model.
- Material risks: identified risk of financial loss from inadequate partner assessment during the transition to a fairer, more inclusive society due to multi‑sector, multi‑geography exposure.
- Forced/child labor exposure in portfolios: indirect risk via asset management; LBP AM mapped salient human rights risks in 2023 following OECD/UNGP guidance and disclosed methodology/results; most critical risk identified is violation of fundamental workers’ rights in the downstream value chain.

nodes.title: Material IROs and links with strategy and business model
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.3.1 Material IROs and links with strategy and business model
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale considers that all workers in the value chain may be subject to material impacts, through the financed entities or projects.
nodes.summary:
- Describes La Banque Postale’s responsible purchasing governance, including annual external audits, direct consultations with employees/representatives, and attainment of the RFAR label in September 2023 based on the 20400 standard.
- Details supplier relationship safeguards: contractual clauses on employee rights, working conditions, and personal data; commitment not to impose harmful commercial terms; ongoing internal/external audits, risk mapping, and a confidential whistleblowing system.
- Reports no severe human rights incidents identified in the upstream value chain.
- Defines scope of “workers in the value chain” primarily through financed entities (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, Louvre Banque Privée), with assessment tools such as the Impact Weighting Factor and ESG controversy management.
- Explains that while social/environmental targets are embedded in governance and risk policies, impacts on value-chain workers do not directly shape the Group’s strategy/business model; no significant opportunities identified from these impacts.
- Identifies material risk of financial loss from inadequate assessment of financed partners’ working conditions, heightened by multi-sector, multi-geography exposure.
- Highlights risks of forced and child labor within investment portfolios; notes LBP AM’s 2023 mapping of salient human rights risks under UNGP/OECD guidance, with violations of fundamental workers’ rights as the most critical risk.
- Summarizes double materiality findings: negative impacts (degraded working conditions; forced/child labor); positive impacts (improved working conditions, diversity, inclusion via minimum requirements, training, and charters).
- Describes transmission of human-rights-related risks to financial performance and reputation; notes Louvre Banque Privée’s moderate risk due to liquid, largely European large-cap exposure and ability to divest quickly.
- Outlines 2024 controversy management process in the Responsible Financing and Investment Charter, excluding clients/prospects with severe or repeated ESG controversies, including human rights violations, guided by UNGP, ILO, and OECD frameworks; prioritizes high-risk groups (child, forced, migrant labor, conflict zones, precarious work).
- Acknowledges the vulnerability of certain worker groups while stating the Group has no direct impact on portfolio companies’ workers.
- Lists applicable policies and exclusions:
  - La Banque Postale’s Responsible Financing and Investment Charter (core tool for detecting and managing negative impacts/controversies).
  - Exclusion lists targeting activities misaligned with sustainable development, health, and well-being objectives.
  - CNP Assurances exclusions using Freedom House and Transparency International country lists; excludes UNGC non-compliant firms and those linked to tobacco or controversial/prohibited weapons.
  - LBP AM’s SFDR-aligned approach (Article 8/9 thresholds, DNSH checks), systematic human rights due diligence, and standards-based exclusions across open-ended funds and selected mandates.
  - Louvre Banque Privée’s ESG Charter promoting human rights in the downstream value chain, with systems to identify serious controversies and non-compliance with UNGC/OECD principles.
- Emphasizes continuous improvement and stakeholder dialogue (Purchasing Committee consultations, mediation with suppliers) as integral to responsible purchasing and human rights risk management across supply and investment chains.

nodes.title: Applicable policies
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.3.2 Applicable policies
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale’s Responsible Financing and Investment Charter aims, among other things, to minimise and prevent the negative impacts of degraded working conditions and cases of forced labour or child labour in portfolio companies.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Social information within La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, centered on human rights and working conditions across credit and investment portfolios.
- Double materiality findings: 
  - Main negative impacts: degraded working conditions and risks of forced or child labor in portfolio companies.
  - Main positive impacts: improved working conditions, diversity, and inclusion via minimum requirements, training, and charters.
  - Material risks: financial loss from inadequate partner assessment; human rights issues potentially affecting investee value; moderate reputational/valuation risk for Louvre Banque Privée mitigated by liquid, large-cap European exposure.
- 2024 controversy management: A new process under the Responsible Financing and Investment Charter screens for severe or repeated ESG controversies, explicitly including human and labor rights, guided by UN Guiding Principles, ILO conventions, and OECD Guidelines. Priority risk groups include child, forced, migrant, conflict-zone, and precarious workers; the Group notes no direct interaction with these workers.
- Applicable policies and exclusions:
  - La Banque Postale: Responsible Financing and Investment Charter as the main tool for ESG controversy detection and management; exclusion list aligned with sustainable development, health, and well-being.
  - CNP Assurances: Country exclusions based on Freedom House and Transparency International; excludes UN Global Compact violators and companies tied to tobacco and prohibited/controversial weapons.
  - LBP AM: SFDR-aligned methodology for Article 8 and 9 products with minimum thresholds, “do no significant harm” checks on human rights, and standards-based exclusions across funds to prevent/mitigate negative human rights impacts.
  - Louvre Banque Privée: ESG Charter aligned with international standards, screening for serious controversies and violations of UN Global Compact/OECD Guidelines.
- Compliance and commitments: No reported non-compliance with UN Guiding Principles or ILO Declaration involving downstream workers. Group-level Human Rights policies (La Poste Group, CNP Assurances, LBP AM) reaffirm commitments; Louvre Banque Privée limits investments to France/Europe to reduce exposure.
- Dialogue mechanisms: No direct engagement with workers in financed value chains due to scale and diversity of holdings; a global worker interaction system is not currently feasible.
- Reporting and remediation: In line with OECD expectations, investors are directly linked to investee impacts and should influence companies to prevent/mitigate harms; responsibility to remedy lies with companies causing or contributing to impacts. LBP AM uses stewardship to support remedies. The Group relies on investee reporting and commitments and maintains whistleblowing protections that prevent reprisals against employees of financed entities.

nodes.title: Dialogue mechanisms
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.3.3 Dialogue mechanisms
nodes.start_phrase: To date, La Banque Postale Group does not interact directly with workers in the value chain of its financed activities.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (CSR/Sustainable performance – Social information), with a glossary reference on page 808.
- Compliance status: No reported non-compliance with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights or the ILO Declaration involving downstream workers within La Banque Postale Group.
- Human rights governance: La Poste Group’s Human Rights policy covers the full value chain (including downstream). Additional policies exist at CNP Assurances and LBP AM.
- Updated charter: In December 2023, La Banque Postale updated its Responsible Financing and Investment Charter to manage serious or repeated controversies, treating human and fundamental labor rights violations as serious controversies, aligned with UNGPs, ILO core conventions, and OECD Guidelines.
- Subsidiary measures: 
  - CNP Assurances is a UN Global Compact signatory (since 2003).
  - LBP AM maintains a human rights risk map and an exclusion policy.
  - Louvre Banque Privée limits investments to France and Europe to reduce exposure.
- Risk focus: Identification of higher-risk worker groups and contexts, including child labor, forced labor, migrant labor, conflict zones, and precarious work.
- Stakeholder dialogue: Due to diversified, global investments across thousands of companies, the Group does not directly interact with workers in financed value chains and lacks a universal interaction mechanism at this stage.
- Reporting and remediation: 
  - Based on OECD Guidelines, investors—even minority holders—can be directly linked to negative human rights impacts and are expected to assess risks and use leverage to prevent/mitigate them; remediation responsibility lies with the companies causing or contributing to impacts.
  - LBP AM uses its influence to enable or support remedy in line with its Human Rights policy.
  - The Group relies on financed entities’ reporting and commitments in the absence of direct worker engagement.
  - Anti-retaliation measures exist for employees of financed entities using Group whistleblowing channels, with further details in the whistleblowing section.

nodes.title: Reporting and remediation process
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.3.4 Reporting and remediation process
nodes.start_phrase: The general approach to preventing negative impacts on workers in the value chain is mainly relevant to LBP AM.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines La Banque Postale Group’s approach to human rights within its sustainable performance and social information disclosures for 2024.
- It reports no cases of non-compliance with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights or the ILO Declaration involving downstream workers.
- La Poste Group has a formal Human Rights policy covering its global value chain; subsidiary policies (CNP Assurances, LBP AM) complement this framework.
- In December 2023, La Banque Postale updated its Responsible Financing and Investment Charter, establishing a process to manage serious controversies, especially human and labor rights violations, aligned with UNGPs, ILO conventions, and OECD Guidelines.
- Subsidiary commitments include: CNP Assurances’ participation in the UN Global Compact since 2003; LBP AM’s human rights risk mapping and exclusion policy; Louvre Banque Privée’s focus on France/Europe to limit exposure.
- The Group identifies high-risk worker categories for enhanced vigilance: child labor, forced labor, migrant labor, conflict zones, and precarious work.
- Due to the breadth of holdings and geographies, the Group does not directly engage with workers in financed entities’ value chains; this complexity precludes a universal interaction system.
- Investors, including minority holders, may be directly linked to human rights impacts per OECD Guidelines; they are expected to integrate risks and incentivize prevention/mitigation, while remediation responsibility lies with the companies causing or contributing to harm.
- LBP AM uses its influence to support remedies when material impacts occur and relies on investee disclosures in the absence of direct worker dialogue.
- Protections exist against reprisals for employees of financed entities who use the Group’s whistleblowing channels.
- Group-wide actions include 2024 e-learning for all employees on fundamental human rights, forced labor, and child labor.
- CNP Assurances incorporates human rights via ESG ratings (LBP AM’s GREaT methodology), prioritizing working conditions and respect for human and trade union rights in asset selection.
- LBP AM integrates human rights into asset management through SRI ratings, controversy checks aligned with SFDR (Articles 8 and 9), exclusion policies, and active shareholder engagement guided by UN Global Compact, UNGPs, and OECD Guidelines.
- Louvre Banque Privée manages material risks/opportunities via ESG data providers to flag controversies and an internal ESG network for qualitative assessment.
- Monitoring effectiveness relies on LBP AM’s SRI governance: the GREaT Committee (steers engagement/exclusions, standards policy, watchlists, escalation) and the ESG Committee (weekly trend/risk monitoring, prioritizing enhanced due diligence and engagements).
- Proprietary SRI methodologies and decision tools integrate human rights risk assessment into issuer selection and ongoing monitoring.

nodes.title: Action plans and resources
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.3.5 Action plans and resources
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group as a whole implements ambitious and consistent policies to prevent, mitigate and remedy negative impacts on human rights, based on approaches adapted to its various entities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale Group’s human-rights due diligence within its financing and investment activities, including action plans, monitoring, incidents, resources, and targets (Social information, Sustainable performance).
- Group-wide actions: 2024 rollout of an e-learning module for all employees on human rights, including preventing forced and child labor.
- Subsidiary frameworks tailored to activities to prevent negative human-rights impacts in downstream value chains.
- CNP Assurances: Integrates human-rights considerations into asset selection via LBP AM’s GREaT ESG methodology, prioritizing working conditions and respect for fundamental rights.
- LBP AM: Human Rights policy aligned with SFDR and international standards; integrates human-rights risk into SRI analysis, applies controversy screening and exclusions, and conducts active shareholder engagement.
- Louvre Banque Privée: Applies strengthened qualitative ESG analysis, uses external ESG data to flag controversies, and leverages internal ESG expertise.
- Monitoring effectiveness: Governance via GREaT and ESG Committees; proprietary SRI rating methodologies embedded in investment decisions; use of SFDR Main Adverse Impact indicators, controversy monitoring, and a standards watchlist.
- 2024 results: Exclusion of three companies for severe workers’ rights violations in supply chains; written AGM questions to two companies after insufficient engagement progress; targeted engagement campaigns in personal care products and automotive sectors to mitigate severe supply-chain risks.
- Resources: Dedicated Sustainability Department team to manage controversies and engage clients to remediate detected negative impacts.
- Targets: No measurable targets yet for poor working conditions, forced labor, or child labor due to data/methodology gaps; ongoing monitoring of controversies with operational adjustments to the Responsible Financing and Investment Charter.

nodes.title: Targets
nodes.heading: 2.3.2.3.6 Targets
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale has not defined a measurable target related to the negative impacts of poor working conditions, forced labour or child labour within the portfolio companies.
nodes.summary:
- Explains how ESG ratings are used in SRI fund selection to address human rights risks via: SFDR Principal Adverse Impact (PAI) indicators, controversies monitoring, and a standards watchlist overseen by the GREaT Committee for ongoing issuer monitoring and engagement effectiveness.
- Details 2024 actions on severe human rights issues: LBP AM excluded three companies for serious supply‑chain labor rights violations; submitted AGM questions to two companies after insufficient progress; launched engagement following a major personal care sector controversy; intensified engagements with automotive and components firms to curb severe supply‑chain human rights risks.
- Describes controversy management and resources: dialogue with business customers to seek rapid remediation when negative impacts are detected; a dedicated Sustainability Department team operates the controversy process.
- Notes absence of quantitative targets on poor working conditions, forced labor, or child labor in portfolios due to methodological and data gaps; ongoing monitoring of controversies and adjustments to the Responsible Financing and Investment Charter as needed.
- Defines scope of potentially affected communities: people near La Banque Postale’s regional network and downstream communities (including indigenous peoples) linked to financed/invested companies.
- Outlines material negative impacts from exposure to high‑risk sectors (conflict zones, privacy/freedom of expression breaches, environmental pollution, health and human rights harms) across diversified portfolios of La Banque Postale, CNP Assurances, LBP AM, and Louvre Banque Privée; highlights heightened vulnerability of certain groups; mitigation through responsible investment strategies.
- Highlights positive community impacts: alignment with Caisse des Dépôts priorities (economic development, territorial cohesion/housing, social cohesion, ecological transition); regional presence ensuring banking access, including in underserved areas; financing for local authorities and associations; societal programs such as L’Envol, solidarity team building, and Déclic.
- States financial materiality conclusion: affected communities topic deemed non‑material with no significant risks or opportunities identified, including for specific groups.
- Summarizes policy framework: Responsible Financing and Investment Charter excludes financing of sensitive sectors and entities with serious/repeated ESG controversies and avoids capital contributions to countries that do not respect fundamental rights and international standards to protect affected communities.

nodes.title: Material IROs and links with strategy and business model
nodes.heading: 2.3.3.1 Material IROs and links with strategy and business model
nodes.start_phrase: The communities likely to be affected by significant impacts related to the activity of the Group and its subsidiaries or projects financed through investment or credit activities are presented in the information published under the ESRS 2 heading.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Identifies communities potentially affected by La Banque Postale Group’s own operations (people around its extensive regional network and societal initiatives) and by financed activities (downstream communities, including indigenous peoples, impacted by portfolio companies), aligned with ESRS 2/S3.

- Material negative impacts: Linked to investments in high-risk sectors (conflict-related operations/materials, privacy and freedom of expression breaches, environmental pollution, health and Human Rights harms). Exposure spans La Banque Postale, CNP Assurances, LBP AM, and Louvre Banque Privée due to diversified, multi-sector, multi-geography portfolios. Particularly vulnerable groups include indigenous peoples, women, children, displaced persons, and populations in conflict or high-risk areas. Mitigation via responsible investment strategies.

- Positive impacts: Strategy aligned with Caisse des Dépôts priorities—economic development and sovereignty, territorial cohesion and housing, social cohesion, and ecological transition. The Group’s regional network enhances banking access in rural/underserved areas; financing supports local authorities and associations for infrastructure renovation, local services, ecological/social initiatives, and inclusion/solidarity projects. Societal programs (e.g., L’Envol for youth from low-income backgrounds) and employee engagement initiatives (solidarity team building, Déclic) reinforce positive community impact.

- Risks and opportunities: The “affected communities” topic is non-material from a financial standpoint; no significant risks or opportunities identified for the Group or for specific groups.

- Commitments/policies for negatively affected communities: Acknowledges potential adverse impacts from financed activities in critical-risk sectors. The Responsible Financing and Investment Charter guides lending and investment, excluding financing of sensitive sectors or entities involved in serious/repeated ESG controversies, and prohibiting capital contributions to countries that do not respect fundamental rights and international standards—aimed at protecting affected communities.

nodes.title: Commitments to communities negatively affected by financed activities
nodes.heading: 2.3.3.2 Commitments to communities negatively affected by financed activities
nodes.start_phrase: This section reviews the negative impacts on the financed activities, particularly in relation to investments in sectors with critical levels of risk: operations and materials from conflict zones, breaches of privacy and freedom of expression, environmental pollution, impacts on health, Human Rights, etc.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and framework: ESRS S3 coverage of communities affected by La Banque Postale Group’s own operations and by financed activities across its value chain, including indigenous peoples; references to ESRS 2 disclosures.
- Who is affected: People near the Group’s extensive regional banking network and beneficiaries of societal initiatives (own operations), and communities downstream of investment/credit activities (financed activities).
- Material negative impacts: Potential harms linked to investments in high‑risk sectors and contexts—conflict zones, privacy and freedom of expression risks, environmental pollution, health impacts, and Human Rights issues—across diversified portfolios of La Banque Postale, CNP Assurances, LBP AM, and Louvre Banque Privée. Vulnerable groups include local and indigenous communities, women, children, displaced persons, and populations in conflict or high‑risk areas; sectors named include agri‑food, metals/mining, and energy/utilities.
- Mitigation approach: Adoption of responsible investment strategies to prevent and minimize adverse impacts, including application of a Responsible Financing and Investment Charter that excludes financing of sensitive sectors, companies with serious or repeated ESG controversies, and capital contributions to countries not respecting fundamental rights and international standards.
- Positive impacts: Alignment with Caisse des Dépôts Group priorities (economic development and sovereignty, territorial cohesion and habitat, social cohesion, ecological transformation). The Group’s regional presence promotes banking access in rural/underserved areas; financing supports local authorities and associations for infrastructure renovation, local services, and ecological/social initiatives. Societal sponsorships (e.g., L’Envol for education, solidarity team building, Déclic) enhance inclusion, solidarity, and employee engagement.
- Risks and opportunities: The topic is non‑material from a financial perspective; no significant risks or opportunities identified for the Group or specific groups related to affected communities.
- Forward reference: Further detail on positive impact commitments is provided in Section 2.3.3.3.

nodes.title: Applicable policies
nodes.heading: 2.3.3.2.1 Applicable policies
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale’s Responsible Financing and Investment Charter sets out the fundamental principles that guide the Bank’s lending and investment decisions.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale Group’s commitments and practices regarding communities affected by its operations and, especially, by financed activities, within the Group’s CSR framework (ESRS S3).
- Scope of affected communities: 
  - Own operations: people near the Group’s extensive regional network and beneficiaries of societal initiatives.
  - Financed activities: downstream communities, including indigenous peoples, potentially affected by portfolio companies.
- Material negative impacts: 
  - Linked to investments in high‑risk sectors (conflict-zone links, privacy/freedom of expression breaches, environmental pollution, health and Human Rights issues).
  - Vulnerable groups highlighted (indigenous peoples, women, children, displaced populations, those in conflict/high‑risk areas).
  - Entities concerned: La Banque Postale, CNP Assurances, LBP AM, Louvre Banque Privée; mitigation via responsible investment strategies.
- Positive impacts:
  - Regional presence ensuring access to banking, including rural/underserved areas.
  - Financing supports local authorities/associations (public infrastructure renovation, local services, ecological/social initiatives, inclusion and solidarity).
  - Societal sponsorship and employee engagement (e.g., L’Envol education program, solidarity team building, Déclic).
- Financial materiality: Affected communities topic deemed non‑material for financial risks/opportunities; no specific group-level risks/opportunities identified.
- Policies and standards:
  - Responsible Financing and Investment Charter: exclusions for sensitive sectors and serious ESG controversies; no capital to countries violating fundamental rights.
  - LBP AM Human Rights Policy; CNP Assurances due diligence with impact mapping across own activities, suppliers, and investments.
  - Alignment with UN Global Compact, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, ILO Conventions, OECD Guidelines; no 2024 non‑compliance identified.
- Targets: No specific targets set to manage negative impacts on affected communities (no direct interaction claimed); controversies handling used to monitor Charter implementation.
- Dialogue mechanisms:
  - Regular engagement with local authorities via La Poste’s local presence and specialized public-sector business centers to identify needs and build trust.
  - Investor stewardship: LBP AM engages portfolio companies to address human rights issues; breadth of holdings limits systematic, direct community interaction.
- Remediation/influence approach:
  - Use “sphere of influence” to:
    - Assess company responses to halt/remedy negative impacts.
    - Set expectations, support corrective actions, and monitor measures.
  - Companies are expected to create action plans, remedy impacts they cause/contribute to, and actively consult affected stakeholders, demonstrating integration of their views.

nodes.title: Targets
nodes.heading: 2.3.3.2.2 Targets
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale has not established targets to manage the material negative impacts of the communities affected by the financed activities.
nodes.summary:
- Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (CSR/Sustainable performance – Social information) focused on human rights governance in financing and investment.
- LBP AM Human Rights Policy referenced (with detailed mechanisms in Section 2.3.4.3); CNP Assurances describes a due-diligence mapping of human-rights, health/safety, and environmental impacts across own operations, suppliers, and investments, with control systems.
- Strong alignment with international standards: UN Global Compact, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, ILO conventions, and OECD Guidelines; commitment to comply with applicable laws and France’s international agreements.
- 2024 outcome: no identified non-compliance with UNGPs, ILO fundamental principles, or OECD Guidelines affecting communities.
- Targets: no specific targets set for managing material negative impacts on affected communities due to lack of direct interaction; instead, controversies are monitored and addressed under the Responsible Financing and Investment Charter.
- Dialogue mechanisms: ongoing, localized engagement with authorities via La Poste’s network to identify regional needs (public facilities, energy renovation, local economy) and build trust; in investments, stakeholder dialogue is conducted through LBP AM’s stewardship, acknowledging limits to systematic, direct engagement with all potentially affected communities given investment breadth.
- Remediation and influence approach: LBP AM uses its “sphere of influence” to engage companies identified via standards-based reviews or ESG Committee decisions to mitigate and remedy human-rights impacts. Objectives include assessing company responses, clarifying expectations, monitoring measures, and supporting remediation. Engaged companies are expected to develop action plans, cease/mitigate and remedy impacts they cause or contribute to, and actively consult affected stakeholders, demonstrating integration of their views.

nodes.title: Dialogue mechanisms
nodes.heading: 2.3.3.2.3 Dialogue mechanisms
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale maintains regular dialogue with local authorities to better understand their challenges and adapt its solutions.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on La Banque Postale Group’s human rights approach within its Sustainable Performance/Social Information section, including LBP AM and CNP Assurances.
- Due diligence and risk mapping: identification and control of potential infringements on human rights, fundamental freedoms, health/safety, and the environment across own operations, suppliers, and investments.
- Alignment with international standards: UN Global Compact, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, ILO Conventions, and OECD Guidelines; no cases of non-compliance identified in 2024.
- Targets: no specific targets set for managing negative impacts on affected communities due to lack of direct interaction; reliance on controversy handling and the Responsible Financing and Investment Charter.
- Stakeholder dialogue: ongoing engagement with local authorities via La Poste’s on-the-ground network; responsible investment strategy leverages LBP AM’s influence over invested companies; no systematic direct interaction with all potentially affected communities due to investment breadth.
- Engagement and remediation approach: use of investor “sphere of influence” to push companies to stop, mitigate, and remedy human rights impacts; expectations include action plans, stakeholder consultation, avoiding immediate relationship severance when impacts are remediable, and strengthening due diligence; effectiveness tracked through engagement outcomes.
- Grievance mechanisms: expectation that portfolio companies implement culturally appropriate whistleblowing channels, with sector-specific guidance (e.g., oil and gas); monitoring via engagements and an annual report; consultation with external stakeholders; policies to prevent reprisals for whistleblowers; LBP relies on financed entities’ reporting given its indirect relationship with communities.
- Controversy monitoring and exclusions: pre-investment and ongoing checks for ESG controversies; severe/repeated human rights violations trigger exclusion from future investments and potential restriction of financing relationships.
- CNP Assurances’ ESG integration: application of Ostrum AM’s GREaT methodology in equity and bond selection, assessing social pillars such as working conditions and respect for human rights.

nodes.title: Action plans and resources
nodes.heading: 2.3.3.2.4 Action plans and resources
nodes.start_phrase: According to the OECD, investors may be linked to the negative impacts on Human Rights caused by the invested companies.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale Group’s social responsibility approach to affected communities, with emphasis on human rights due diligence, grievance mechanisms, engagement and exclusion policies in investment, and positive local impacts via financing and sponsorship.

- Expectations for investee companies:
  - Prefer engagement and remediation over immediate relationship termination; strengthen due diligence to prevent recurrence.
  - Establish accessible, culturally appropriate whistleblowing and grievance channels; sector-specific guidance (e.g., oil and gas) for local community alerts.
  - Demonstrate effective remediation aligned with UN Guiding Principles and OECD Guidelines, especially in sensitive/conflict areas.

- Monitoring and evaluation:
  - Track responses and corrective actions from engagement campaigns; publish annual engagement reports.
  - Consult external stakeholders (local communities, experts) to test channel effectiveness.
  - Non-retaliation and independence of whistleblowing systems are reinforced.

- Investor responsibility and action:
  - Recognizes OECD view that investors are “directly linked” to impacts; uses influence to prevent/mitigate, while remediation lies with companies.
  - When material impacts are found, LBP AM consults local experts/affected communities, promotes action plans, strengthens company policies, and monitors remedies.

- Controversy screening and exclusions:
  - Pre- and post-investment checks for ESG controversies under a Responsible Financing and Investment Charter; serious/repeated controversies can trigger exclusion or relationship surveillance.
  - CNP Assurances uses Ostrum AM’s GREaT ESG methodology, including social pillars on working conditions and human rights.

- Governance, tools, and methodologies:
  - Two SRI committees drive policy: GREaT Committee (engagement and exclusions) and ESG Committee (trend/risk monitoring, awareness).
  - Exclusion decisions consider severity, company linkage, preventive/remedial measures, and likelihood of future violations.
  - Human rights integrated into investment analysis and SFDR “do no significant harm” checks; formal exclusion and engagement policies; active bilateral/collective dialogues.
  - Participation in sector initiatives: Coalition for Ethical AI, Ranking Digital Rights, Access to Medicine Foundation, ChemSec.

- Operating posture:
  - As a financial institution/asset manager, the Group does not directly engage communities affected by financed activities but relies on investee reporting and leverages influence to uphold due diligence and remediation.

- Resources and 2024 outcomes:
  - Dedicated SRI Solutions team (10 experts, including a human rights lead), SRI rating tools, and internal guidance on risk mapping and salient issues.
  - No serious human rights incidents concerning affected communities reported in 2024.

- Positive impact commitments:
  - Through sponsorship, a nationwide branch network, and financing of local authorities/associations, the Group supports regional development and social value creation.
  - CLDB-led initiatives include:
    - Local Finance Steering Committee (advisory/observatory role).
    - Strong partnership with the social and solidarity economy; advisors support 4,000 major associations.
    - “Advance on subsidy” cash-flow solution for associations.
    - Green/social financing solutions (e.g., responsible real estate, access to essential services) with accessible social loans.
    - “Donation collection” offer to boost online fundraising; 100+ partnerships with leading NGOs/foundations.
  - Goal: support associations in a just and sustainable transition.

nodes.title: Commitments to affected communities to generate a positive impact
nodes.heading: 2.3.3.3 Commitments to affected communities to generate a positive impact
nodes.start_phrase: This section reviews the positive impact of the La Banque Postale Group in connection with its societal sponsorship actions, its regional network and the financing of local authorities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Sustainable performance/Social information from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, with CSR term definitions referenced.
- LBP AM’s human rights approach as an asset manager:
  - Uses investor influence to promote remediation of significant human rights impacts, aligned with OECD Guidelines and UNGP.
  - Expects portfolio companies to consult affected stakeholders, implement accessible and culturally appropriate whistleblowing/complaints systems, and align grievance mechanisms with international standards.
