  - Heightened expectations for companies in sensitive/conflict areas, including proof of effective recourse mechanisms.
- Governance and resources for human rights integration:
  - Dedicated SRI Solutions team (10 experts, including a human rights lead) coordinating across investment, risk, and CSR functions.
  - SRI rating tools incorporate salient human rights risks; internal guides support risk mapping and investment decision-making.
  - Reported no serious human rights incidents concerning affected communities in 2024.
- Positive impact commitments toward affected communities:
  - Through financing activities: strong role in funding local authorities and associations to drive regional development and social value.
  - Through own operations: societal sponsorship and extensive regional network to support local communities.
- Financing and support for local authorities, associations, and the local economy (via CLDB):
  - Ongoing engagement with public-sector stakeholders through a Local Finance Steering Committee (elected officials, former MPs, experts) providing risk assessment, monitoring, and service recommendations.
  - One in ten French associations is a client; 4,000 major associations supported across health, education, charity, and social-purpose sectors.
  - Targeted solutions:
    - 2020: “Advance on subsidy” to bridge cash-flow gaps before public payments.
    - 2022: Green and social financing for responsible real estate and essential services (health, education, housing) via accessible social loans from €50,000.
    - 2023: “Donation collection” offer to enhance online fundraising with an end-to-end donor journey.
  - Partnerships with 100+ recognized public-interest associations/foundations (e.g., French Red Cross, Hospitals Foundation).
  - Strategic objective to help associations transition toward a just and sustainable model.

nodes.title: Financing of local authorities, associations and the local economic sector
nodes.heading: 2.3.3.3.1 Financing of local authorities, associations and the local economic sector
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale, through the Corporate and Local Development Banking (CLDB), implements strategic initiatives and concrete actions aimed at maximising positive impacts for the affected communities and is committed to local authorities and associations.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on human rights integration by LBP AM (La Banque Postale Asset Management) in line with OECD Guidelines and UN Guiding Principles: requires portfolio companies to consult affected stakeholders, provide accessible whistleblowing/complaints channels, and demonstrate effective remediation, with heightened expectations in sensitive/conflict areas. Dedicated SRI Solutions team (10 experts, including a human rights lead) and tools/risk mapping guide investment decisions. No serious human rights incidents reported in 2024.

- Commitments to affected communities through financing and operations: Corporate and Local Development Banking (CLDB) supports local authorities, associations, and the local economy. Ongoing dialogue via a Local Finance Steering Committee. Product innovations include “advance on subsidy” for associations, green/social loans (from €50,000) for essential services and responsible real estate, and an end-to-end donation collection solution; extensive partnerships with major nonprofits. Objective: enable a just and sustainable transition for the sector.

- Financing local authorities: 25% market share; comprehensive offer from cash management and bond solutions to short/long-term loans. Emphasis on responsible/social financing and Subzen grant-seeking support. Targeted impacts: modernizing public infrastructure, advancing sustainable mobility, supporting energy transition, and reducing regional disparities, including rural/remote areas.

- Support for other local public sector players: financing for hospitals and medico-social establishments (including Ségur de la Santé projects), nursing homes, and social housing (partners with 8/10 social housing operators; solutions for rent collection, receipts reconciliation, cash investments, and responsible production/renovation finance; second-largest commercial bank in the market). Ongoing financing for associations in social inclusion, health, and social protection.

- Tailored financial instruments to regional needs: real estate and equipment leasing, factoring, and asset securitization to enhance liquidity and reinvestment capacity.

- Capacity building for local decision-makers: publications, conferences, and tools (e.g., DOB budgeting aid); 2024 studies presented to the French Congress of Mayors; partnership with I4CE on climate action financing challenges; joint studies with the French Hospital Federation on hospital investments.

- Regional network impact: leveraging La Poste’s extensive footprint to maintain essential services, prevent banking deserts, support local development projects, and strengthen financial inclusion, with coordinated outreach to promote sustainable finance—especially in small towns and rural areas.

- Societal sponsorship: L’Envol program supports around 100 underprivileged youths for 3–8 years with mentoring and personalized monitoring; effectiveness assessed annually. Resources include a €2 million annual budget, dedicated staff (4 FTEs plus a work-study student) and community outreach hours (439 in 2023).

- MicroDon subsidiary enables embedded giving: checkout rounding (over €47.7 million raised to date), payroll giving, and time donations to associations, fostering a culture of solidarity and skills-based volunteering.

- Broader civic and ESG partnerships: strong engagement with the social and solidarity economy (150,000 association clients), participation in national campaigns (Téléthon, Breast Cancer Awareness, Pièces Jaunes), collaboration platforms on banking inclusion and budgeting education, WWF partnership for decarbonization, and ongoing dialogue with consumer associations.

nodes.title: Regional network
nodes.heading: 2.3.3.3.2 Regional network
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale, through its integration within La Poste Group, plays a role in maintaining the regional network of essential services in France.
nodes.summary:
- Role of La Banque Postale’s regional network within La Poste Group:
  - Maintains essential banking and postal services nationwide, including rural and remote areas, via a dense post office and retail network.
  - Prevents “banking deserts,” ensures service continuity where other financial institutions are absent.
  - Supports local development and environmental transition through financing for regional planning and essential infrastructure (schools, hospitals, social housing).
  - Promotes financial inclusion with tailored solutions such as controlled-rate loans and inclusive banking products.
  - Synergy with La Poste: leverages postal presence to engage local elected officials on sustainable financial solutions; adapts services through ongoing dialogue with local authorities.

- Societal sponsorship and community impact:
  - L’Envol programme:
    - Long-term support (3–8 years) for ~100 youths per year from modest backgrounds to foster academic success, social inclusion, and access to higher education.
    - Personalized mentoring by monitoring officers and La Poste volunteers; oversight by the Deputy General Manager; annual satisfaction surveys to assess effectiveness.
    - Resources mobilized: €2 million annual budget; 439 outreach hours in 2023; 4 FTEs plus a work-study student seconded to the association.
  - MicroDon subsidiary (embedded giving):
    - Checkout rounding: over €47.7 million raised since inception.
    - Payroll giving: small, recurring donations from employees.
    - Donation of time: skills-based sponsorship and volunteering during work hours.
  - Broader commitments:
    - Banking partner to the social and solidarity economy, serving 150,000 association clients (around one in ten associations in France).
    - Supports major national campaigns (Téléthon, Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Pièces Jaunes) and partners with leading NGOs (Secours Populaire, French Red Cross, Fédération des Banques Alimentaires).
    - Collaborative initiatives via Alliance Dynamique and the Club de l’Initiative contre l’Exclusion Bancaire on community causes, banking inclusion, and budgeting education.
    - WWF partnership since 2021 to advance decarbonization and sustainable solutions.
    - Regular engagement with consumer associations to bolster mutual aid and social inclusion.

nodes.title: Societal sponsorship
nodes.heading: 2.3.3.3.3 Societal sponsorship
nodes.start_phrase: Through its L'Envol programme, La Banque Postale implements practical actions which have positive impacts on society.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on La Banque Postale’s social and regional role within La Poste Group, emphasizing its dense regional network as an essential-services backbone for small towns and rural areas.
- Prevention of “banking deserts” via universal access to banking/postal services; support for local initiatives (environmental transition, regional planning, and essential infrastructure such as schools, hospitals, social housing); and financial inclusion through controlled-rate loans and inclusive products.
- Synergy with La Poste to maximize impact, including using post offices to inform local elected officials about sustainable financial solutions; ongoing dialogue with local authorities and adaptation of services to regional needs.

- Societal sponsorship:
  - L’Envol program: multi-year support (3–8 years) for around 100 youth from modest backgrounds annually, promoting academic success, social inclusion, and access to higher education via personalized monitoring, mentoring, and educational opportunities; supervised by a Deputy GM; annual effectiveness assessment through satisfaction surveys.
  - Resources for L’Envol: €2 million annual budget; 439 hours of employee community outreach in 2023; 4 FTEs plus one work-study student seconded to the association.
  - MicroDon: “embedded” giving solutions including checkout rounding (over €47.7 million raised since launch), payroll giving, and donation of time/skills; fosters a culture of community engagement.
  - Broader charity commitments: banking partner to 150,000 associations (about one in ten nationwide); support for national campaigns (Téléthon, Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Pièces Jaunes) and major NGOs (Secours Populaire, French Red Cross, Food Banks); participation in coalitions (Alliance Dynamique, Club de l’Initiative contre l’Exclusion Bancaire); WWF partnership since 2021 for decarbonization; regular dialogue with consumer associations.

- Impact finance monitoring:
  - Lending to local authorities, social/health sectors, associations, and local economic operators to fight inequality, expand access to essential services, and drive a just transition across regions.
  - Community loans tracked via sub-indicators for social housing, health, associations, and local economy; include green (Taxonomy-aligned), social, and impact loans.
  - All indicators improved from 2023 to 2024; annual origination to local authorities exceeded the 2025 target ahead of schedule.

- Acting in the interest of consumers and end-users:
  - Scope includes all customers/end-users (retail, corporate, local public entities) across financing, insurance, investment, and banking services.
  - Material impacts include data protection/privacy risks (banking secrecy, GDPR) and potential consumer health/safety impacts linked to financed activities.
  - Focus on vulnerable customers (youth, elderly, financially fragile, disabled, low financial literacy) through inclusive offers, accessible bancassurance services, and responsible marketing; positive impacts particularly benefit these groups.

- Impact finance metrics (2023 → 2024 → 2025 target):
  - Annual loan premium income with local authorities (€bn): 4.5 → 5.8 → 4.5
    - Of which green and social loans (€bn): 1.6 → 1.87 → 1.1
  - Social housing, healthcare, non-profit sectors (€bn): 1.00 → 1.53 → 2.5
    - Of which sustainability loans (€bn): 0.4 → 0.71 → 0.3
  - Local economy sector (€bn): 1.9 → 1.94 → 2.4
    - Of which sustainability loans (€bn): 0.5 → 0.32 → 0.3

nodes.title: Monitoring indicators for impact finance commitments
nodes.heading: 2.3.3.4.1 Monitoring indicators for impact finance commitments
nodes.start_phrase: The origination of loans to local authorities, the social sector, health, associations and local economic operators forms part of the Group’s commitments to supporting the regions.
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt is from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Social information) and references a glossary of CSR terms.
- It details additional entity-specific indicators, focusing on monitoring impact finance commitments. The Group emphasizes loan origination to local authorities, the social sector, healthcare, associations, and local economic operators to support regions, reduce inequalities via access to essential services, and advance a just transition.
- Community loan monitoring includes sub-indicators covering social housing, health and associations, and the local economy, encompassing green loans aligned with the EU Taxonomy, social loans, and impact loans.
- All impact finance indicators improved from 2023 to 2024; annual origination to local authorities already exceeded the 2025 target.
- Under “Acting in the interest of our consumers and end-users” [S4], the scope includes all customers and end-users (individuals, companies, local public entities) potentially affected by La Banque Postale Group’s financing, insurance, investment, and banking services, in line with ESRS 2 [S4_SBM_3_01].
- Material impacts highlighted:
  - Risks to all customers from personal data protection incidents (e.g., data leaks) and service failures.
  - Specific focus on vulnerable customers (youth, elderly, financially constrained, disabled, or with low financial literacy), who benefit from inclusive offers, accessible bancassurance services, and responsible marketing.
  - For credit and investment activities, potential impacts on users of financed operators’ goods/services if activities harm consumer health or safety [S4_SBM_3_02].
  - Privacy risks tied to sensitive data shared for bancassurance; positive impacts stem from inclusive, accessible, and responsible commercial practices, especially aiding vulnerable customers [S4_SBM_3_03].
- Key impact finance metrics (2023 → 2024 vs. 2025 targets):
  - Annual loan premium income with local authorities: 4.5 → 5.8 €bn (target 4.5); of which green/social: 1.6 → 1.87 €bn (target 1.1).
  - Social housing, healthcare, non-profit: 1.0 → 1.53 €bn (target 2.5); of which sustainability loans: 0.4 → 0.71 €bn (target 0.3).
  - Local economy: 1.9 → 1.94 €bn (target 2.4); of which sustainability loans: 0.5 → 0.32 €bn (target 0.3).
- Overall, the section connects impact finance performance and consumer/end-user safeguards to the Group’s CSR strategy, evidencing progress toward targets and reinforcing commitments to inclusivity, data protection, and responsible financing.

nodes.title: Material IROs and links with strategy and business model
nodes.heading: 2.3.4.1 Material IROs and links with strategy and business model
nodes.start_phrase: All customers and end-users, whether natural or legal persons (individuals, companies, local public entities), likely to be affected by material impacts related to the activities of La Banque Postale Group (financing, insurance, investment, banking services) are covered by the information disclosed under ESRS 2.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Social information), focusing on ESRS S4 (consumers and end-users) and impact finance monitoring.

- Impact finance monitoring indicators:
  - Lending to local authorities, social housing, health, associations, and the local economy supports regional development, combats inequality, and advances a just transition.
  - Community loans tracked via sub-indicators: green loans aligned with the EU Taxonomy, social loans, and impact loans.
  - All indicators improved from 2023 to 2024; annual origination to local authorities already exceeded the 2025 target.

- Key metrics (2023 → 2024 vs 2025 target):
  - Annual loan premium income with local authorities: €4.5bn → €5.8bn (target €4.5bn) – surpassed.
  - Of which green & social: €1.6bn → €1.87bn (target €1.1bn) – surpassed.
  - Social housing, healthcare, non-profits: €1.0bn → €1.53bn (target €2.5bn) – progressing.
  - Of which sustainability loans: €0.4bn → €0.71bn (target €0.3bn) – surpassed.
  - Local economy: €1.9bn → €1.94bn (target €2.4bn) – progressing.
  - Of which sustainability loans: €0.5bn → €0.32bn (target €0.32bn) – target met.

- Scope of S4 (consumers/end-users):
  - Covers all customers and end-users of banking, insurance, investment, and services, including users of financed companies’ products.
  - Special focus on vulnerable customers (youth, elderly, financially fragile, disabled, low financial literacy).
  - Universal exposure to privacy risks due to sensitive data (banking secrecy, GDPR).

- Material impacts:
  - Negative (one-off):
    - Service activities: data leaks/cybersecurity incidents affecting sensitive personal data.
    - Financed activities: potential harm to consumer health/safety from financed operators; complex global value chains make detailed monitoring difficult; responsible investment strategies mitigate.
  - Positive:
    - Improved customer service, accessibility of bancassurance, and protection of customers’ financial security.
    - Strong emphasis on inclusion and support for vulnerable customers; regional development via public financial division partnership and local public player focus.

- Risks (consumers/end-users):
  - Abusive commercial/marketing practices (compliance and reputational risks).
  - Financial loss from inadequate customer protection practices.
  - Financial loss from insufficient partner assessment amid social inclusion transition.
  - Customer service failures.
  - No material opportunities identified in this scope; risks can affect all customers, not only vulnerable groups.

- Governance and stakeholder engagement:
  - Supervisory Board oversight of vulnerable customer issues.
  - Ongoing dialogue via the “Club de l’Initiative contre l’Exclusion Bancaire” to address banking exclusion.
  - In 2024, La Banque Postale is the only bank in France entrusted with a banking accessibility public service mission.

- Policies and ethics:
  - As a mission-led company (since 2022), LBP pursues social and environmental goals for a fair, accessible transition.
  - Group entities (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, Louvre Banque Privée, Retail Banking, LBP Consumer Finance) implement policies to maximize positive customer impact and reduce data security/confidentiality risks.
  - Ethical code of conduct (updated 2024) centers customer interests, fairness, transparency, accountability, regulatory compliance, and avoidance of conflicts of interest; available internally and publicly.
  - CNP Assurances’ code reinforces customer protection and ethical business practices.

nodes.title: Applicable policies
nodes.heading: 2.3.4.2.1 Applicable policies
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale, a major international financial player and a mission-led company since 2022, places its customers at the heart of its model.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document covering CSR social information on consumers and end-users, including material impacts, risks, opportunities, policies, human rights, and stakeholder dialogue.
- Material impacts:
  - Service activities: key negative impact risk is data breaches/cybersecurity incidents due to sensitive personal data handling.
  - Financed activities: potential negative impact from financing activities that undermine consumer health/safety across complex global value chains.
  - Positive impacts: enhanced customer service, accessibility of bancassurance, protection of customers’ financial security, inclusive/sustainable products, support for vulnerable customers, and regional development via Caisse des Dépôts affiliation.
- Key risks identified for banking services: abusive sales/marketing practices; financial loss from weak or unmet customer protection; partner assessment failures amid social inclusion transition; customer service failures. No material opportunities identified.
- Focus on vulnerable customers: topic overseen by the Supervisory Board; engagement through the “Club de l’Initiative contre l’Exclusion Bancaire”; La Banque Postale acts as France’s public service operator for banking accessibility in 2024.
- Customer-centric policies and governance: mission-led company since 2022; updated 2024 Ethical code of conduct (fairness, transparency, avoidance of conflicts of interest); customer protection embedded across entities (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, Louvre Banque Privée, Retail Banking, LBP Consumer Finance).
- Inclusion and accessibility measures:
  - Banking: “Simplicité” account package, “Atout Simplicité” program, universality of Livret A, transparent pricing, financial education tools.
  - Consumer finance: LBP CF policy (Dec 2024) to detect/support vulnerable customers, prevent over-indebtedness, and adapt offers.
  - Insurance: CNP Assurances commits to accessible, tailored protection solutions.
- Data protection and cybersecurity: Group IT Systems Security policy and ISS framework (annual updates; Group Risk Management Committee oversight); GDPR compliance, professional secrecy, CNIL notification protocols; Privacy by Design at CNP Assurances; internal codes and regular audits at Louvre Banque Privée.
- Responsible investment and exclusions:
  - LBP AM SRI Charter excludes financing with significant negative consumer health/safety impacts; ESG due diligence to prevent controversies and promote responsible consumption.
  - Louvre Banque Privée exclusion policy on hazardous chemicals (pesticides), pornography, controversial weapons, gambling, and tobacco.
  - Risks integrated into the Group risk matrix with reduction action plans; compliance ensured via internal procedures.
- Human rights commitments: alignment with UN Global Compact, UN Guiding Principles, ILO Conventions, and OECD Guidelines; pre-investment checks for ESG/human rights controversies; LBP AM human rights policy and engagement-based remedy approach; signatory to seven international agreements.
- Stakeholder dialogue and feedback mechanisms:
  - Retail banking: Customer Council (16 members) meets three times per year; local roundtables in specialised areas (e.g., real estate loans, protected adults, savings).
  - “Voice of the Customer” program: benchmark surveys (BVA Insight), post-contact and journey-specific surveys; results shared via dashboards to inform corrective actions and “irritant” resolution.
  - Corporate and local development banking: no current satisfaction survey; projects underway to measure satisfaction and centralize complaints.
  - CNP Assurances: periodic customer dashboards to the Executive Committee; service quality and perceived quality tracked via indicators including NPS and CES.
- Overall: The Group emphasizes proactive risk management, inclusive access to financial and insurance services, rigorous data protection, responsible investment screens, and structured customer dialogue to enhance experience and mitigate impacts.

nodes.title: Respect for Human Rights
nodes.heading: 2.3.4.2.2 Respect for Human Rights
nodes.start_phrase: As a subsidiary of La Poste Group, a signatory to the UN Global Compact since 2006, La Banque Postale upholds the principles set forth by the Global Compact on Human Rights, labour standards, environmental protection and the fight against corruption.
nodes.summary:
- Human rights commitment: As part of La Poste Group and a UN Global Compact signatory, La Banque Postale aligns with UN Guiding Principles, ILO Conventions, and OECD Guidelines, complying with legal and international standards.
- Responsible financing and investment: The bank’s charter screens investments/financing for ESG controversies, prioritizing avoidance of human rights violations; LBP AM maintains a specific Human Rights policy.
- Remedy and engagement: LBP AM uses its influence to enable or support remedies when investee companies cause or contribute to material human rights impacts, in line with its Human Rights and Engagement policies.
- International standards: La Banque Postale is a signatory to seven international agreements reinforcing its social and environmental responsibility positioning.
- Customer and end-user dialogue: Daily interactions occur via branch networks, complaints, and surveys; for end-users of invested companies (LBP AM), engagement is indirect through legitimate representatives.
- Customer Council and round tables: A 16-member Customer Council meets three times a year to advise on offers, service quality, and experience; specialized round tables at CREC (e.g., real estate loans, protected adults, savings) gather feedback and escalate out-of-scope issues nationally.
- Voice of the Customer program: Ongoing BVA Insight benchmarking vs. competitors, plus post-contact and journey-specific satisfaction surveys (e.g., account opening, home loans, insurance). Results feed management dashboards and drive corrective actions, including a structured program to identify and resolve recurring “irritants.”
- Business customer feedback: No current satisfaction survey for Corporate and Local Development Banking; projects are underway to establish measurement and monitoring, including a procedure to centralize business customer complaints.
- CNP Assurances dialogue: Integrates customer perspectives via a dashboard to the Executive Committee tracking service quality (phone accessibility, complaint and decision times) and perceived quality (NPS, CES).

nodes.title: Dialogue mechanisms with customers and end-users
nodes.heading: 2.3.4.3 Dialogue mechanisms with customers and end-users
nodes.start_phrase: On a day-to-day basis, interactions with customers take place directly within the network, either through complaints channels or through surveys.
nodes.summary:
- Human rights commitments: La Banque Postale adheres to the UN Global Compact, UN Guiding Principles, ILO Conventions, and OECD Guidelines, and complies with relevant laws and international agreements. Its Responsible Financing and Investment Charter screens investments for ESG controversies, especially human rights. LBP AM uses its influence to support remedies for actual or potential human rights impacts per its Human Rights and Engagement policies. The bank is a signatory to seven international agreements reinforcing its social and environmental responsibility.

- Customer and end‑user dialogue: 
  - Retail Banking: A 16‑member Customer Council meets three times a year; regular round tables at Customer Relations and Expertise Centres address specialized topics. Extensive “Voice of the Customer” research (benchmarking, post‑contact, and journey‑specific surveys) informs corrective actions, dashboards, and governance. A program targets and tracks resolution of recurring “irritants.”
  - Corporate and Local Development Banking: No current satisfaction survey; projects are underway to measure and monitor satisfaction and to formalize centralized handling of business customer complaints.
  - CNP Assurances: Uses a customer dashboard for Executive Committee oversight; tracks service quality and perceived quality via NPS, CES, and CSAT; runs email surveys and twice‑yearly overall satisfaction checks; operates the “You & Us” online community for co‑creation and insights; follows up with dissatisfied respondents; does not use intermediaries.
  - LBP AM: Cannot engage directly with end‑consumers but incorporates stakeholder and end‑user perspectives into its Human Rights policy and company engagement; participates in initiatives such as Ranking Digital Rights, the Coalition for Ethical AI, and the Access to Medicine Foundation to inform engagement.
  - Louvre Banque Privée: Uses an annual satisfaction barometer; no specific measures for particularly vulnerable consumers due to its wealth‑management focus.

- Support for customers facing financial difficulties: Engagement with stakeholders through an Initiative Against Banking Exclusion think‑tank. Spot NPS measures satisfaction of customers supported by the L’Appui banking and budget platform. A QR‑code pilot collects feedback from cash‑counter users, with nationwide rollout targeted for September 2025. LBP Consumer Finance proactively contacts “vulnerable” customers and a dedicated Support division offers tailored solutions and referrals (e.g., CRESUS, Banque de France, social services).

- Reporting and remediation: 
  - LBP Consumer Finance’s Customer Relations Centre manages complaints and escalates to a Complaints Department, with regular reporting to the Quality Committee and root‑cause analysis.
  - Retail Banking has a dedicated complaints department focused on continuous improvement and processing times. Multiple channels are available (call centers, online banking, social media, in‑branch and remote advisory, Business Centres). The Supervisory Board and Risk Committee conduct annual regulatory monitoring of complaints.

nodes.title: Reporting and remediation process
nodes.heading: 2.3.4.4 Reporting and remediation process
nodes.start_phrase: In the event of a negative impact, La Banque Postale has several departments tasked with providing solutions to customers.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on customer satisfaction measurement across Group entities:
  - CNP Assurances uses email surveys (since 2015), twice‑yearly overall satisfaction checks (since 2022), NPS and CSAT tracking, follow‑ups to dissatisfied respondents, and the “You & Us” online community for co‑creation, forums, workshops, and surveys.
  - Louvre Banque Privée runs an annual satisfaction barometer (quantitative/qualitative by year).
  - La Banque Postale runs spot NPS for customers supported by the L’Appui banking/budget platform; pilots QR‑code surveys for cash counter users (nationwide rollout targeted for Sept 2025).

- Stakeholder dialogue and integration of end‑user perspectives:
  - LBP AM embeds stakeholder and end‑user views in its Human Rights policy and corporate engagement; consults external stakeholders; participates in sector initiatives (Ranking Digital Rights, Coalition for Ethical AI, Access to Medicine Foundation).
  - Louvre Banque Privée has fewer vulnerable consumer profiles given its wealth‑management focus and no specific measures for such groups.

- Support for vulnerable customers and those facing financial difficulties:
  - La Banque Postale set up an “Initiative Against Banking Exclusion” think‑tank.
  - LBP Consumer Finance proactively contacts customers flagged as vulnerable and operates a dedicated Support division to assess situations and propose tailored solutions or referrals (e.g., CRESUS, Banque de France, social services).

- Complaints and remediation mechanisms:
  - LBP Consumer Finance: Customer Relations Centre triages and forwards to a Complaints Department; regular reporting and root‑cause analysis.
  - Retail Banking: dedicated complaints department; multiple access channels (call centres, online, social media, face‑to‑face and remote advisory); supervisory oversight by the Supervisory Board and Risk Committee.
  - Insurance (CNP Assurances): leverages Brazilian consumer/government platforms (Reclame Aqui, Procon, consumidor.gov); enhanced service (incl. WhatsApp); RA1000 certification and award nomination.
  - LBP AM: published Complaints Management policy with multiple channels.

- Communication and accessibility of channels:
  - Extensive physical network (17,000+ retail outlets, including 7,000 post offices; 43 corporate/local development business centres).
  - Complaints can be filed via Customer Service or a dedicated online form.

- Request management and continuous improvement:
  - Daily triage of emails/letters; SLA checkpoints (10, 35, 60 days).
  - “Footprint Labs” to review response quality; root‑cause analysis of major complaints; PEPS continuous improvement deployed across Customer Relations and Expertise Centres.
  - Dedicated team analyzes customer journeys; monitoring of service quality (phone accessibility, post‑contact NPS).
  - Corporate and Local Development Banking customers briefed on complaint processes.

- Whistleblowing:
  - Group‑wide whistleblowing system open to consumers and end‑users, in line with duty‑of‑vigilance requirements.

- Cybersecurity governance and incident management:
  - Defined process for security event/incident management with anticipation (threat monitoring) and reaction (incident response) pillars; crisis management procedures for critical ISS/cyber cases; post‑incident reviews and action plans.

- Action plans addressing privacy and cybersecurity risks:
  - 2021–2027 cybersecurity strategic plan (50 key projects): continuous monitoring/detection (SOC) and deployment of safeguards to protect data.
  - Crisis unit for incident handling (including potential system lockdowns), eradication, and regulatory notifications as required.
  - Ongoing employee training and anti‑fraud awareness.

- Personal data protection and GDPR compliance:
  - Privacy by Design integrated into product/service development; tools (customer dictionary, marketing plan) to personalize communications and avoid mass campaigns; staff GDPR training.
  - Subsidiaries:
    - CNP Assurances: Privacy by Design with upfront privacy risk analyses and technical/organizational safeguards.
    - Louvre Banque Privée: data confidentiality policies, consent management, limited retention, and regular audits.

- Governance and assurance:
  - Annual updates to security policies validated by the Group Risk Management Committee; General ISS policy and topical policies; regular internal audits of controls’ effectiveness.

- Monitoring of effectiveness and resources:
  - Use of indicators (including for vulnerable populations) to track outcomes.
  - Monthly committee monitoring Online Banking and Mobile App incidents to prioritize fixes and drive continuous customer‑experience improvements.

nodes.title: Actions taken to address negative impacts
nodes.heading: 2.3.4.5.1 Actions taken to address negative impacts
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale and its subsidiaries, including CNP Assurances and Louvre Banque Privée, have implemented action plans to manage risks related to privacy and cybersecurity, which are recognised as potential material negative impacts.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: CSR/Social information focusing on action plans, resources, and outcomes related to privacy, cybersecurity, customer accessibility, and inclusion across La Banque Postale Group and subsidiaries (CNP Assurances, Louvre Banque Privée).

- Managing negative impacts (privacy and cybersecurity):
  - Cybersecurity strategic plan 2021–2027 with 50 key projects:
    - Threat identification via a 24/7 monitoring and detection center.
    - Deployment of safeguards to protect customer information and personal data.
  - Incident management:
    - Dedicated crisis unit, potential partial/total IS lockdown, eradication actions, post-incident analysis, regulatory notifications as needed.
  - Training and awareness:
    - Anti-fraud team with preventive measures and regular staff training to identify risky behaviors.
  - Data protection and GDPR:
    - Privacy by Design embedded in products/services.
    - Tools (customer dictionary, marketing plan) to personalize communications and avoid mass campaigns.
    - Employee training on GDPR.
  - Subsidiaries:
    - CNP Assurances: Privacy by Design, privacy risk analyses at project launch, technical/organizational safeguards.
    - Louvre Banque Privée: confidentiality policies, consent management, limited retention, regular audits overseen by Legal and Compliance.
  - Governance and audits:
    - Annual updates to security policies validated by the Group Risk Management Committee (General ISS policy, topical policies).
    - Regular internal audits of compliance and effectiveness.

- Monitoring effectiveness and resources:
  - Use of indicators to assess impacts on consumers, including vulnerable populations (referenced in Section 2.2.1.11.1).
  - Monthly committee overseeing incidents on Online Banking and Mobile App, prioritizing fixes and continuous customer experience improvement.

- Generating positive impacts (accessibility, protection, financial security):
  - Commitment to quality service, universal access to bancassurance, and customer protection.
  - Accessible banking mission:
    - State-entrusted mission ensuring universal, non-discriminatory access to essential banking.
    - Livret A as a universal, free product; withdrawals/deposits from €1.50; authorized transfers for benefits and essential bills; additional free services.
    - 1.2 million customers excluded from traditional banking served.
  - Access to products and services:
    - Simplified contractual documents for better understanding.
    - Banking/insurance products:
      - Simplicité low-cost account for 1.7 million customers in difficulty, with capped annual fees (€1,500).
      - CNP Assurances: 14 inclusive insurance products (2024), 828,000 policyholders; affordable funeral cover (up to €2,500); microinsurance in Latin America for low-income families; Italian offers enabling credit to low-income retirees with repayments capped at 20% of pension.
      - Clear language governance for customer documents (since 2024); 24% of management letters revised in 2024.
      - Broad distribution via post offices (France) and lottery points (Brazil) for reach into remote areas.
    - Credit solutions:
      - Youth-focused loans (e.g., one-euro-a-day driving licence loan; Student and Apprentice Loans).
      - Personal microloans via associations (CCAS, Restos du Cœur) for social reintegration projects.
      - Professional microloans for small businesses and micro-entrepreneurs to combat exclusion and support activity.
      - Temporary personal loan for temp workers.
      - Three-instalment financing via Django app using open banking analytics.
      - Home loans including no down-payment options and social home loans for low-income households.
  - Protection of vulnerable customers:
    - Dedicated systems and services to safeguard and support vulnerable clients.

nodes.title: Actions implemented to generate positive impacts
nodes.heading: 2.3.4.5.2 Actions implemented to generate positive impacts
nodes.start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group is committed to generating positive impacts for its customers by placing their needs at the heart of its priorities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of the section: actions implemented to generate positive impacts for customers as part of La Banque Postale Group’s CSR/social commitments—quality service, universal accessibility to banking/insurance, and customer protection/financial security.
- Universal banking accessibility mission: as State-appointed custodian, guarantees non-discriminatory access to essential services centered on the Livret A (universal eligibility, €1.50 cash transactions in post offices, payment of essential bills and welfare transfers, free associated services). Serves about 1.2 million people excluded from traditional banking.
- Accessible products and clearer information: simplification of contractual documents to improve customer understanding.
- Inclusive banking and insurance:
  - Simplicité low-cost account option for 1.7 million customers in financial difficulty, including an annual fee cap of €1,500 on incident-related charges.
  - CNP Assurances: 14 inclusive insurance products covering 828,000 policyholders by end-2024; affordable funeral cover with ATD Fourth World (up to €2,500); microinsurance in Latin America (illness, death, property damage) and solutions in Italy enabling low-income retirees to access consumer credit.
  - Plain-language governance at CNP since 2024; 24% of management letters revised; multichannel distribution via post offices and lottery points in France and Brazil to reach remote areas.
- Credit inclusion:
  - Youth-focused loans (e.g., “€1/day” driving licence, student/apprentice loans).
  - Personal microloans via partners (CCAS, Restos du Cœur) for social reintegration.
  - Professional microloans for very small businesses/micro‑entrepreneurs to tackle unemployment and exclusion.
  - Temporary workers’ personal loan; Django three-instalment solution using open banking analytics.
  - Home loans without personal contribution and social home loans to widen access to home ownership.
- Protection of vulnerable customers:
  - L’Appui free banking/budget support (330,000+ people helped since 2013).
  - Educational tools (BGV, Dilemma) and staff training to detect/respond to vulnerability.
  - Pooled long‑term care contracts by CNP (no medical screening; population-based pricing; €100–€500 monthly payments) for broad accessibility.

- Regional proximity: 7,000+ retail outlets ensure geographic accessibility, including rural and priority neighborhoods; CNP distributes via post offices/lottery points in France and the Correios postal network in Brazil.
- Structured assistance for customers in financial difficulty: early detection (including 400 specially trained online advisors), right‑to‑an‑account services, fee reductions, microloans, solidarity offers, over‑indebtedness support, personalized guidance and referrals to relevant organizations.
- Enabling a just transition:
  - Systematic ESG integration through a mandatory product design checklist (updated 2021) covering customer experience and civic ambition for the just transition; products scoring >50/100 labeled “community-friendly.”
  - 2024 results: 30% of reviewed offers labeled (20% Retail Banking, 25% CLDB, 100% Transaction Banking); target 80% sustainable products by 2025; monitoring via annual citizen‑certified offers, independently assured.
  - Impact products: Créa‑Sol financing for social entrepreneurs; Green Vehicle/Green Works loans; Avance Rénovation (PAR); impact real estate loan; impact bank card that channels spending to energy renovation and biodiversity preservation.
- Governance and outcomes: no severe human rights incidents involving consumers/end‑users in 2024; consumer/end‑user targets managed via mission‑led indicators (e.g., NPS for financially vulnerable customers, access metrics) and CNP’s purpose metrics (e.g., number of inclusive products), plus customer satisfaction indicators like CES.

nodes.title: Targets
nodes.heading: 2.3.4.6.1 Targets
nodes.start_phrase: The Group’s targets related to consumers and end-users are managed through La Banque Postale’s mission-led company indicators (for example, the NPS of customers experiencing financial difficulties) and CNP Assurances’ company purpose (for example, the number of products improving access to insurance for vulnerable groups).
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Social information) outlining how the Group advances accessibility, customer protection, and the just transition through ESG-integrated products and impact finance.

- Geographic and social accessibility:
  - Over 7,000 retail outlets ensure nationwide access, including rural areas and priority neighborhoods.
  - CNP Assurances broadens access for vulnerable populations: distribution via post offices and lottery points in France; life and health microinsurance via Brazil’s Correios network in Latin America.

- Enabling customer participation in the just transition:
  - Development and promotion of products incorporating ESG or positive-impact criteria.

- ESG assessment of offers (ESG checklist):
  - Checklist launched in 2008, revised in 2021; mandatory in Product Review Committees; co-developed with Utopies and WWF France.
  - Two pillars: customer experience/satisfaction (clarity, satisfaction, traceability, journey) and civic ambition for the just transition (reduce inequalities, build virtuous ecosystems, foster citizenship/responsibility).
  - Scoring out of 100; >50 points earns “community-friendly” label.
  - 2024 labeling outcomes: 30% of examined offers labeled (20% Retail Banking, 25% CLDB, 100% Transaction Banking); target is 80% sustainable products by 2025.
  - Applied during impact card design to enhance environmental performance.
  - Annual indicator of new “citizen-certified” offers published in the mission-led company report and third-party assured.

- Impact product suite:
  - Small professionals: Créa-Sol program for social entrepreneurs and local sustainable projects.
  - Retail customers: Green Vehicle and Green Works loans; Avance Rénovation (PAR) for energy efficiency; impact real estate loan tied to stringent environmental criteria.
  - Impact banking: impact card contributing to energy renovation (including thermal strainer remediation) and biodiversity preservation.

- Customer protection and incidents:
  - No severe human rights incidents involving consumers/end-users reported in 2024.

- Targets and performance management:
  - Group targets anchored in La Banque Postale’s mission-led indicators (e.g., NPS for financially vulnerable customers) and CNP Assurances’ company purpose (e.g., number of products improving access for vulnerable groups).
  - Use of performance insights to adjust commercial targets and advisor guidance for community-based financing.
  - Customer metrics used by CNP: CES (effort), NPS (recommendation/loyalty), CSAT (satisfaction).

- Negative impact monitoring:
  - Trialing indicators for potential negative impacts (e.g., cybersecurity, information/security of consumers), not disclosed for confidentiality.

- Stakeholder involvement:
  - Indirect involvement of consumers/end-users via mission-led status and public-service role, with the State guiding activities in the general interest.

- Alignment with international standards:
  - Integration of UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, ILO standards, and UN SDGs.

- Additional indicators and recent results:
  - Proportion of new offers identified as sustainable via the ESG checklist declined from 39% (2023) to 30% (2024); target 80%.
  - Banking and insurance inclusion metrics (2023 → 2024 → 2025 target):
    - Sustainable new offers (ESG checklist): 39% → 30% → 80%.
    - Change in NPS among financially vulnerable customers: 3 → 9 → (target not specified here).
    - CNP products/partnerships improving access for vulnerable populations: 9 → 14 → 15.

structure.summary:
- Accessibility of services
  - Commitment to physically accessible banking via post offices and ATMs.
  - 98% of ATMs accessible to people with reduced mobility; 100% accessible to the blind/visually impaired.
  - Customer assistance in French Sign Language via Deafi, with 6,044 deaf/hearing‑impaired customers assisted in 2024.

- Ethical and responsible business conduct
  - Corporate culture anchored in accessibility, fairness, proximity, and service; mission-led company status since 2022.
  - Group-wide Code of Conduct, periodic reviews, Confirmodoc acknowledgement tool; CNP Assurances maintains its own code and secure whistleblowing channel.
  - No political financial or in-kind contributions in 2024; lobbying overseen by Chief Risk & Compliance Officer and General Secretariat.
  - Key advocacy topics in 2024: Basel 3 (CRR3/CRD6), CMDI, Retail Investment Strategy, FiDA, digital euro/legal tender, PSD3/PSR, AI Act, SFDR review, CS3D, Solvency II review; national focus on inheritance banking fees.
  - Compliance with transparency rules: registrations in EU Transparency Register and France’s HATVP.
  - Public administration involvement: APE representative on Supervisory Board; Government Commissioner attends boards/committees in advisory capacity.
  - Participation in industry bodies (FBF, AMAFI, ASF, AFG, France Assureurs).

- Anti-corruption governance and performance
  - Governance bodies (Supervisory Board, Risk Committee, Executive Board) oversee the anti-corruption framework, risk mapping, controls, and reporting.
  - Policies aligned with Sapin II and UN Global Compact; zero-tolerance stance, internal whistleblowing accessible to all employees and third parties.
  - Annual corruption risk mapping; accounting controls; tailored training across entities and geographies.
  - 2024 results: zero convictions and zero fines for corruption/bribery.
  - Ongoing enhancements: strengthened controls, procedures on whistleblowing and conflicts of interest, third‑party assessments, accounting controls; sponsorship policy formalization and beneficiary assessment tool rollout.

- Whistleblowing system
  - Group platform (third-party hosted) accessible to employees and external stakeholders; Ethics Officer oversight; independence of investigations with a three‑level validation process.
  - CNP Integrity Line available 24/7 with response within three months post-acknowledgment (extendable for complex cases).
  - Strong protections for whistleblowers (confidentiality, anti-retaliation) under Sapin II and EU Directive 2019/1937; unitary control of alerts reported to governance from 2024.

- Employee awareness and training
  - Induction and recurring training on ethics, AML/CFT, conflicts of interest, data confidentiality, and systems use.
  - New 2024 training module on ethics, anti-corruption, and influence peddling; widespread deployment across employees and those acting on behalf of the bank.
  - High completion rates: 99% completion of ethics/anti-corruption e‑learning among target population by end‑2024; 98.7% AML/CFT training (LBP SA scope); 99% of roles classified as “at‑risk” (LBP SA scope) covered.
  - Entity-specific programs (CNP, LBP AM, La Financière de l’Échiquier) and ESG/culture training for Supervisory Board members.

- Supplier relations and responsible purchasing
  - Supplier dependency management with a 25% alert threshold; monitoring, diversification support, and orderly exit planning.
  - Commitment to timely supplier payments: RFAR charter signatory; Group responsible purchasing policy; risk mapping and action plan oversight.
  - Monthly dashboards since 2021; SME officer and SME-specific tracking added in 2025; internal Supplier Relations Mediator (no 2024 referrals).
  - 2024 payment metrics: average payment term 51.6 days; invoices paid on time—SMEs 81.2%, ISEs 84%, large corporates 80.5%, unspecified 69.8%; no legal proceedings for late payments.
  - Integration of ESG criteria in procurement: EcoVadis assessments at CNP; AFNOR sectoral CSR criteria (typically ~10% weighting); ISO 20400-aligned approach; equal treatment and transparent selection; contract clauses on ethics, ESG compliance, audit rights, and termination for non‑compliance.

- EU Green Taxonomy (GAR) disclosure
  - Presentation of assets included in the Green Asset Ratio calculation across loans, debt securities, and equity instruments for financials, non-financials, households, and local governments.
  - Breakdown by environmental objectives (climate change mitigation/adaptation, water & marine resources) and instrument types (including use‑of‑proceeds, enabling, transitional).
  - Highlights of household exposures (notably residential real estate and renovation loans) and taxonomy‑eligible/aligned portions across portfolios.

It also specifies included accounting categories (amortised cost, FVOCI, FVTPL designated/mandatorily, investments in subsidiaries/joint ventures/associates) and real estate collateral obtained through possession.
- GAR coverage: Assets included in both numerator and denominator total €148,050m.
- Breakdown by counterparty/product (gross carrying amounts; highlights):
  - Financial undertakings: €24,301m, including credit institutions (€14,795m), other financial corporations (€9,506m), and insurance undertakings (€8,494m, largely equity). Limited taxonomy‑aligned shares; minor Use‑of‑Proceeds/enabling amounts.
  - Non‑financial undertakings: €30,115m, with taxonomy‑eligible €9,551m and smaller taxonomy‑aligned portions across CCM/CCA/WMR; limited enabling/UoP.
  - Households: €83,631m, taxonomy‑eligible €78,355m; significant CCM‑aligned component (€8,907m) largely from:

    - Building renovation loans: €3,215m (CCM‑aligned €4m)
    - Motor vehicle loans: €4,510m (CCM‑aligned €4m)
  - Local governments financing: €10,003m.
- Methodological notes: Alignment is reported primarily by targeted environmental objective; the template isolates taxonomy‑eligible vs taxonomy‑aligned exposures and identifies Use‑of‑Proceeds, transitional, and enabling categories, which are generally small in this extract. A glossary of CSR terms is referenced for definitions.

nodes.title: Tables on the European Green Taxonomy

- Purpose: Details the assets included in both the numerator and denominator of the GAR, showing taxonomy eligibility and alignment by environmental objective and by counterparty/product.
- Methodology:
  - Based on the EU Taxonomy turnover metric.
  - Alignment shown by environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), and Water & Marine Resources (WMR).
  - Breaks out “use‑of‑proceeds,” “transitional,” and “enabling” categories.
- Scope of assets:
  - Banking book exposures: loans and advances, debt securities (incl. use‑of‑proceeds financing), and equity instruments.
  - Counterparties: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, insurance undertakings), non‑financial undertakings (incl. SMEs), households (residential real estate, renovation loans, motor vehicles), and local governments/municipalities (house financing).
  - Accounting categories included: amortised cost; fair value through OCI; investments in subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates; designated and non‑trading mandatorily FVTPL; and real estate collateral obtained by taking possession.
- Headline figures (€ millions):
  - Total gross carrying amount of GAR‑covered assets: 148,050.
  - Households: 83,631 total; major share from residential mortgages (75,285 total; 75,285 taxonomy‑eligible; 8,900 taxonomy‑aligned).
  - Non‑financial undertakings: 30,115 total; 9,551 taxonomy‑eligible; 728 taxonomy‑aligned.
  - Financial undertakings: 24,301 total; 4,456 taxonomy‑eligible; 631 taxonomy‑aligned (with sub‑breakdowns for credit institutions, other financial corporations, and insurance undertakings).

  - The template clarifies inclusions/exclusions and ensures comparability of GAR inputs across product and counterparty types.

nodes.title: Assets included in the GAR calculation
nodes.heading: 2.5.1.1 Assets included in the GAR calculation
nodes.start_phrase: This table shows the information used to calculate the GAR, by type of product and counterparty.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, “Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report,” focused on European Green Taxonomy disclosures and the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).

- GAR methodology and scope:
  - Detailed templates showing assets included in the GAR numerator and denominator and those excluded from the numerator but in the denominator.
  - Coverage spans loans and advances, debt securities, equity instruments (banking book), and specific household products (mortgages, renovation, motor vehicle loans) plus local governments.
  - Environmental objectives reported: climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), water and marine resources (WMR), circular economy (CE), pollution prevention and control (PRP), and biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO), with sub‑categories for use‑of‑proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Accounting categories: amortised cost, FVOCI, FVPL (designated/mandatory), investments in subsidiaries/JVs/associates, and repossessed real estate.

- Two calculation bases and timeframes:
  - GAR disclosures presented “Based on turnover” and “Based on CapEx.”
  - Comparative data for the reporting date (T) and prior period (T‑1).

- Key quantitative structure (illustrative figures for T):
  - Total assets: ~€321.3bn; total GAR assets: ~€180.1bn; GAR‑covered assets (numerator/denominator): ~€148.1bn.
  - By counterparty within GAR‑covered assets: financial undertakings (~€24.3bn), non‑financial undertakings (~€30.1bn), households (~€83.6bn; taxonomy‑relevant ~€78.4bn, largely mortgages).
  - Assets excluded from numerator but in denominator include SMEs and non‑NFRD entities, non‑EU counterparties, derivatives, interbank on‑demand, cash, and other assets.
  - Assets not covered for GAR: central governments/supranationals, central bank exposures, and trading book.

- Off‑balance sheet disclosures:
  - Financial guarantees and assets under management (AUM) with taxonomy‑eligible and aligned breakdowns across the six objectives, including separate views for debt securities and equities; shown for T and T‑1.

- Sector (GAR) information:
  - Banking book exposures mapped to 4‑digit NACE sectors, indicating gross and “environmentally sustainable” amounts (primarily for CCM) for NFRD‑subject corporates and SMEs/others.
  - Examples include electricity (D35), construction (F41–F43), vehicle manufacturing (C29), waste (E38), and selected manufacturing and trade sectors; sectors lacking sufficient granularity are grouped on a final row.

- Methodological notes and caveats:
  - Institutions with non‑EU subsidiaries must provide best‑effort separate GARs for non‑EU exposures using estimates/proxies and explain assumptions/limitations.
  - Motor vehicle loans are included only if originated after the disclosure’s application date.

- High‑level takeaways:
  - Taxonomy‑relevant exposure is dominated by retail mortgages; reported taxonomy‑aligned volumes concentrate in climate objectives, with comparatively limited amounts for water, circular economy, pollution, and biodiversity.
  - Use‑of‑proceeds green instruments are identified separately.

nodes.title: GAR sector information
nodes.heading: 2.5.1.2 GAR sector information
nodes.start_phrase: This table shows banking book exposures to sectors covered by the European Green Taxonomy, with the counterparty’s economic activity or the activity concerned by the project financed by the Bank identified by the relevant NACE code.
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt is from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report) and presents EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures.

- It provides detailed GAR sector information for the banking book at NACE 4‑digit level, shown:
  - Based on turnover and, separately, based on CapEx.
  - Split between non‑financial corporates subject to the NFRD and SMEs/other non‑financial corporates not subject to the NFRD.
  - By environmental objectives: climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), water and marine resources (WMR), circular economy (CE), pollution prevention and control (PRP), and biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO).
  - For each sector: gross carrying amounts in € millions and the share “of which environmentally sustainable (CCM).”

- The sectoral breakdown highlights significant exposures (and, where available, CCM‑sustainable portions) across:
  - Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning (D35.*) with notable CCM‑sustainable amounts.
  - Real estate activities (L68.*), including large volumes in L68.2.0.
  - Construction (F41–F43), transport and storage (H49–H53), air transport (H51), wholesale trade (G46), retail trade (G47), information and communications (J61), and professional/technical services (M70–M71).
  - Waste collection, treatment and disposal (E38.*).
  - An “Other” row aggregates exposures where the required NACE granularity is not available.

- Methodology notes clarify:
  - Counterparty assignment is based solely on the immediate counterparty’s principal activity (relevant NACE code).
  - For exposures incurred jointly by multiple obligors, classification reflects the obligor most relevant/determinant for granting the exposure.
  - Information is disclosed at the required level of disaggregation; where granularity is unavailable, amounts appear in the final “Other” line.

- The CapEx‑based view generally mirrors the turnover‑based view but shows different “of which environmentally sustainable (CCM)” amounts for several sectors, notably:
  - Higher CCM‑sustainable amounts in electricity (D35.*), real estate (L68.2.0), and waste activities (E38.3.2).

- GAR Technical Reserves KPI (based on turnover) summarizes the ratio of Taxonomy‑aligned assets to covered assets, with breakdowns by counterparty/instrument:
  - Shows the proportion of total covered assets that fund Taxonomy‑relevant sectors (eligible) and those that are Taxonomy‑aligned, across CCM, CCA, and WMR.
  - Indicates components “of which” use‑of‑proceeds, transitional, and enabling (largely negligible in the presented data).
  - Illustrates contributions from financial undertakings (including credit institutions and insurance), non‑financial undertakings, households, and local governments.
  - Notable household details: loans collateralised by residential property are fully covered (100%), with an indicated c. 11.8% CCM share; building renovation and motor vehicle loans show small CCM shares (~0.1%).

- Overall, most reported sustainability alignment appears under climate change mitigation (CCM), with limited amounts disclosed for other environmental objectives in the presented tables.

- A glossary on page 808 is referenced for definitions of key CSR terms.

nodes.title: GAR Technical Reserves
nodes.heading: 2.5.1.3 GAR Technical Reserves
nodes.start_phrase: Based on the information presented in Section 2.5.1.1, the B ank indicates in these tables the ratio of Taxonomy-aligned assets to covered assets.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report), detailing EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures.
- Scope covered:
  - 2.5.1.3 GAR Technical Reserves: KPIs based on turnover and on CapEx, for the current year (T) and prior year (T‑1).
  - 2.5.1.4 GAR Flow: turnover‑based KPIs on flows of eligible assets during the period.
  - References to the CSR glossary and methodological notes (templates, coverage, replication for turnover and CapEx).

- What is disclosed and how:
  - Proportions of covered assets that are Taxonomy‑eligible and Taxonomy‑aligned across environmental objectives: climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), water and marine resources (WMR), circular economy (CE), pollution prevention and control (PRP), and biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO).
  - Breakdowns by portfolio segment and instrument: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, insurance undertakings), non‑financial undertakings, households, local governments; loans and advances, debt securities including Use‑of‑Proceeds (UoP/green bonds), equity; with retail detail for mortgages, renovation loans, and motor vehicle loans.
  - “Of which” flags for Use‑of‑Proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Proportion of total assets covered by the GAR.

- Headline results (Technical Reserves):
  - Based on turnover:
    - T: total eligible GAR assets 51.4% of covered assets; Taxonomy‑aligned 5.7% in total, largely CCM (about 5.0%), with marginal CCA and WMR (~0.1% each).
    - T‑1: total eligible 54.7%; aligned 5.5% (mostly CCM ~5.2%; negligible for other objectives).
  - Based on CapEx:
    - T: total eligible 51.7%; aligned 6.0% (primarily CCM ~5.0%; small CCA and WMR ~0.1% each).
    - T‑1: total eligible 53.7%; aligned 5.7%.
  - Observations: eligibility is concentrated in households (notably residential mortgages) and non‑financial undertakings; equity exposures are negligible; enabling and transitional shares are largely nil.

- Headline results (GAR Flow – turnover):
  - T: flows of eligible assets represent 18.5%; flows that are Taxonomy‑aligned 1.7% overall, mostly CCM with small contributions from CCA and WMR.
  - Flow breakdowns mirror stock metrics, with a notable role for UoP/green bonds in non‑financial undertakings and consistent contributions from household mortgage flows.

- Methodological notes:
  - KPIs are calculated from the covered assets template using prescribed formulas; templates are replicated for turnover and CapEx.
  - Credit institutions may additionally present the proportion of assets funding Taxonomy‑relevant sectors that are environmentally sustainable (Taxonomy‑aligned) to enrich the KPI.
  - Glossary reference provided for CSR terms.

nodes.title: GAR Flow
nodes.heading: 2.5.1.4 GAR Flow
nodes.start_phrase: •This template discloses the GAR KPIs on the technical reserves of loans, calculated based on the data disclosed in template 1 on covered assets, and by applying the formulas proposed in this template.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report) detailing EU Taxonomy disclosures and Green Asset Ratio (GAR) flow KPIs.
- Scope and methodology: Presents GAR flow metrics calculated both on a turnover basis and a CapEx basis, using prescribed templates and formulas derived from “template 1” (covered assets). Breakdowns follow EU Taxonomy environmental objectives and sub-classifications (use‑of‑proceeds, transitional, enabling). A glossary reference is provided.
- Environmental objectives covered: Climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), water and marine resources (WMR), with placeholders for circular economy (CE), pollution prevention (PRP), and biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO) largely unfilled.
- On-balance-sheet GAR Flow (turnover basis):
  - Total GAR assets: about 18.5% taxonomy‑eligible; taxonomy‑aligned shares are low (around 1.7% in aggregate across objectives).
  - By counterparty/instrument:
    - Financial undertakings/credit institutions: mid‑20% eligibility; near‑zero alignment.
    - Non‑financial undertakings: ~17.6% eligibility; alignment primarily in CCM (~3.9%); higher eligibility/alignment seen in debt securities including use‑of‑proceeds.
    - Households: mortgages 100% taxonomy‑eligible with ~5.4% aligned (CCM); overall household line shows ~92% eligibility and ~4.9% aligned; building renovation and vehicle loans show eligibility but no aligned share reported.
- On-balance-sheet GAR Flow (CapEx basis):
  - Total GAR assets: about 18.5% taxonomy‑eligible; taxonomy‑aligned modestly higher than turnover basis (~1.9%).
  - Patterns mirror turnover basis with slightly higher eligibility/alignment for some non‑financial debt securities (use‑of‑proceeds) and similar low alignment for financial counterparties; households/mortgages again 100% eligible with ~5.4% aligned (CCM).
- Off-balance-sheet exposures:
  - Templates disclose KPIs for financial guarantees (FinGuar KPI) and assets under management (AuM KPI), on both turnover and CapEx bases.
  - Turnover basis: indicative figures show FinGuar ~2.7% eligible; AuM ~13.5% eligible with ~1.4% aligned to CCM (small shares in other objectives).
  - CapEx basis: FinGuar ~5.46% eligible; AuM ~15.94% eligible with alignment primarily to CCM; alignment shares across use‑of‑proceeds/transitional/enabling are minimal or zero.
- Notes: Institutions are to replicate these templates for both turnover and CapEx; results are computed from covered‑assets data using the prescribed formulas.

nodes.title: Off-balance sheet exposures
nodes.heading: 2.5.1.5 Off-balance sheet exposures
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables show off-balance sheet exposures calculated on the basis of data published in the table on covered assets.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report) presents EU Taxonomy-related disclosures focused on off-balance sheet exposures and exposures to nuclear and fossil gas activities. It details:
- KPIs for off-balance sheet exposures—financial guarantees and assets under management—calculated from “covered assets” (Template 1), with results shown on two bases (turnover and CapEx). Metrics report the proportion of total eligible off-balance sheet assets that fund Taxonomy-relevant sectors, distinguishing Taxonomy-eligible vs. Taxonomy-aligned activities.
- Breakdowns by environmental objectives: climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), water and marine resources (WMR), circular economy (CE), pollution prevention and control (PRP), and biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO), including “of which” categories for use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities, plus aggregate totals across all objectives. The templates are intended to be replicated for technical reserves and flow KPIs.
- A qualitative disclosure (Template 1) on nuclear and fossil gas-related activities, stating the bank’s exposures arise via general purpose financing to companies in these sectors, whose main counterparties are committed to SBTi-aligned low-carbon pathways. In line with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214, it flags that quantitative Taxonomy-alignment indicators are also required. The checklist confirms exposures across nuclear R&D/innovative generation, construction and operation of new and existing nuclear installations, and fossil gas electricity and heat generation (construction, refurbishment, and operation).

nodes.title: Nuclear and fossil gas-related activities
nodes.heading: 2.5.1.6 Nuclear and fossil gas -related activities

nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines La Banque Postale’s sustainability disclosure on exposures to nuclear and fossil gas activities within its 2024 Universal Registration Document. It explains that the Bank’s exposure arises mainly through general-purpose financing to companies in these sectors, which are committed to Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) low‑carbon pathways. In line with EU Delegated Regulation 2022/1214, the Bank notes that quantitative EU Taxonomy alignment indicators will also be published in addition to this qualitative disclosure. A template table confirms the Bank “has exposures” (YES) across six activity categories: nuclear R&D and innovative generation; construction and safe operation of new nuclear installations (including for heat and hydrogen) and related safety upgrades; safe operation and upgrades of existing nuclear installations (including for heat and hydrogen); and fossil gas activities covering construction/operation of electricity generation, combined heat/cool and electricity generation, and heat/cool generation, including construction, refurbishment, and operation.

    - Nuclear: R&D/innovation in nuclear generation; construction and safe operation of new installations; safe operation and upgrades of existing installations.

- Quantitative Taxonomy alignment for GAR denominator (Template 2):

    - Section 4.28 activities: €108m (0.1%) total; €96m (0.1%) under climate change mitigation (CCM); no climate change adaptation (CCA).

    - Sections 4.26, 4.29, 4.30, 4.31: €0.
    - Other Taxonomy-aligned activities (not 4.26–4.31): €10,716m (6.0%); CCM €10,738m (6.0%); CCA €1m (0.0%).
    - Total applicable KPI denominator: €180,087m (100%).

- Key takeaway: The Bank’s EU Taxonomy-aligned exposures to nuclear and fossil gas activities constitute a very small share (~0.1%) of the GAR denominator, while “other” aligned activities represent around 5.6% (turnover basis) to 6.0% (CapEx basis).

nodes.title: Taxonomy-aligned economic activities (denominator) [Template 2]

- Context and scope: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report), presenting EU Taxonomy-aligned economic activities for the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) using Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139, Annexes I and II, Sections 4.26–4.31 (nuclear and gas). Data are shown per regulatory templates for the GAR denominator (Template 2) and numerator (Template 3), split by turnover and CapEx, and by climate objectives: climate change mitigation (CCM) and adaptation (CCA).
- Denominator (Template 2):
  - Total applicable KPI (turnover and CapEx): €180,087m (100%).
  - Nuclear/gas sections:
    - Turnover: 0 for 4.26, 4.27, 4.29, 4.30, 4.31; €108m (0.1%) in 4.28 (mainly CCM: €96m, 0.1%).
    - CapEx: 0 for 4.26, 4.29, 4.30, 4.31; €16m (0.0%) in 4.27 (CCM €14m), €97m (0.1%) in 4.28 (CCM €78m).
  - Other Taxonomy-aligned activities (outside 4.26–4.31):
    - Turnover: €10,158m (5.6%).
    - CapEx: €10,716m (6.0%).
  - Indicative aligned share of denominator: ≈€10.27bn (~5.7%) on turnover basis; ≈€10.83bn (~6.0%) on CapEx basis.
  - Climate objective split: almost entirely CCM; CCA negligible (€1m, ~0.0%).
- Numerator (Template 3):
  - Total Taxonomy-aligned activities:
    - Turnover: €10,267m (100%).
    - CapEx: €10,831m (100%).
  - Nuclear/gas sections:
    - Turnover: €108m (1.1%) in 4.28 (CCM €96m); 0 in 4.26, 4.27, 4.29, 4.30, 4.31.
    - CapEx: €16m (0.2%) in 4.27 (CCM €14m); €97m (0.9%) in 4.28 (CCM €78m); 0 in other sections.
  - Other Taxonomy-aligned activities (outside 4.26–4.31):
    - Turnover: €10,158m (98.9%).
    - CapEx: €10,716m (98.9%).
  - Climate objective split: overwhelmingly CCM; CCA is minimal (€1m, ~0.0%).
- Key takeaway: The Bank’s Taxonomy alignment is driven almost entirely by activities outside the nuclear/gas sections (4.26–4.31), with negligible exposure to those transitional activities; alignment is predominantly for climate change mitigation, with adaptation immaterial. A glossary of CSR terms is referenced on page 808.

nodes.title: Taxonomy-aligned economic activities (numerator) [Template 3]
nodes.heading: 2.5.1.6.3 Taxonomy-aligned economic activities (numerator) [Template 3]
nodes.start_phrase: This table presents the amounts and proportions of the GAR’s numerator represented by T axonomy-aligned activities referred to in Sections 4.26 to 4.31 (nuclear and gas) of Annexes I and II of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139.

- Source and scope: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report), covering EU Taxonomy disclosures for the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- What’s reported: Amounts and proportions of Taxonomy-aligned activities in the GAR numerator (Template 3) and Taxonomy-eligible but not aligned activities in the GAR denominator (Template 4), with splits by:
  - Turnover and CapEx bases
  - Climate objectives: climate change mitigation (CCM) and climate change adaptation (CCA)
  - Specific EU Taxonomy sections 4.26–4.31 (nuclear and gas) and “other” activities
- Key results – Taxonomy-aligned (numerator):
  - Based on turnover: €10,267m aligned (100% of numerator); 98.9% in “other aligned activities,” 1.1% in Section 4.28; zero in 4.26, 4.27, 4.29–4.31. Strongly mitigation-driven (€10,266m CCM; €1m CCA).

- Key results – Eligible but not aligned (denominator, turnover basis):

  - Minimal amounts in nuclear/gas-related sections: 4.28 (€2m), 4.29 (€22m), 4.30 (€2m); none in 4.26, 4.27, 4.31; negligible CCA.
- Overall takeaways: Nuclear and gas activities contribute negligibly to both aligned and eligible-not-aligned amounts; almost all aligned exposure is in other Taxonomy activities and is overwhelmingly mitigation-focused. A glossary reference for CSR terms is provided (page 808).

nodes.title: Eligible economic activities not aligned with the Taxonomy (numerator) [Template 4]

nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, Notes to the sustainability report, covering EU Taxonomy disclosures tied to the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) denominator. References Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139, Annexes I–II, Sections 4.26–4.31 (nuclear and gas). Points readers to the CSR glossary (p. 808).
- Template 4 (Taxonomy-eligible but not Taxonomy-aligned activities):

nodes.title: Taxonomy-non-eligible activities [Template 5]

nodes.summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report), covering EU Taxonomy disclosures, notably non-eligible activities and KPIs by business segment.
- Taxonomy-non-eligible activities (Template 5, GAR denominator):

  - Turnover-based denominator:
